articles.title: Tokyo can create means of delivering nuclear weapons, China says
articles.body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan has the industrial and technical potential to develop delivery systems for nuclear weapons, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
According to him, Japan has been actively expanding its military capabilities in recent years by acquiring advanced US weapons. Besides, it has its own technologies that can be used for military purposes, Dai Huaicheng said.
"Japan has long held a leading position in the world in the field of large launch vehicles, has mastered the key technologies necessary for the development of medium-and long-range ballistic missiles, such as guidance and reentry systems, and also has the technical base for the development of ships with a nuclear power plant," he said.
"This means that if it makes the relevant political decision, Japan will face no insurmountable industrial and technical obstacles either in the field of nuclear warheads or in their delivery systems.
"Japan is the only non-nuclear-weapon state party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons that possesses nuclear fuel reprocessing technologies, is capable of extracting weapons-grade plutonium and has operating fuel reprocessing facilities, as well as the only country outside the nuclear club that has a full-fledged nuclear fuel cycle. In addition, Japan has a powerful industrial base and economic potential, which theoretically enable it to produce and obtain nuclear materials using existing reactors and reprocessing technologies to manufacture nuclear explosive devices."
According to Dai Huaicheng, Japan has been building up its military potential in recent years with support from the US military industry.
"As for the means of delivery, the F-35A, F-15 and F-2 fighters in service with the Japan Air Self-Defense Forces are potentially capable of carrying nuclear bombs. Japan has also decided to purchase several hundred Tomahawk cruise missiles, modify the launchers on ships equipped with the Aegis combat information management system, and deploy US Typhon medium-range ground-based missiles," he said.

articles.title: Qatari mediators hand Iran new proposal to end the war
articles.body:
Live Updates: Iran rejects "unacceptable" ideas as Qatari mediators say they presented new draft deal to Tehran
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iran's foreign minister said Wednesday the country "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" after Reuters earlier reported Tehran rejected Qatar's latest peace proposal, saying they had come with "unacceptable" ideas.
- Israelis voted Tuesday in a national election set to shape the country's next government, with the Iran war looming large. Exit polls projected that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition but neither side had a clear margin of victory.
- The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.
Hezbollah says it doesn't care who wins Israeli election
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said Wednesday the Iran-backed Lebanese movement was not concerned with the results of Israel's election, vowing to continue its "resistance" against the neighbouring country no matter who wins.
With 85% of ballots counted, the right-wing bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a slight lead over the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, but was still short of a majority after Tuesday's election.
"We do not concern ourselves with who governs Israel, but let it be perfectly clear that it cannot continue its occupation and must leave our land," Qassem said in a written statement.
"The resistance will continue ... and will stand up to the aggression directed against it and against Lebanon, and there is no room to discuss the disarmament" of Hezbollah "as long as the occupation persists and its aggression continues," he added.
The group, which once dominated political life in Lebanon, has been weakened by the two wars it has waged against Israel since 2023.
U.K. seeks to give households "breathing space" this winter over Iran war energy price spike
U.K. Treasury chief John Healey used his first budget Wednesday to offer households and businesses some support with energy bills this winter in the face of what he termed "global economic storms."
He said that his "choice in the budget today is to give families and businesses some breathing space now," as the consequences of the Middle East conflict play out.
"For families, that means higher prices at the pump, higher energy bills and higher mortgages," he said in his statement, one of the main dates of the parliamentary calendar. "For businesses, higher running costs and more expensive loans. And the impact is felt in the public finances, too."
Among the measures announced was a 100-pound ($133) one-off payment this winter for 20 million lower- and middle-income households, proportionately more of whom live in the electoral battlegrounds in northern England.
Other measures include the extension of a cut in the sales tax on electricity bills and the abolition of a charge paid on gas bills.
Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of stealing election, widespread fraud
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the Arab parties of stealing the election through widespread fraud and called on Shin Bet, Israel's security agency, to investigate.
"We demand from the police and the Shin Bet a thorough investigation into the election theft by the Arab parties and the full prosecution of the criminals," Netanyahu's Likud party shared on his X account, translated from Hebrew. "This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens. The law enforcement agencies must act with an iron fist and in an immediate manner."
Netanyahu's party leads in the latest vote counts, but all of the parties will fall short of the majority needed to control the Knesset, Israel's parliament. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%, according to official election data.
Local media projected 53 seats for the Likud party, 48 seats for the Yahar and other opposition parties and 19 seats for the Arab-led parties. In order to reach a majority (61 of 120 seats) and pick a prime minister, deals will have to be made.
Iran continues to review ideas for peace agreement, foreign minister says
Amid reports Iran had rejected the latest proposal for peace from Qatari intermediaries, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that his country continues to review ideas for a diplomatic solution to the eight-month war.
"While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," Araghchi wrote. "We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week."
The seven-day plan was presented to the U.S. shortly after the U.N. General Assembly in September. However, President Trump rejected the idea presented by Iran for a seven-day ceasefire and then phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas, Reuters reported.
A source had earlier reported there were concerns Israel could begin a new bombing campaign after its election, according to Reuters.
Kuwait summons Iran ambassador over "interference"
Kuwait summoned Iran's envoy in protest on Wednesday, after Tehran denied one of its citizens, sentenced to death in Kuwait, was involved in an assassination plot targeting a top government figure.
Earlier this week, two Kuwaiti judicial sources told the AFP news agency that the Gulf state had condemned three Shia men to death for plotting the assassination of Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Fahad al-Yousef, collaborating with Iran; and for membership in Hezbollah.
Iran's embassy in Kuwait said earlier Wednesday it "rejects the Kuwaiti government's claim regarding the involvement of an Iranian citizen in a plot to assassinate figures or in any other act that could harm Kuwaiti national security."
It added that the person in question had been outside Kuwait for 10 years.
It said it regretted a "negative approach towards Iran, manifested, among other things, in the repetition of flimsy and worn-out scenarios concerning Iranian interference in Kuwaiti affairs."
In response, Kuwait summoned Iranian ambassador Mohammad Toutounji over the statement, which it said "constituted blatant interference in the internal affairs of the State of Kuwait and an infringement upon its sovereignty and the independence of its judiciary."
Abdulredha Haydar Dahqani was among those who had been sentenced to death, the judicial sources told AFP.
Dahqani, an Iranian national, had already been handed the death penalty in 2016 after he was tried in absentia along with 25 Kuwaitis. He was convicted of spying for Iran and plotting attacks.
Another was Hussein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Kuwait's most influential Shia movement, the sources said.
CBS/AFP
Israeli defense minister slams Eisenkot's call for military to resist Netanyahu's pressure
Israel's defense minister on Wednesday denounced opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot for urging the military to resist post-election pressure from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has threatened new strikes on Iran.
"His call to senior military officials not to obey the directives of the prime minister or me or of other relevant security authorities, on the grounds that 'they have his support,' is an anti-democratic statement detached from reality," Israel Katz wrote on X.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, said in a speech to supporters after Tuesday's election that Netanyahu was a caretaker prime minister lacking a mandate and the military should serve the state rather than the premier.
"Stand firm in the face of any attempt to challenge you. You have my unequivocal backing. Netanyahu, do not dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Netanyahu has repeatedly threatened in recent days to renew strikes on Iran.
Media reports, denied by Netanyahu, said military chief Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir pushed back immediately before the election on the prime minister's new plans on Iran.
Eisenkot's comments were the latest in "a campaign of lies" about tension between Netanyahu and the military over Iran, Katz said.
Yemen's transport ministry warns of civil aviation risks after sixth Houthi attack on Aden airport
Yemen's Ministry of Transport has warned of risks to civil aviation safety after Aden International Airport was targeted in a missile attack attributed to the Houthi group for the sixth time, Saudi Arabia's Asharq News reported.
The missile strike shook parts of the southern city, raising fresh concerns over the safety of airport operations and the potential threat to civilian air traffic.
Airport authorities had evacuated all employees and workers from the facility following Houthi threats to target the airport.
Iran, Russia near agreement on joint development of small modular nuclear reactors
Iran is finalizing a protocol with Russia to accelerate joint development of small modular nuclear reactors, Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman and deputy for international, legal and parliamentary affairs at the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, has announced.
Speaking to Iran's Shabakeh Khabar television network, Kamalvandi said the agreement would facilitate closer cooperation on the construction of small modular reactors, a technology attracting growing international interest as countries seek reliable, low-carbon electricity sources. SMRs are far smaller than traditional large-scale reactors.
Kamalvandi also highlighted rising global electricity demand, driven in part by artificial intelligence, digital technologies and the electrification of transport. He said nuclear power could provide stable baseload electricity while helping reduce emissions.
He claimed Iran's nuclear industry had reached a mature stage and said the country had developed substantial domestic capabilities in nuclear plant construction, fuel-cycle technology and nuclear safety. He also stated political pressure had delayed some Iranian projects but had not halted the country's nuclear activities.
Kamalvandi made the remarks while discussing Iran's participation in an international ministerial conference on nuclear energy in South Korea. He said the Iranian delegation was using the event to promote international cooperation and argue that countries party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty should have their rights respected alongside their obligations.
Iran warns any Israeli-led attack would be "devastating" for global markets
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Wednesday that any Israeli-instigated attack in the Gulf region would have a "devastating impact" on global markets.
"Devastating impact on int'l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Persian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers," Araghchi said in a post on X.
The United States and Israel have in recent days raised the prospect of renewed attacks on Iran in the war, which began in late February with strikes on the Islamic republic.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to form a new government after close elections, said on Wednesday he could work with President Trump to eliminate the "existential threat" posed by Iran.
CBS/AFP
Iranian embassy in Kuwait denies assassination plot allegations against Iranian citizen
Iran's Embassy in Kuwait has categorically rejected the Kuwaiti government's allegation that an Iranian citizen was involved in a plot to assassinate public figures or in any other activity that could undermine Kuwait's national security.
The embassy said in a statement that it "categorically rejects the allegation made by the Kuwaiti government regarding the involvement of an Iranian citizen in a plot to assassinate public figures or in any other act that could undermine Kuwait's national security, and recalls that the aforementioned individual has not been present in Kuwait at any time during the past ten years."
A Kuwaiti State Security and Terrorism Criminal Court sentenced three men to death on Monday over an alleged plot to assassinate First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad Al-Yousef, with prosecutors accusing the defendants of spying for Iran, communicating with Iranian-linked entities and joining Hezbollah, two judicial sources told the AFP news agency Tuesday.
The court also sentenced eight other defendants to varying prison terms.
According to Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Rai, the defendants were accused of communicating with Iran and entities allegedly operating in its interests, including Lebanese group Hezbollah, to carry out hostile acts against Kuwait following the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on Feb. 28, at the beginning of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Saudi strike kills 14, Houthis say, as group targets Aden
Iran-backed Houthi rebels said Wednesday Saudi Arabia killed dozens of people with strikes in Yemen. The group also said it had targeted the perimeter of an airport in government-held Aden
Houthi broadcaster Almasirah reported 14 dead "and 10 wounded, including women and children in a preliminary toll," in attacks blamed on Saudi Arabia that hit a market and a petrol station in the northwestern Jawf province.
In Aden, a Houthi missile fell inside the perimeter of the airport shortly before the Iran-backed group issued a call to evacuate the area, a local police source told the AFP news agency.
The source added that the strike hit while a Saudi military aircraft was at the airport, but the plane "was not hit and took off shortly afterward."
He spoke on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a post on Telegram that the cargo plan was "transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people."
The Houthis have targeted Aden several times in recent weeks. They have also intensified attacks on their Saudi foe, while they battle the government it backs in Aden.
CBS/AFP
U.S. reportedly warns Gulf allies to prepare for brief, intense campaign against Iran post-midterms
The United States has told its Gulf allies to prepare for a brief but intense campaign against Iran after the midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the matter.
The U.S. military is shipping a Patriot antimissile system from Texas to Israel and has transferred troops off bases where they may have been vulnerable, officials familiar with the decisions told the outlet.
American forces across the Middle East have been restocking munitions and aircraft have been preparing for strikes, the paper reported, while an additional aircraft carrier strike group and Marine unit are set to join the 20 or so warships in the region, though some other vessels could be withdrawn.
Houthis call for immediate evacuation of Yemen's Aden airport
The Houthis have called on people in Aden International Airport in southern Yemen to evacuate immediately, claiming that a Saudi military cargo aircraft is transporting weapons there intended to kill Yemenis.
Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a post on X: "Our armed forces call on those present at Aden Airport to evacuate the airport immediately, due to the presence of an enemy Saudi military cargo aircraft transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people."
Aden is the seat of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, and has been since the Iran-backed Houthis took the country's capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
Senior Iranian official denies Qatar presented new peace proposal, says ideas "unacceptable"
A senior Iranian official denied Wednesday that Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal, saying instead that Qatar had come with "unacceptable" ideas, the Reuters news agency reported.
Reuters reported earlier Wednesday that Qatari mediators handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war on Sunday, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Dismissing the idea that they had been given a new peace proposal, the Iranian official speaking to the news agency said Tehran would show no flexibility on the nuclear issue.
Qatari mediators hand Iran new proposal to end the war, Reuters reports
Qatari mediators on Sunday handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war, the Reuters news agency reported, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Tehran is considering the proposal and set to respond by the end of the week, the agency reported Wednesday.
The source added that there were concerns in Tehran before the meeting on Sunday that Israel could resume its bombardment of Iran this week.
Cost of Iran war rises to an estimated $47 billion
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.
Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.
According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.
Israeli election exit polls show race headed toward stalemate
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

articles.title: Iran war costs US taxpayers $47.1 billion
articles.body:
The U.S. war with Iran has cost American taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion, according to new Pentagon figures submitted to Congress, as the conflict's financial toll fuels debate ahead of the midterm elections and President Donald Trump signals that further military action remains possible.
The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion.
The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week's midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump's last two years in office.
The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks. As the war’s costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll.
The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal. The White House is also asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities.
Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress.
"Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. "Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House.”
In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war's costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army’s Patriot and THAAD systems, with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars.
The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force's costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army's are more than $2 billion. The Navy's costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September.
When asked why the Navy’s cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates.
The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The Pentagon’s official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or the disposal of Iranian drones.
While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or "finish them off,” a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. The Trump administration also has reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel.

articles.title: Ethiopia receives its first Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets
articles.body:
- Ethiopia has received its first 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets, a year ahead of schedule, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said on Oct. 28.
- Abiy said Ethiopia will also receive four S-400 air defense batteries but did not disclose the deal’s value or delivery timeline.
Ethiopia has taken delivery of its first 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will also receive four batteries of the S-400 long-range air defense system, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said on social media on Oct. 28.
Abiy said the jets arrived under an earlier agreement with the Russian government and a year ahead of the agreed schedule, and he thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for the early delivery. He did not disclose the value of the deal, its terms, or when the S-400 batteries will arrive, Addis Standard reported.
“In accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have today taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets,” said Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The announcement came while Abiy was in Russia for the third Russia-Africa Summit, according to Ethiopian state broadcaster Fana Media Corporation, which reported that he witnessed the official handover of the aircraft. Abiy described the purchase as a major boost to the defense forces and said it puts Ethiopia in the lead among Sub-Saharan African nations.
The Su-35 is Russia’s most advanced fighter in export service after the Su-57. It is a single-seat, twin-engine multirole jet built for both air combat and ground attack, with thrust-vectoring engines that let it maneuver sharply and a long-range Irbis-E radar. Sukhoi calls it a “4++ generation” aircraft, meaning a heavily upgraded fourth-generation design that stops short of the stealth features of fifth-generation fighters.
The S-400 is a long-range surface-to-air missile system designed to shoot down aircraft and some missiles. A battery typically includes radars, a command post and several launcher vehicles.
Ethiopia’s interest in the Su-35 first surfaced a year ago. In October 2025, a hacker group called Black Mirror published internal files from Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec that listed Ethiopia as having signed a contract for six Su-35s, alongside larger orders for Iran and Algeria. Neither Rostec nor the Ethiopian government commented at the time. The 12 jets Abiy announced are double the number in the leaked documents, and his description of them as the “first” twelve suggests more could follow, though he did not say how many Ethiopia has ordered in total.
The new jets will join an air force that has flown Russian Sukhoi fighters for more than 25 years. Ethiopia received Su-27s in the late 1990s and used them in its 1998 to 2000 border war with Eritrea. In January 2024, it inducted Su-30K fighters, believed to come from a batch originally built for the Indian Air Force, along with Turkish Akinci drones.
Only a handful of countries have received the Su-35 for export. China took delivery of 24 aircraft between 2016 and 2018, and Algeria received its first units in March 2025, Army Recognition reported. The S-400 is in service with China, India and Turkey, and Turkey’s purchase led the United States to impose sanctions on its defense procurement agency in 2020 under a law targeting significant arms deals with Russia.
Tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have risen this year, and Russia has offered to host talks between the two countries, Addis Standard reported. Abiy said the new equipment would allow Ethiopia to deter aggression and support regional stability.

articles.title: Putin adviser says Frederiksen deserves to lose Greenland
articles.body:
Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian envoy involved in negotiations over the war in Ukraine and an adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin on economic and international affairs, said Tuesday that Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen deserves to lose Greenland.
Dmitriev made the comment in a post on the social media platform X, alongside a video in which Frederiksen criticized Finnish and Norwegian leaders for speaking by phone with Putin.
“She (Mette Frederiksen, ed.) deserves to lose Greenland. The warmongers will lose. Dialogue will prevail,” Dmitriev wrote.
The comments came after Finnish President Alexander Stubb announced Tuesday morning that he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre had spoken with Putin by phone.
The call received a mixed response from the countries’ allies. Frederiksen was among those who criticized the decision to speak with the Russian president.
“I am very skeptical of this Norwegian and Finnish own initiative. It is not coordinated with the rest of us,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcaster TV 2 during a meeting of the Nordic Council in Finland.
“I think one should keep Europe together instead of going solo,” she added.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also expressed doubts about the call.
“Holding talks that risk dividing the European voice, that is risky,” he said Tuesday, according to Swedish media.
Støre later rejected the criticism, saying the talks were conducted with other countries’ knowledge.
“We do not speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves, but it has been thoroughly consulted, and all our partners and allies were informed in advance and have also received a thorough summary afterwards,” he told Norwegian media outlet VG on Tuesday.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took a more positive view of the talks. In a post on X, he said he was “grateful” for Norway and Finland’s active diplomatic work.
Copenhagen Airport says tighter security checks and staffing shortfalls contributed to long queues
An order from the Danish Transport Authority led to additional baggage checks from October 8. Some passengers missed flights, and SAS reported rebooking 352 travelers.
Copenhagen Airport introduced additional security checks following an order from the Danish Transport Authority and underestimated staffing needs on some days in October, the airport said Wednesday after long queues caused passengers to miss flights.
The airport received the order on October 6 and introduced the measures two days later. The changes meant more passengers had their baggage checked manually, it said in a press release.
The airport did not explain why the authority issued the order or give details of its requirements.
There were periods of long waits on October 8, October 22 and October 23, the airport said. Passengers also faced waits of up to an hour early on Saturday, October 24.
Danish media have reported lengthy queues, particularly over the past five days, with some passengers reaching their flights too late to depart as booked.
The airport acknowledged that it had underestimated staffing needs on some days during October. It said “it is naturally not satisfactory” that some passengers had had “a bad experience”.
SAS said on October 23 that it had rebooked 352 passengers because of the long waits. Passengers were also urged to arrive earlier than usual and allow extra time for security.
Norwegian also offered affected customers rebooking.
The American singer-songwriter will perform at next year’s Northside festival in Aarhus, joining a lineup that already includes The Strokes and Danish singer Mille.
The festival confirmed the booking in a press release, announcing ten other acts alongside the 32-year-old musician.
Northside will take place at Eskelunden in Aarhus from June 10 to June 12, 2027.
Organizers praised Bridgers’ songwriting and her ability to combine emotional themes with humor.
“Few songwriters manage to hit both the heart and dark humor as precisely as Phoebe Bridgers,” the festival said.
“With fragile vocals, detailed lyrics, and her ability to unite melancholy with quirky humor, the American singer-songwriter has established herself as one of the most prominent voices of her generation,” organizers added.
Bridgers made her solo debut in 2017 with the album Stranger in the Alps, followed by Punisher in 2020.
Her third album, Lost Weekend, was released earlier this year. Her songs include “Scott Street,” “Motion Sickness” and “Lost Boys.”
Danish fans will also have an opportunity to see Bridgers before next summer’s festival. She is scheduled to perform at Royal Arena in Copenhagen this December.
Other newly announced Northside acts include Danish band Kind mod Kind, Canadian rock duo Angine de Poitrine, African group Tinariwen and American soul musician Jalen Ngonda, whose music draws inspiration from Motown.
Northside said the latest bookings reflect its earlier promise to increase spending on its music program.
The festival had previously confirmed American rock band The Strokes and Danish singer Mille for its 2027 edition.
Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.
Ukrainian embassy disputes Danish lawmaker’s claim of unanswered meeting request
A disagreement has emerged between Ukraine’s embassy in Copenhagen and independent Danish lawmaker Jacob Harris over attempts to arrange a meeting ahead of his planned talks with Russia’s ambassador.
In a written statement to Ritzau, Denmark’s news agency, the embassy said it had offered Harris two possible meeting dates but received no reply.
“We were surprised to hear these claims from Member of Parliament Jacob Harris,” the embassy said.
“After receiving an email from Jacob Harris requesting a meeting, we suggested two possible dates to him in the near future. However, we have not received any response.”
Harris maintains that he never received the embassy’s reply but said he was “glad that contact has been made”.
“Now I will write to them again with a view to arranging a meeting,” he said.
The embassy also stated that Harris had visited twice without an appointment, hoping to meet the ambassador.
On both occasions, the ambassador was attending previously scheduled events and was not at the embassy.
Harris confirmed the visits, saying he had hoped to arrange a meeting.
The disagreement follows Harris’ announcement Thursday that he plans to meet Russia’s ambassador in Copenhagen on November 10.
In a Facebook post, Harris called for “more diplomacy, more dialogue, and less war rhetoric”.
The planned meeting drew criticism from politicians across Denmark’s political spectrum.
Harris also wrote that he had repeatedly contacted Ukraine’s ambassador without receiving a response.
He now hopes to meet the Ukrainian ambassador before his scheduled meeting with Russia’s representative.
The Ukrainian embassy expressed appreciation for Danish political support and thanked the Danish public for its continued solidarity with Ukraine.
Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.

Putin adviser says Frederiksen deserves to lose Greenland
Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian envoy involved in negotiations over the war in Ukraine and an adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin on economic and international affairs, said Tuesday that Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen deserves to lose Greenland.

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.
Electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex recalled over electric shock risk
Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.

Customers will receive a full refund even if they no longer have their receipt.

Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.

Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.

Veteran Venstre lawmaker expelled over party discipline dispute
Preben Bang Henriksen has been expelled from Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, after refusing to promise that he would follow the party’s position in future parliamentary votes.
The lawmaker confirmed his expulsion Tuesday following a meeting at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing.

He has served as the party’s justice spokesperson and chaired parliamentary committees overseeing legal affairs and intelligence services.

Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.

At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.

Norwegian to cut 123 jobs at Copenhagen Airport as it reduces locally based aircraft

Three senior doctors leave Rigshospitalet after being sent home following patient safety warnings

Bank deposits in Denmark fall for two consecutive months

New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news

Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.

Danish publisher bans AI tools for work on manuscripts

Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak

Power fault causes train delays and cancellations across Zealand

Strong winds and high water to ease as calmer weather reaches Denmark

The strongest winds Monday morning were along Jutland’s west coast between Blåvandshuk and Skagen, Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Mette Zhang said.
Some areas continued to experience storm-force gusts, although the wind was expected to weaken during the day.
DMI maintained warnings for elevated water levels around the Wadden Sea, the central western coast of Jutland and parts of the Limfjord.
Water levels in the Wadden Sea reached more than three meters above normal overnight but were beginning to fall.
Western Denmark will experience the most clouds Monday, while eastern areas will have clearer conditions. Showers are expected in several places before conditions improve later in the day.
Temperatures will range from 9 to 13 degrees Celsius.
A new front will bring clouds, rain and stronger southerly winds overnight into Tuesday. Winds could reach gale force along the west coast, although less rain is expected than during the weekend.
Wednesday will bring a mixture of rain, showers and sunshine.
A high-pressure system is expected to stabilize the weather from Thursday, bringing less wind, drier conditions and more sunshine.
Fog may form overnight into Thursday and Friday. Clearer skies will also increase the risk of overnight frost, particularly heading into Saturday.
Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.
Danish Crown confirms slaughter without stunning at Polish subsidiary
Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.
The method is legal in Poland but has been prohibited in Denmark since 2014, when prior stunning became mandatory.
Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.
Several animal welfare organizations criticized the company’s involvement.
Søren Kent Pedersen, a veterinarian with animal welfare organization Dyrenes Beskyttelse, described the practice as animal cruelty and accused Danish Crown of hypocrisy because the company publicly emphasizes animal welfare.
Danish Crown’s website states that “good animal welfare is the core of our business” and that the company protects animals’ well-being from farms through slaughter.
Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.
Danish Crown did not say whether it would continue permitting the practice.
Parents urged to check children’s electric scooters after illegal riding cases
Danish road safety authorities are urging parents to check electric scooters used by their children after police stopped underage riders and scooters capable of greatly exceeding the legal speed limit.
Riders must be at least 15 years old to use an electric scooter alone in traffic. Scooters may travel no faster than 20 kilometers per hour, and helmets are mandatory.
Children under 15 may ride in traffic only when accompanied by an adult.
The Danish Road Safety Council identified 21 reported cases between September 13 and October 13 involving children who were too young or scooters that could travel too fast.
The figure came from media coverage and police reports rather than a complete national count.
Children as young as nine were stopped, while some scooters could reach speeds of up to 90 kilometers per hour.
“Parents should take it seriously and check the rules before saying yes to an electric scooter,” council chief executive Jakob Bøving Arendt said.
Emergency departments in Odense and Svendborg have treated 811 people injured in electric scooter accidents since 2021. Twenty-five percent suffered serious injuries.
Odense University Hospital physician Jens Lauritsen said crashes can cause severe injuries even at legal speeds.
Modified scooters capable of traveling 60, 80 or 100 kilometers per hour could endanger both riders and others, he said.
Denmark to cull 27,000 turkeys after bird flu outbreak on Lolland
Danish authorities will cull 27,000 turkeys Monday after highly pathogenic avian influenza was detected in a flock in Stokkemarke on the island of Lolland.
It is Denmark’s second confirmed outbreak of the highly contagious disease within one week, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration said.
Another outbreak was identified Friday in a flock in Bøgelunde in Slagelse Municipality.
“It is therefore extra important at this time of year that everyone who keeps poultry or other birds does everything to prevent contact between their animals and wild birds,” agency veterinarian Mette Kirkeskov Sie said.
Owners should prevent wild birds from reaching their animals, drinking water and feed. The agency also recommends changing footwear before entering areas where birds are kept.
Authorities have established protection and surveillance zones around the infected flock on Lolland. Poultry owners within those areas must follow stricter disease control requirements.
The restrictions will remain until authorities complete their investigations and determine that the risk of further transmission has declined.
The agency said avian influenza only very rarely spreads to humans.
However, people should avoid touching sick, weakened or dead wild birds.
Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.
Queen Margrethe receives medal for 25 years of design work at Tivoli
Queen Margrethe has received a 25th anniversary medal recognizing her work as a costume and set designer for Copenhagen’s Tivoli Gardens.
Tivoli chief executive Susanne Mørch Koch presented the medal during a private ceremony at Fredensborg Palace.
“Queen Margrethe has had a truly exceptional significance for Tivoli’s performing arts,” Koch said.
The former Danish monarch has contributed to nine productions at Tivoli during the past 25 years.
Seven were staged at the Pantomime Theatre, while two appeared in Tivoli’s Concert Hall.
Her first production was Hans Christian Andersen’s “Love in the Dustbin” in 2001, for which she created costumes, scenery and an interpretation of the story.
“Queen Margrethe’s contribution has become part of Tivoli’s cultural heritage,” Koch said.
Margrethe has also contributed costumes and set designs to a new production of “The Nutcracker,” opening at Tivoli’s Concert Hall on November 26.
Three ballet dancers were honored during the ceremony. Tori Cooper and Allan Clausen marked 25 years at Tivoli, while Tommy Edvardsen celebrated 50 years at the Pantomime Theatre.
All three have performed in productions involving Margrethe, including “The Tinderbox,” “The Swineherd” and “Cinderella.”
Margrethe, 86, became Denmark’s monarch in 1972 and abdicated in favor of her son, King Frederik, on January 14, 2024.
Copenhagen Airport continues to expect busyness and longer waiting times than normal at security during periods over the weekend.
The airport’s press department stated this on Saturday morning.
On Saturday around 08:45, the waiting time for security is down to between five and seven minutes. This appears from Copenhagen Airport’s website.
Earlier in the morning there was longer waiting time, in periods up to between 45 minutes and an hour, the airport states.
Several media outlets have on Thursday and Friday described long queues at security in Copenhagen Airport.
The reason for the long queues is that an inspection from Trafikstyrelsen has led to the airport temporarily having to introduce extra measures.
Neither Trafikstyrelsen nor Copenhagen Airport has wished to elaborate on what has led to the supplementary measures at security.
For security reasons, Copenhagen Airport also does not wish to disclose when Trafikstyrelsen asked the airport to introduce the temporary measures.
Copenhagen Airport recommends that passengers stay updated on waiting times and recommendations on both the airport’s own website and with the individual airline.
The airport recommends travelers arrive two hours before departure when traveling within the Schengen area, and three hours before departure when traveling outside the Schengen area.
RITZAU
Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.
Source: Ritzau
Denmark delays new citizenship screening model – what it means for applicants
The expert group tasked with examining the possibilities for a screening model for citizenship applicants is facing further delays in its work.
The Ministry of Immigration and Integration writes this in a press release.
– Due to the scope and complexity of the work, we cannot manage to deliver our recommendations around the turn of the year. Instead, I expect that we will conclude our work in mid-March next year, says Henrik Thomassen, chairman of the expert group, in the press release.
The granting of citizenship in particular has taken up a significant amount of the political debate recently.
Most recently, the Danish People’s Party entered the debate because the party wants a Pakistani man removed from an upcoming bill that next year will make 2,055 foreigners Danish citizens.
DF’s citizenship spokesperson, Mikkel Bjørn, has found a Facebook post from 2016 in which the man, according to DF, supported an Islamic execution.
– The government should strip him of the opportunity to obtain citizenship. If they are not willing to do that, they must at the very least be willing to let us meet this man eye-to-eye so we can see the matter for ourselves, Mikkel Bjørn told DR on Thursday.
Last week, Liberal Alliance found a woman who, according to the party, has repeatedly praised Hamas and the former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Therefore, the party wants the person summoned for an interview with the Folketing’s Naturalisation Committee.
The central element in the debate regarding a bill granting citizenship to 2,055 new individuals has been whether they have been sufficiently investigated for anti-democratic views.
Every six months, a bill is introduced in the Folketing granting new individuals Danish citizenship after an often lengthy and comprehensive application process.
This also applied to the then SVM government.
But the latest granting of citizenship coincided with the calling of the general election held in March of this year, and the bill regarding the citizenship of the 2,055 individuals was therefore postponed.
A screening model must be created for people who apply for Danish citizenship to investigate whether they have anti-democratic views. The government announced this earlier in October.
However, the government has ultimately decided that it will introduce the bill before a screening model is ready.
The original bill had its first reading in the Folketing on 5 February, but three weeks later Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen (S) called a general election.
The expert group was established in 2025 and was initially given ten months to complete its work.
RITZAU
Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.
Source: Ritzau
Data on 525,000 people compromised in KU cyberattack
The University of Copenhagen (KU) has been subjected to a cyberattack.
The hackers have gained access to information on approximately 525,000 individuals. Among this is information such as full name, CPR number, work telephone number, private telephone number, and private email address.
The university stated this in a press release on Friday evening.
The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, just as “other relevant authorities are being kept closely informed”.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness and the Agency for Public Security write in a press release Friday evening that the authorities are monitoring the cyber incidents at the University of Copenhagen and Aarhus University.
The ministry and the agency are working closely with the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalisation and other relevant authorities on the handling, it is stated.
– The incidents emphasize once again that the cyber threat against Denmark is serious, states Minister for Public Security and Emergency Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen (SF) in a written comment to Ritzau and continues:
– The Agency for Public Security generally assesses that universities in Denmark are exposed to the threat of cyberattacks. Among other things because they are leaders within a range of research areas. I know that the universities are working actively to counter that threat.
The minister states that “relevant higher education institutions have been informed about the incidents and have received advice from the Agency for Public Security.”
The attack against the University of Copenhagen was discovered on Tuesday and “was subsequently brought under control”.
The university is in the process of analyzing the exact scope and preventing similar or further attacks from taking place, it is stated.
KU further writes in the press release that at present they have no further comments on the cyberattack, but that “there will be follow-up with further information when a clearer picture of the incident is available”.
Aarhus University stated on Thursday that the educational institution had been subjected to a hacker attack.
The hacker gained access to one of the university’s servers.
Afterwards, the hacker attempted to gain access to and change passwords for approximately 1,700 users – both current and former employees and students.
This did not succeed, as the unauthorized access to the system was discovered.
RITZAU
Hundreds of passengers rebooked after long queues at Copenhagen Airport
At least 352 passengers booked on SAS flights have been rebooked after long queues at security control at Copenhagen Airport caused them to miss their departures.
“We understand the frustration and inconvenience that the situation causes, and share our passengers’ frustration. We know that Copenhagen Airport is working hard to resolve the problem,” she said.
Rival airline Norwegian has also been affected. Country Manager Sara Neergaard told Danish broadcaster DR that 200 passengers missed their flights on Thursday, with a further 30 missing their departures on Friday.
“Unfortunately, we cannot do much other than ask people to arrive more than two hours early,” Neergaard told DR.
Norwegian has offered affected passengers the option of rebooking their flights.
Long queues were reported at Copenhagen Airport on Thursday evening and again on Friday morning. The Danish Transport Authority said on Thursday that an inspection had led the airport to introduce additional security measures temporarily.
SAS has advised passengers to arrive earlier than usual and allow extra time to pass through security.
Kaoukji said the situation appeared to have improved by midday Friday, but SAS was hoping the airport could maintain sufficient capacity as passenger traffic increased later in the afternoon.
Copenhagen Airport’s Head of Communications, Lise Agerley Kürstein, told TV 2 on Friday that the airport did not yet know how long the temporary measures would remain in place.
However, the airport hopes to have a solution in place at the beginning of next week.
Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.
Jacob Harris has been banned from managing or sitting on the board of a company for three years following a ruling by the probate court in Roskilde on Friday.
TV 2 reported the decision, citing trustee and bankruptcy lawyer Morten Bjerregaard.
The ban also means Harris, an independent member of the Danish parliament, cannot own a company unless he accepts personal liability.
The ruling concerns Harris’ activities in Krokodille ApS, a company for which his wife, Tetiana Harris Nielsen, served as director. The court declared the company bankrupt in the autumn of 2025.
According to TV 2, Harris’ wife has also received a three-year bankruptcy ban. The ruling was reportedly based on the couple’s conduct in the company, whose bookkeeping was deficient and entirely absent for 2025.
Krokodille ApS was founded in Hedehusene, west of Copenhagen, in December 2021 under the name Vostok Sokol ApS. A holding company owned by Tetiana Harris Nielsen is registered as its founder. The company changed its name in March 2022 and moved its registered address from the couple’s home to an address in Ringsted in October 2025, shortly before its bankruptcy.
Harris was elected to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, for Borgernes Parti in the March election but was expelled from the party days later. The party said he had “not provided truthful information to the party and, moreover, repeatedly acted contrary to the party’s values.”
Harris has also faced criticism over plans to meet Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, on 10 November.
Responding to the controversy, Harris wrote on Facebook: “Talking to a foreign ambassador is not treason.”
Danish pension provider ATP will increase lifelong pension payments by 2 percent from 1 January 2027, benefiting all 5.8 million members, including 1.1 million current pensioners.
