Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.
During the debate, opposition party Naleraq proposed putting the agreement to a referendum.
The Greenlandic government holds a majority in Inatsisartut. In Denmark, the government must secure support from other parties to obtain a parliamentary majority for the agreement.
Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.
Netanyahu orders West Bank lockdown after shooting near Hebron
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered an immediate closure of the city of Hebron and instructed the military to prepare to shut down the entire West Bank following a shooting that left at least five people injured.
Netanyahu announced the measures in a post on X, according to the French news agency AFP.
“I have ordered the IDF and the security forces to impose an immediate closure of the city of Hebron and to prepare a full shutdown of all of Judea and Samaria effective from today,” he wrote.
Judea and Samaria are the names Israel uses for the territory known internationally as the West Bank. It remains unclear what the planned shutdown will mean in practice.
Netanyahu said the military had begun “counter-terrorism operations” in the area, including searches of homes belonging to people suspected of involvement in terrorism.
“Soldiers are currently operating inside the homes of terrorists and other suspects,” AFP reported.
The announcement follows a shooting early Friday near Hebron, during which two Palestinian men were shot by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). They are suspected of carrying out an attack that left at least five people injured.
The incident involved an exchange of fire between the two men and Israeli forces at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint near Hebron. According to AFP, the Palestinians were armed with a pistol and an automatic rifle.
Netanyahu praised the military for preventing what he described as “a major terrorist attack” and vowed to pursue Hamas members.
“You have nowhere to hide,” he wrote.
Israel is due to hold parliamentary elections next week. Following the shooting, Netanyahu cancelled all political meetings.
Israel’s National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, also responded to the shooting by calling for the dissolution and demilitarization of the Palestinian Authority.
“We have to act before it is too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dissolved and demilitarized, and its terrorist infrastructure must be completely eradicated,” he said.
The Palestinian Authority administers parts of the West Bank and was established under the Oslo peace agreements. It is led by President Mahmoud Abbas, whose Fatah party is a rival of Hamas.
There is currently no indication that Palestinian Authority officials were involved in the shooting.
Hamas praised the attack but did not claim responsibility, according to AFP.
“The attack is a natural and legitimate response to the ongoing crimes and brutal attacks against our people,” the group said, describing it as “an exceptional heroic operation”.
Retail sales in Denmark rose by 0.4 percent in September compared with August, despite growing pessimism among consumers, according to figures from Statistics Denmark.
The increase is adjusted for seasonal fluctuations, price changes and the number of trading days.
For the third quarter, covering July through September, retail sales rose by 1.6 percent compared with the previous quarter.
Sales trends varied across industries in September. The largest increases were recorded among retailers selling second-hand goods, household equipment, furniture and building materials.
By contrast, sales fell the most at gas stations and pharmacies. Danish supermarkets also recorded a slight decline.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said the increase in retail sales was encouraging given the growing pessimism among Danish consumers.
On Thursday, Statistics Denmark’s consumer confidence indicator stood at minus 17.2, down from minus 13.7 in September.
A negative reading indicates that consumers have a pessimistic view of the country’s current and future economic situation.
Despite the decline in confidence, Morten Granzau, deputy director at the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri), believes retail sales could continue to grow in the coming months.
“Consumers’ purchasing power is fundamentally good. High employment, growth in real wages, and the lower electricity tax provide breathing room in many households’ budgets. This creates good opportunities for retail sales to maintain progress through the autumn,” he wrote in a comment.
Danish military to fund four bus routes to attract and retain staff
Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.
The initiative is outlined in a funding document approved by the Folketing’s Finance Committee, a parliamentary body that approves certain government spending outside the annual Finance Act.
The Armed Forces will receive 2 million kroner in 2026 to establish the routes. The initiative is planned to run for three years, with a total budget of 17 million kroner.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said the routes would help make military employment more attractive at garrisons in remote parts of Denmark, where public transport services are inadequate.
“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.

Strong winds, heavy rain and potentially elevated sea levels are forecast across parts of Denmark on Sunday, with the west coast of Jutland expected to experience the worst conditions.
According to Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, wind gusts could locally reach storm force, particularly along the North Sea coast.
“One should consider whether it is worth going outside when the wind is blowing the most,” DMI meteorologist Hans Ole Wanner told Ritzau.
Southerly winds are expected to strengthen overnight into Sunday as a warm front brings widespread rain.
During Sunday, winds will shift toward the southwest and intensify, bringing strong gusts and severe gales to coastal areas.
DMI warns that the conditions could affect traffic on several Danish bridges.
Higher water levels are also possible along Jutland’s west coast, particularly around the Wadden Sea.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a storm system moving toward Denmark from the British Isles over the weekend.
DMI advises residents to secure loose outdoor items, including garden furniture and trampolines, before the strongest winds arrive.
The institute also recommends clearing leaves from gutters and drains to help prevent problems during heavy rainfall.
Wind gusts are expected to weaken Monday, although breezy conditions will continue.
Wanner said the forecast reflects Denmark’s transition into its windier autumn and winter months.
“We are genuinely entering the windy season in Denmark. It is not at all unthinkable that there will be more episodes with storm-like conditions leading up to and throughout the winter,” he said.
DMI will continue monitoring the weather and publishing updated forecasts as the storm approaches.

US warns Gulf states to brace for 'intense' Iran war after midterms
The US has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible short but intense military campaign against Iran following next week's US midterm elections, according to a report published by The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday.
The warnings, delivered through diplomatic and military channels, come as the US and Israel make preparations for renewed strikes against Iran, potentially targeting the country's nuclear facilities and other critical infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on launching another military operation, but is leaning towards a major attack after the 3 November elections, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with his thinking.
The preparations are intended to give Trump military options while Washington continues to pursue an agreement with Tehran.
The US military is transferring an additional Patriot missile defence system from Texas to Israel, according to flight-tracking data and officials familiar with the deployment.
American forces have also relocated personnel from vulnerable military bases across the Middle East, replenished ammunition stockpiles and prepared bombers and fighter aircraft for potential operations.
An additional aircraft carrier strike group and Marine expeditionary unit are expected to join approximately 20 American warships already operating in the region next month, although some vessels could be withdrawn.
Israel has also reportedly identified targets and prepared plans for another military offensive, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continuing to advocate further strikes against Iran.
The White House declined to discuss the reported preparations.
"President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon," it said.
Trump has previously said he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday, he suggested that further developments involving Iran could follow within weeks.
"You'll see Iran in a couple of weeks, if you don't mind," Trump said.
Gulf states face renewed threat
The reported preparations come as Gulf governments attempt to prevent another regional war while confronting the prospect of Iranian retaliation against their territory.
Iran has warned that further American or Israeli attacks would provoke strikes against economic and military targets across the region.
During the previous phase of the war, Iranian missiles and drones targeted American military facilities, diplomatic installations, energy infrastructure and airports in Gulf countries.
Another confrontation could expose Gulf states to renewed attacks at a time when Washington and its regional allies are attempting to replenish missile defence systems depleted during earlier fighting.
Despite extensive American and Israeli bombardment, Iran retains substantial missile capabilities and has reportedly been rebuilding its military arsenal and air defences.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February, with Iranian responding with attacks on what it said were US facilities in the region and closing the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington subsequently intensified economic pressure through sanctions and a naval blockade that have severely restricted Iranian oil exports and international trade.
Renewed diplomatic efforts
The prospect of renewed attacks comes amid diplomatic efforts by regional governments to secure an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have recently participated in high-level consultations with Iranian officials, while other regional mediators have attempted to revive negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme.
However, the talks have made little progress, with Washington insisting on restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities and Tehran maintaining its own conditions for negotiations.
The International Atomic Energy Agency said on Tuesday that it had identified no evidence of reconstruction at Iranian nuclear facilities damaged during previous American and Israeli attacks.
However, agency chief Rafael Grossi warned that inspectors had been unable to access the damaged sites or verify the status of Iran's nuclear material.
Analysts have also questioned whether further military action would compel Tehran to make concessions, warning that renewed attacks could instead strengthen Iran's determination to rebuild its military capabilities.
The reported American preparations therefore leave Gulf governments confronting the possibility of another major regional conflict, even as diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed fighting continue.

articles.title: EU, US, allies urge North Korea to abandon nuclear, missile programs
articles.body:
Burak Bir
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
A group of countries including the US, the UK, Japan as well as the EU on Wednesday reiterated their demand for North Korea to abandon its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs and urged all UN member states to fully implement sanctions.
In a statement, the EU, the US, Canada, the UK, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Japan, Australia, New Zealand,and South Korea reaffirmed their commitment to the "complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization" of North Korea.
The statement noted that the EU, Australia and the US implemented sanctions in October to target North Korea’s "use of overseas workers, malicious cyber activities, and actors involved in unlawful DPRK (North Korea)-Russia cooperation."
"Their actions represent their efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s ability to support its unlawful development of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missiles, and to counter unlawful DPRK-Russia military cooperation," it added.
The statement said the designations build on detailed reporting published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), which monitors and reports on North Korea's non-compliance with UN Security Council resolutions.
"The MSMT and EU reaffirm our commitment to the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the DPRK, calling on it to abandon its unlawful WMD and ballistic missile programs, and taking action to counter DPRK attempts to violate and evade UN sanctions."
It added: "We continue to strongly support the implementation of all DPRK-related UN Security Council resolutions."
The signatories also urged all UN member states, especially permanent members of the Security Council, to fully implement the resolutions.

articles.title: F-16 Jets to Add Startup Castelion’s Hypersonic ‘Blackbeard’ Missile
articles.body:
The Air Force has awarded Castelion, a venture capital-backed defense startup founded in 2022, a contract to integrate its hypersonic Blackbeard missile onto the F-16 Fighting Falcon.
The announcement, which came from the company via social media on Oct. 26, marks a major advancement in the Air Force’s work on hypersonic munitions.
Neither the Air Force Research Laboratory, which awarded the contract, nor Castelion immediately responded to a request for comment.
The same day, the service awarded a $694 million contract to Lockheed Martin, a longtime defense prime, to begin production of the hypersonic Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
The Blackbeard missile has drawn strong interest across the Pentagon, with the Navy pushing to field the rocket-powered, boost-glide strike weapon with a nearly 500-mile strike range on the sea service’s F/A-18 Super Hornet.
Navy Development
The Navy’s Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 used the Super Hornet to conduct carriage and separation tests of Blackbeard on Sept. 18 at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Md., which validated the weapon’s compatibility and flightworthiness on the aircraft.
The service selected Blackbeard as the winner in its Multimission Affordable Capacity Effector program, which shifted it to a program of record under framework contract orders of up to $200 million.
The company won a $105 million contract to integrate the missile on the F/A-18 Super Hornet in April.
The MACE initiative sought an affordable hypersonic missile about the size of an AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missile.
In June, the service awarded the company its first production contract, worth $23.4 million, for 50 early operational capability pre-production prototype Blackbeard missiles.
Subsequent delivery orders from the Navy aim to speed up Blackbeard pre-production prototypes to EOC status and field the low-cost hypersonic weapon.
USAF Spending and Development
For its part, the Air Force has spent nearly $21 million to date on Blackbeard research and development, and AFRL added $16.4 million in a September contract modification for the missile.
Those dollars cover development through June 2028 under current spending and contractual agreements.
The USAF contract modification also pursues compatibility with the F-35A.
While the F-35 is the services’ main fifth-generation tactical fighter, the F-16, like the Navy’s workhorse Super Hornet, are workhorse fourth-gen fighters that can carry more munitions without worrying about compromising stealthy characteristics.
The Air Force has more than 600 F-16s in the fleet and recently moved forward with plans to upgrade the decades-old software system for those crucial aircraft, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
The Big Picture
The Air Force now has a three-pronged approach to hypersonic munitions.
These include Castelion’s Blackbeard, an air-to-air missile; the Lockheed Martin AGM-183A ARRW, a strategic strike-focused, exquisite, long-range hypersonic missile; and the Raytheon/Northrop Grumman Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile, a cruise missile option to strike ground or maritime targets.
ARRW successfully completed booster and All-Up-Round tests and is poised to add terminal seeker and data-link integration for moving-target tracking in its Increment 2 tests. The strategic strike missile is envisioned for the B-52 Stratofortress and B-1B Lancer.
The AHM-4A HACM is built for internal or external carriage and geared for both fighter and bomber use to add high-volume magazine depth to the fleet. The missile achieved milestone flight tests over an undisclosed Australian range in late September, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. Initial operational delivery of HACMs is slated for 2027.
Additionally, AFRL recently posted a request for white papers on developing a more advanced hypersonic rocket engine for its current and future munitions dubbed the Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine.
If successful, the more affordable, mass-produced engine could extend ranges, increase speed, and up the payload for future hypersonic, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.

articles.title: Israeli firm turned Starlink traffic into espionage tool across 105 countries
articles.body:
Israeli firm turned Starlink traffic into espionage tool across 105 countries
Netanyahu loses his majority, Eisenkot cannot win one, and the wars go on
TEHRAN — Recent disclosures from digital defense watchdogs have exposed an obscure Tel Aviv-registered advertising company, Discover-Tech, running aggressive online ad campaigns designed to geolocate and track users of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network across more than 100 countries.
Investigative research by TrendAI, a division of Tokyo-based Trend Micro, revealed that Discover-Tech became the dominant global bidder for ad space displayed to Starlink terminals, according to a Reuters report on Oct. 27.
Operating under the internal threat codenamed "Shadow-Earth-79," the Israeli firm captured an implausibly high share of ad auctions in restricted or conflict-heavy jurisdictions including Syria, Libya, Yemen, South Sudan, and Venezuela.
By harvesting the metadata embedded in real-time bidding requests, Discover-Tech systematically turned routine browser traffic into an active intelligence pipeline.
From ad impressions to silent infiltration
Programmatic ad auctions rely on instant exchanges of telemetry. Every time an advertisement loads on a web page or mobile application, a bid request transmits the user's IP address, device model, software configuration, autonomous system number, and exact location parameters to participating ad networks.
Discover-Tech leveraged this routine infrastructure to build a comprehensive tracking map.
TrendAI concluded that the firm’s bidding behavior reflected a dedicated tracking operation rather than commercial marketing, noting that legitimate Western advertising demand in heavily sanctioned states is virtually non-existent.
On observed Starlink connections, Discover-Tech accounted for nearly 13 percent of winning ad bids worldwide.
The surveillance mechanism went far beyond passive location mapping. Concurrent technical investigations by Canada’s Citizen Lab and ad-security firm Confiant exposed a sophisticated exploitation vector named "AdFection."
Discover-Tech's proprietary ad platform served as a conduit, connecting mainstream advertising exchanges directly to mercenary spyware operators. When a targeted device loaded a background advertisement, Discover-Tech servers screened the incoming telemetry.
High-value targets were served malicious JavaScript that delivered zero-click attack payloads without requiring any user interaction, while ordinary users received empty responses.
Citizen Lab confirmed with high confidence that at least 45 devices belonging to news personnel at Al Jazeera were targeted with Candiru spyware through this ad-driven vector.
Starlink and the military-industrial infrastructure
The focus on Starlink underscores how low-Earth-orbit satellite constellations have become central to Western military strategy and intelligence operations.
SpaceX's Starlink network bypasses land-based telecommunications gateways, routing data through satellite links to circumvent national regulatory frameworks and local internet blocks.
The U.S. Department of "War" and NATO forces have integrated Starlink and its military-grade derivative, Starshield, into frontline combat operations. In Ukraine, the technology provides primary battlefield command architecture, directing artillery, facilitating real-time satellite coordination, and guiding long-range combat drones.
This deep integration into Western military operations makes Starlink terminals prime targets for intelligence agencies.
Intelligence outfits seek to identify, geolocate, and compromise satellite terminals operating inside sensitive sovereign territory.
Israeli-owned firms were already pitching commercial clients on specialized methodologies to map and deanonymize Starlink subscribers by exploiting commercial ad data.
The Discover-Tech operation confirms that these theoretical pitches were already operationalized at a global scale, turning satellite terminals into beacons for military intelligence gathering.
The broader ecosystem of Israeli cyber warfare
Discover-Tech represents the latest evolution of a commercial cyber-arms ecosystem cultivated by the Israeli regime.
For decades, intelligence entities such as Unit 8200 and Mossad have maintained an institutional pipeline into private surveillance vendors, enabling former Israeli operatives to commercialize state-funded hacking techniques.
Discover-Tech’s corporate history shows direct ties to veteran surveillance executives, including past directors associated with Circles, an affiliate of NSO Group, and Senpai Technologies, linked to the Intellexa consortium.
This ecosystem includes a wide network of offensive vendors. NSO Group gained global infamy through its Pegasus software, which infected the phones of diplomats, political opponents, and human rights defenders.
Candiru, operating under various corporate names such as Saito Tech and Integrity Labs, specialized in zero-click desktop compromises. Paragon Solutions markets its Graphite interception software, while Intellexa and Cytrox developed the Predator spyware suite.
Other key players include Cognyte, Cytrox, Cellebrite, and Black Cube, the private intelligence agency staffed by former Israeli operatives specializing in deception and corporate espionage.
These entities routinely establish international shell companies across Europe to bypass nominal export restrictions and maintain access to global markets.
Industry self-censorship and structural vulnerability
Despite the scale of Discover-Tech’s operations, accountability remains hindered by self-censorship within the commercial security sector.
TrendAI initially omitted Discover-Tech’s name from its public report, opting instead for the "Shadow-Earth-79" alias after corporate executives raised legal concerns.
This practice allows offensive operators to evade immediate platform bans and legal scrutiny.
Following the public identification by Citizen Lab and news outlets, major tech platforms including Google, Comcast's Beeswax, Vungle, and Eskimi cut off Discover-Tech’s access, while IAB Europe suspended the firm from its approved vendor list.
Internal inquiries were also launched by a major U.S. technology corporation and an international organization to evaluate potential employee targeting.
These platform removals disrupt specific operational routes, but the underlying vulnerability remains unaddressed.
Discover-Tech operated inside approved industry registries for years, utilizing standard European data privacy frameworks to collect targeting parameters.
As long as commercial advertising exchanges permit real-time data harvesting, state-aligned surveillance contractors will continue to use programmatic ad bidding as an unregulated, low-cost vector for global espionage.

articles.title: Hegseth and Koizumi agree on new Japanese missile production line
articles.body:
- Japan and the United States agreed on Oct. 28 to build an AMRAAM air-to-air missile final assembly plant in Japan.
- Defense chiefs Shinjiro Koizumi and Pete Hegseth also agreed to share technical data to expand SM-3 Block IIA interceptor production.
Japan will host a final assembly plant for the AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missile after Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth agreed on Oct. 28 to build the facility as part of joint U.S.-Japanese missile production, Nikkei reported.
The two met for about 30 minutes in Cebu, the Philippines, on the sidelines of an expanded meeting of Southeast Asian defense ministers. The facility, known as a final assembly and check-out plant, or FACO, is where completed components are put together into finished missiles and tested before delivery, Financial News reported, citing the Asahi Shimbun and NHK. Hegseth welcomed Japan’s work to strengthen its defense production base, and the two sides also agreed to expand joint exercises, including live-fire drills.
The ministers also agreed to share technical information to expand production of the SM-3 Block IIA, a ship-launched interceptor that destroys ballistic missiles in space, Nikkei reported. The Japanese side said Hegseth did not press for a specific increase in Japan’s defense budget, and the Defense Ministry said the talks were not held with any particular amount or outcome in mind.
The AMRAAM is a radar-guided missile that fighters fire at enemy aircraft beyond visual range, and it guides itself to the target after launch, so the pilot can turn away or engage another threat. It arms U.S. and allied F-15, F-16, F/A-18, F-22 and F-35 fighters, including the F-35s that Japan is buying, and it also serves as the main interceptor for the ground-based NASAMS air defense system. Raytheon builds the missile in the United States and in February agreed with the U.S. Department of War to raise annual AMRAAM production to at least 1,900.
The plant would take a years-long effort a step further. The United States and Japan first agreed in July 2024 to explore joint production of the AMRAAM and the PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptor, and Japan’s Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency then ran a feasibility study with Mitsubishi Electric and Raytheon. In April, the two governments identified circuit card assembly, the production of the missile’s electronic boards, as part of Japan’s share, with a final assembly plant in Japan raised as a possibility, Mitsubishi Electric said. Japan is also a major AMRAAM customer: in January 2025, the U.S. State Department approved the sale of up to 1,200 AIM-120D-3 and AIM-120C-8 missiles to Japan, valued at an estimated $3.64 billion.
The SM-3 Block IIA has a longer history as a shared program. Raytheon and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries developed it jointly, and it entered full-rate production in 2024. In March, the two governments agreed to quadruple production of the interceptor in Japan, and Japan now pays for a large share of new orders, covering nearly half the immediate funding in a $745 million contract for SM-3 Block IIA missiles awarded this summer.
During the meeting, Koizumi briefed Hegseth on Japan’s plan to revise its three main national security documents by the end of 2026. He said Japan would strengthen what it calls denial defense, the ability to stop an invading force from succeeding, along with deterrence intended to discourage an attack in the first place. The ministers also agreed to step up cooperation against cyberattacks, The Japan Times reported.

articles.title: Russian troops liberate two communities in Ukraine operation over past day — top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated two communities in the Kharkov and Sumy Regions over the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units liberated the settlements of Alisovka in the Kharkov Region and Barilovka in the Sumy Region through active operations," the ministry said in a statement.
Kiev loses 1,160 troops along engagement line in past day - latest figures
The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,160 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 195 troops and six motor vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, more than 240 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and over 155 troops and two armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost over 335 troops and nine armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, more than 215 troops and two armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and roughly 20 troops and a jamming station in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 195 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 195 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed six enemy motor vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade and an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Izbitskoye, Stary Saltov, Bugayevka and Rubezhnoye in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.
In the Sumy direction, Battlegroup North units struck formations of a mechanized brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Luzhki and Sukhodol in the Sumy Region, it said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 195 personnel and six motor vehicles in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 240 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 240 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup West units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades in areas near the settlements of Glushchenkovo, Studenok, Monachinovka and Smorodkovka in the Kharkov Region and Bogorodichnoye in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 240 personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 15 motor vehicles, two field artillery guns, a Grad multiple rocket launcher and six electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it said.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 155 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 155 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed two enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup South units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on formations of a mechanized brigade, an air assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Semyonovka, Slavyansk, Kamyshevakha and Kramatorsk in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 155 personnel, two armored combat vehicles, 31 motor vehicles and three artillery guns in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 335 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 335 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed nine enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Center units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades of the Ukrainian army, two marine infantry brigades and two National Guard brigades in areas near the settlements of Belozerskoye, Bokovoye, Kalinino, Shilovka and Viktorovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic, Ivanovka and Novopavlovka in the Dnepropetrovsk Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 335 personnel, nine armored combat vehicles, 10 motor vehicles and two electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 215 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 215 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed two enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup East units advanced into the depth of the enemy’s defenses and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two air assault brigades, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Berestovoye, Novoukrainka, Tersyanka and Sergeyevka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 215 personnel, two armored combat vehicles, seven motor vehicles and an artillery gun in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 20 Ukrainian troops in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 20 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy jamming station in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on formations of a mechanized brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Orekhov and Preobrazhenka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
"Up to 20 Ukrainian military personnel, five motor vehicles and an electronic warfare station were destroyed," it said.
Russian troops strike energy, transport sites used by Ukrainian army in past day
Russian troops struck energy and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army and enemy deployment areas over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck energy and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, ammunition depots, workshops producing and sites storing unmanned aerial vehicles, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 142 locations," the ministry said.
Russian air defenses intercept 617 Ukrainian UAVs, two Neptune missiles over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 617 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and two Neptune missiles over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down two Neptune long-range missiles and 617 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 273,040 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,439 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,794 multiple rocket launchers, 36,830 field artillery guns and mortars and 75,823 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

articles.title: Italy puts Ukraine weapons package on hold – media
articles.body:
Italy puts Ukraine weapons package on hold – media
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has put a major new weapons package for Ukraine on hold until after the US midterm elections, according to La Repubblica. The move comes as her ruling coalition faces mounting resistance to arming Kiev.
The long-delayed 13th military aid package remains stuck despite repeated assurances that Rome will continue to support Ukraine, the Italian outlet reported on Tuesday. Initially expected in July, the shipment was pushed back to September, then delayed again, with a decision now potentially postponed until after the November 3 US congressional elections.
La Repubblica noted that the delay has cast doubt on whether Meloni will deliver on promises made to French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to send more Aster 30 interceptor missiles for Kiev’s SAMP/T air defense systems by the end of October.
The Italian parliamentary intelligence committee has yet to review the decree authorizing the shipment, while Rome continues to declare its support for Ukraine without specifying when the weapons will be delivered.
Earlier this week, Italian media reported that Meloni’s government is split over further arms supplies to Kiev. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, leader of the League party, has opposed further weapons deliveries, while Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti, also from the League, has reportedly resisted signing off on the package. In December 2025, Tajani rejected Italy’s immediate participation in the US-led PURL scheme, under which NATO members bankroll American weapons for Kiev, citing ongoing peace talks. “If we reach an agreement and the fighting stops, weapons will no longer be needed,” he said.
Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and Defense Minister Guido Crosetto, meanwhile, have pushed for continued military assistance, leaving Meloni caught between her government’s commitments to Kiev and opposition from a key coalition partner.
According to La Repubblica, Rome is also holding off on further arms deliveries until the US midterms, which could strip President Donald Trump’s Republicans of their control of Congress. The November 3 vote will determine control of both chambers, with Democrats leading Republicans 53% to 44% in an October 22-26 Reuters/Ipsos poll. The delay could stretch even further as Italy heads toward its own elections in 2027. Silver Bulletin’s October 27 forecast also indicated that Democrats were strongly positioned to retake the House, while the Senate remained less certain.
Public opposition to arming Kiev is growing in Italy. A September Termometro Politico poll found that 55.4% of Italians opposed further weapons shipments, against 38.8% in favor. Ukraine’s EU membership bid has also split opinion, with a May survey showing 32% backing eastward enlargement and 26% opposed.
Russia has warned that Western weapons deliveries to Ukraine prolong the conflict and obstruct peace efforts. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has accused European countries of fueling the fighting, while Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has warned that any shipments carrying foreign arms into Ukraine would be considered legitimate military targets.

articles.title: Alliance response must be credible if Russia uses nuclear weapons, former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy says
articles.body:
Alliance response must be credible if Russia uses nuclear weapons, former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy says
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023–2025), made the remarks in an interview with Ukrinform.
“In this hypothetical situation, if Russia uses nuclear weapons, NATO will have to respond... The response must be credible,” Stokes said.
He recalled NATO’s stated readiness to inflict damage far exceeding any potential gains. The response could involve nuclear weapons, conventional weapons, or a combination of both. The decision would be made at a later stage, as it would be unwise to reveal to an adversary where these red lines lie or exactly how a response might be formulated and carried out, the former NATO official emphasized.
Stokes said that in an emergency or during a crisis, the Alliance could make political decisions and implement them very quickly. He added that member states were also capable of acting independently and swiftly. The United States, the United Kingdom, and France could each independently employ their nuclear forces to deter aggression against the Alliance, not just a nuclear attack. Stokes described this as a major advantage for NATO.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and NATO’s designation of Russia as a threat to the Alliance, NATO has been adapting its nuclear deterrence posture, including by modernizing its nuclear forces. Exercises and preparations for a potential NATO nuclear operation demonstrate that the Alliance is capable of carrying one out effectively with its current capabilities and force posture, the former official said.
He noted that NATO aircraft could deliver free-fall nuclear bombs. Some advocate the option of launching missiles from sea-, land-, or air-based platforms. In Stokes’s view, all options should remain on the table.
As previously reported, British and French fighter jets conducted joint exercises over the Mediterranean for the first time in October, involving French nuclear forces and demonstrating deeper defense cooperation between the two countries amid tensions with Russia. In July 2025, the two countries agreed to deepen their cooperation on nuclear deterrence in response to growing threats to Europe and uncertainty over the role of the United States as an ally.

articles.title: US warns Gulf states of possible military action after November 3 — WSJ
articles.body:
NEW YORK, October 28. /TASS/. The United States has warned several Persian Gulf countries of a possible "short, intense military campaign" against Iran following the November 3 midterm congressional elections, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, citing sources.
According to the report, the Pentagon has evacuated US military personnel from Middle Eastern bases where they could be at risk, US forces in the region are replenishing their ammunition stockpiles, and bombers and fighter jets are preparing to carry out strikes.
The Wall Street Journal reported that US President Donald Trump has not yet made a final decision on resuming military operations but is leaning toward launching a large-scale attack after the elections, potentially targeting Iranian infrastructure and nuclear facilities.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing Tehran of violating the terms of the agreements concerning the Strait of Hormuz. Approximately 25% of global oil trade and around 20% of global liquefied natural gas trade pass through the strait. The US administration subsequently effectively signaled an end to the use of large-scale military force against Iran and a shift toward attempting to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

articles.title: German special forces preparing for war with Russia – commander
articles.body:
German special forces preparing for war with Russia – commander
Germany’s elite special forces are preparing for a potential large-scale war with Russia, the unit’s commander told Bild. The remarks come amid tensions between Moscow and NATO over the Ukraine conflict, with German officials warning that the armed forces must be ready for a confrontation by the end of the decade.
The highly secretive unit, known as Kommando Spezialkrafte (KSK), is comparable to Britain’s SAS or the US Green Berets. According to a report from its base in southwestern Germany published on Monday, the commandos are adjusting their training to counter Russian forces equipped with tanks, artillery, drones, and electronic warfare capabilities, including in extreme cold.
“We are orienting ourselves very specifically toward the adversary Russia,” KSK Commander Brigadier General Andreas Kuhne said, adding that his soldiers would have to be prepared to “remain in the field much longer,” potentially “with no end in sight,” if war broke out.
Kuhne also said the unit is preparing to carry out missions before conventional German forces enter combat. “When the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania starts its engines in a real emergency, we want to have already completed our job,” he told Bild.
According to the newspaper, only around a third of the KSK’s 1,500 personnel are commandos, while the rest serve in administrative and support roles.
The unit has been rocked by a series of far-right extremism scandals in recent years. In 2017, an investigation was launched following reports that soldiers performed Nazi salutes and listened to far-right music, among other things.
In 2018, investigations exposed an underground far-right network involving German military and security personnel, some of whom allegedly discussed plans to kill political opponents in the event of a breakdown of public order.
In 2020, police discovered a large cache of weapons, ammunition, explosives, and Nazi memorabilia at the property of a KSK sergeant major. Some of the ammunition was suspected of being stolen from German military stockpiles.
The scandals prompted then-Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer to disband one of the KSK’s four commando companies, the 2nd Company, and introduce sweeping reforms. The special forces command itself remained operational.
Speaking to Bild, Kuhne said disciplinary and conduct-related incidents within the unit have become “extremely rare,” but have not disappeared entirely, insisting that misconduct would no longer be tolerated or covered up.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to transform the German armed forces into Europe’s strongest conventional military force in response to what he describes as threats from Russia. His government has prioritized defense spending and military assistance to Ukraine despite acknowledging that the German economy is in a “structural crisis.”
In July, The Telegraph and Die Welt reported that Berlin was preparing a secret plan to override potential resistance from regional governments to the deployment of NATO troops toward Russia’s borders.
Merz’s military ambitions come amid declining public support for his government. According to an INSA poll published by Bild this week, the chancellor ranked last among 20 prominent German politicians. The surging opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) won state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September, while the socialist Left Party (Die Linke) emerged as the largest party in Berlin’s election.
Russia has denied that it plans to attack NATO countries. In August, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed reports that Moscow intends to attack NATO members as “scare stories” that have “nothing to do with reality.”

articles.title: Houthis say deadly Saudi strikes hit Yemen as they target Aden
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis say deadly Saudi strikes hit Yemen as they target Aden
Yemen's Houthis said Saudi strikes on a petrol station and a market killed more than a dozen people on Wednesday, while the Iran-backed group targeted the airport in government stronghold Aden, wounding several civilians.
The Houthis last month launched a lightning offensive in Yemen, reigniting a long frozen civil war against the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government there.
They have also launched sustained attacks on Saudi Arabia itself, the world's biggest crude exporter, rattling global markets already volatile from the wider Middle East war.
On Wednesday, Houthi broadcaster Almasirah reported 14 dead "and 15 wounded, including women and children in a preliminary toll", in attacks it blamed on Saudi Arabia in the northwestern Jawf province, where it reported strikes on a market and a petrol station.
In Aden, two ballistic missiles struck the perimeter of the airport, leaving several civilians wounded and causing damage, government forces spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili said on X.
He blamed the Houthis for the attack, describing it as "the sixth such attack on the airport".
A local police source told AFP that one missile fell inside the airport perimeter shortly before the Houthis issued a warning for people to evacuate the area.
"Our armed forces call on those present at Aden airport to immediately evacuate due to the presence of a military cargo plane belonging to the Saudi enemy transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Telegram.
The first strike happened while a Saudi military aircraft was at the airport, but the plane "was not hit and took off shortly afterward", the first police source said.
The second attack targeted an area "under Saudi forces' control inside the perimeter of Aden airport", the second Aden police official said.
Both sources spoke on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.

articles.title: The Israeli election hurt Netanyahu, but the country is still stuck
articles.body:
The Israeli election hurt Netanyahu, but the country is still stuck
The parliamentary elections in Israel were a major test of public confidence in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israelis went to the polls in the aftermath of the events of October 7, 2023, the wars in Gaza and Lebanon, the confrontation with Iran, and increasingly strained relations with several international partners. The composition of the next government will decide the direction of Israel’s political and strategic development.
Turnout was exceptionally high – the Central Elections Committee put it at 77.7%, the highest since 1999. The main contest unfolded between Netanyahu’s Likud party and an opposition camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the centrist Yashar party. His potential allies include the parties of Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid (who had shared a rotating premiership in 2021-22), and other parties opposed to the incumbent coalition.
According to updated exit polls conducted by three major TV networks, the opposition bloc is projected to secure 47 seats, Netanyahu’s allies 54, and Arab parties outside either camp 19. Likud nevertheless remains the largest individual party, while other projections are more favorable to the right-wing bloc. The official results are expected to be published on November 4. For now, one thing is evident: Neither side has secured a clear parliamentary majority.
Political mobilization
The turnout reflects a profound political mobilization within Israeli society. Over the past several years, decisions made by the leadership have become increasingly intertwined with questions of personal security, economic well-being, and the future of individual families. As a result, even citizens who previously remained relatively disengaged from politics have become more actively involved.
The events of October 7, 2023 were the decisive catalyst for this transformation. The failure of the national security system severely undermined confidence in the political leadership, and the subsequent wars failed to produce lasting national unity around the government. Instead, they intensified questions of political accountability, the human and economic costs of military decisions, and the absence of a convincing strategy for ending the conflicts. Even supporters of a hardline security approach have grown disillusioned with its effectiveness.
Socioeconomic pressures have also played an important role. Rising military expenditure, the high cost of living, housing difficulties, and prolonged reserve military service have shown the people the price of continuing instability. Particularly contentious has been the exemption of sections of the ultra-Orthodox community from military service, while other segments of society bear the burden.
Israel’s deteriorating international standing has further compounded these challenges. Disagreements with traditional European partners over the war in Gaza, developments in the West Bank, and the policies pursued by far-right members of the government are leaving the country with less and less room for diplomatic maneuvers. Some voters increasingly blame the government for growing diplomatic isolation and economic risks.
The high turnout was not just against Netanyahu. Right-wing voters were also highly mobilized, as was the Arab electorate, whose parties achieved a notable result. Nevertheless, the elections suggest that the existing political situation is no longer widely seen as sustainable.
The coalition struggle
In Israeli politics, electoral success does not necessarily translate into political power. In the 120-seat Knesset, a governing coalition requires the support of at least 61 members, a threshold that neither of the two main political camps is so far projected to reach. The decisive struggle will now move to negotiations between parties.
After the official results are released, President Isaac Herzog will consult parliamentary factions and entrust the task of forming a government to the candidate considered most capable of securing a majority. The initial period for coalition negotiations is 28 days, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. If these efforts fail, another member of the Knesset may be given 28 days to form a government. Subsequently, members of parliament would have 21 days to nominate an alternative candidate with the support of at least 61 legislators, who would then receive a further 14 days to complete the process. Should this final attempt also fail, the Knesset would be dissolved and new elections called.
Under these circumstances, smaller parties have far more power than their number of seats would suggest. In exchange for supporting a coalition, they may demand ministerial appointments, budgetary commitments, and significant policy concessions. Netanyahu’s camp will have to seek additional support beyond its traditional allies, while the opposition faces the difficult task of reconciling the positions of centrists, right-wing opponents of Netanyahu, and more liberal parties.
Arab parties, which are projected to hold 19 seats, could become particularly important. Eisenkot and some of his potential coalition partners, however, have ruled out including them in the government. External parliamentary support or abstention during a confidence vote could theoretically alter the balance, but this would require politically sensitive compromises from the centrist camp.
Netanyahu’s extensive experience in coalition-building gives him considerable opportunities to negotiate with smaller parties and persuade individual political actors to abandon competing alliances. Even if he fails to assemble a majority, he will remain in office as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. His political position has undoubtedly weakened, but this does not yet amount to his removal from power.
The Netanyahu factor
Netanyahu entered these elections with a loyal electoral base intact, but with substantially weakened support beyond the right-wing camp. National security has always been his central political argument. Yet the consequences of October 7 and the prolonged military campaigns have seriously damaged his reputation, raising questions about the effectiveness of his leadership.
With this in mind, reports of preparations for a new military operation against Iran shortly before the elections deserve particular attention. Axios reported on discussions between Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump, the Financial Times described preparations for a large-scale strike in early October, and CNN reported on Israeli efforts to secure American support. According to these accounts, the Trump administration prefers to avoid another major escalation ahead of the US elections scheduled for November 3. Netanyahu denied reports that Trump prevented a planned Israeli attack, and some of the reported details have also been disputed by Israeli media.
A swift and successful military operation against Iran could have unified a substantial part of society around Likud, restored Netanyahu’s image as a decisive defender of national security, and pushed criticism of his domestic policies into the background. While this does not prove that a strike was being planned for electoral purposes, the potential political benefits are obvious.
On the other hand, a short war against Iran would have been an extremely risky gamble. Iranian retaliation, the involvement of Tehran’s regional allies, additional pressure on Israel’s missile defense systems, and potential disruption of global energy markets could have produced another crisis of public confidence. The combination of American constraints and unpredictable military consequences appears to have prevented this from happening before the election.
Ultimately, the election took place without a major military development capable of fundamentally shifting votes. Should Netanyahu remain in power, the most likely outcome would be the continuation of his hardline approach towards Iran and aligned armed groups. Continued dependence on far-right coalition partners could push this policy in an even more confrontational direction. Even so, Israel would still have to take Washington’s position into account, given the importance of American support for major military operations.
The Eisenkot alternative
Gadi Eisenkot, who served as chief of the General Staff of the Israel Defense Forces from 2015 to 2019, has emerged as Netanyahu’s principal political alternative. His main advantage lies in offering a change of leadership without abandoning the centrality of national security. For voters dissatisfied with the incumbent prime minister but unwilling to embrace a fundamental ideological shift, this is an appealing compromise. Eisenkot presents himself as a centrist, institutionally minded political figure with extensive experience in military leadership.
Particular emphasis in his political program is placed on soldiers, reservists, and their families. His party has proposed expanding housing, tax, and education benefits, increasing social assistance, and raising the remuneration of conscripts by 15%, with a 50% increase for combat soldiers in their third year of service. These proposals have the potential to attract military families that have long demanded more equitable social protection. It would, however, be an exaggeration to suggest that Israel’s entire security establishment supports a single candidate.
Another important part of Eisenkot’s electoral base consists of citizens disillusioned with the governing coalition’s style of leadership, its disputes with state institutions, and its dependence on far-right parties. Eisenkot promises to restore confidence in government, broaden the principle of compulsory military or national service, and reduce divisions within society. His political appeal is centered on effective governance rather than ideological transformation.
On the Palestinian question, however, fundamental changes are unlikely. Eisenkot opposes the establishment of a fully independent Palestinian state under present conditions and insists on maintaining Israeli control over essential security matters. Although some Jewish parties support the two-state solution, the core of a new coalition would most likely consist of nationally oriented parties. Nevertheless, Eisenkot’s criticism of illegal settlement outposts and settler violence suggests that a change in political methods is possible.
There is much more room for change in foreign policy. A departure from a government of far-right politicians whose rhetoric has complicated Israel’s relations with European partners and Arab states could, in itself, help reduce diplomatic tensions. A more pragmatic cabinet would have the opportunity to restore working relationships, ease Israel’s international isolation, and pursue a gradual normalization of relations across the region.
However, a more restrained diplomatic approach should not be mistaken for the abandonment of military deterrence. Eisenkot regards Iran’s nuclear program, its missile capabilities, and its network of regional allies as serious threats to national security. Under his leadership, Israel would likely maintain a firm policy of containment while seeking closer coordination with Washington and a more balanced combination of military and diplomatic instruments. This approach could reduce certain risks, but it would not eliminate the underlying confrontation.
The main dilemma emerging from the election is that many Israelis who voted against Netanyahu expect greater stability and a reduction in regional tensions, yet the country’s security environment and the positions of opposition leaders themselves impose significant constraints on any rapid political compromise. Eisenkot could change the style of governance and improve the atmosphere of Israel’s relations with the outside world, but he cannot guarantee peace. Netanyahu, by contrast, would be more likely to continue along the current path.
Until the official results are published and coalition negotiations concluded, it is impossible to predict with confidence who will become the next prime minister. The elections have nevertheless exposed profound public fatigue with a prolonged period of crisis and the absence of a clear political mandate for overcoming it.
The ultimate outcome will determine far more than the composition of the next government. It may also shape the future trajectory of the entire Middle East, influencing whether the region moves towards a period of cautious stabilization or enters another phase of escalating confrontation.

articles.title: US-Iran war bill reaches $47.1 billion
articles.body:
US-Iran war bill reaches $47.1 billion
TEHRAN — The cost of the US war against Iran reached an estimated $47.1 billion by October 16, with bombs, missiles and other munitions accounting for more than 60% of the total, according to figures the Pentagon provided to US lawmakers, The New York Times reported.
The estimate, disclosed to congressional national security committees last week, highlights the mounting financial burden of the military campaign launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on February 28, as well as the pressure on American weapons inventories and military resources.
Despite US President Donald Trump holding back, at least for the time being, from resuming major combat operations, the Pentagon incurred an additional $3.5 billion in costs over approximately six weeks, compared with the estimates previously shared with Congress.
The figures provide an unusual, unclassified breakdown of the expenses incurred by the US armed services, including the costs of deploying forces, maintaining military operations, replacing damaged equipment and transporting supplies.
However, congressional officials cautioned that the $47.1 billion estimate does not represent the full financial cost of the war, with several significant expenditures still excluded from the Pentagon’s accounting.
Munitions account for $29 billion
According to the figures cited by The New York Times, the US military has spent approximately $29 billion on munitions since the war began, making bombs, missiles and other weapons the largest component of the reported expenditure.
The extensive use of ammunition has depleted global inventories of several critical weapons, including Patriot air-defense interceptors, while supplies have also been diverted from US military commands in Europe and Asia to support operations related to the war.
The scale of the expenditure raises questions about the sustainability of prolonged high-intensity military operations and the resources required to replenish depleted stockpiles.
The Pentagon has also spent $6.1 billion replacing dozens of damaged or destroyed combat aircraft, weapons systems, and other military equipment.
These replacement costs illustrate how the financial burden extends beyond the direct expenditure on weapons used in combat to include the loss of valuable military assets.
Air Force, Navy and Army face mounting costs
The Pentagon’s breakdown shows that the US Air Force has spent approximately $7.6 billion operating dozens of fighter and bomber squadrons involved in the military mission.
The Navy has incurred around $1.5 billion in costs associated with deploying more than two dozen warships, including several aircraft carriers, while maintaining Army forces in the region has cost approximately $2.1 billion.
According to US Central Command, more than 50,000 American troops are assigned to the war mission.
The figures also reveal additional expenditures on specialized military operations and logistical support. The Pentagon has spent $645 million to deploy and sustain several thousand Special Operations personnel in the region.
US Transportation Command has incurred $92.2 million in costs for moving supplies and equipment, while US Cyber Command has spent $14 million on cyber support operations.
A congressional official, speaking anonymously to discuss information provided to lawmakers, also disclosed that $24.5 million had been spent on internal medical support for US service members.
The Pentagon has reported that 18 American service members have been killed and more than 860 injured in the war.
Official estimate excludes major expenses
Despite the scale of the reported spending, congressional officials said the actual cost of the war was almost certainly higher than the Pentagon’s estimate.
According to The New York Times, the administration’s calculations excluded $1.5 billion in fuel and other expenses that the Trump administration had requested through a supplemental funding proposal intended to cover the war’s costs.
The estimate also did not include the cost of repairing or rebuilding US military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks, including the US Navy’s base in Manama, Bahrain.
The Pentagon has indicated that some damaged facilities could be closed permanently or left unreconstructed. However, if the US military or host countries decide to rebuild them, congressional officials estimate that the bill could reach tens of billions of dollars.
Such expenses could substantially increase the overall financial burden, particularly if Washington decides to restore damaged infrastructure while simultaneously replenishing weapons inventories and maintaining its regional military presence.
The extent of the additional costs remains uncertain, and the figures disclosed so far should therefore be treated as a partial accounting rather than a final assessment of the war’s financial consequences.
Washington seeks up to $70 billion in additional military funding
The disclosure comes as US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Trump administration seek as much as $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the war against Iran and finance additional weapons and personnel.
The request underscores the growing financial demands associated with the campaign, particularly as the Pentagon faces the dual challenge of sustaining military operations and replacing equipment and ammunition already expended or lost.
The unclassified figures provided to Congress offer a rare glimpse into the financial accounting of a war whose costs have largely remained undisclosed by the Pentagon’s senior leadership.
The reported $47.1 billion in spending, combined with excluded fuel costs, potential reconstruction expenses and the administration’s request for additional funding, indicates that the final bill could rise substantially beyond the amount currently acknowledged.
For Washington, the financial consequences extend beyond the immediate costs of military operations to the long-term task of replenishing strategic weapons reserves, restoring damaged facilities and maintaining military readiness across other regions.
The Pentagon has not immediately responded to The New York Times’ request for comment on the figures.
While the final cost of the war remains undetermined, the disclosed estimates highlight the considerable financial resources consumed by the US military campaign and the additional expenditures Washington may face as it addresses the consequences of the conflict.

articles.title: Ethiopia receives 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets, plans to acquire S-400 air defenses
articles.body:
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced Wednesday that Ethiopia has received 12 advanced Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and plans to acquire four S-400 air defense systems, Anadolu reports.
The announcement comes as tensions with neighboring Eritrea and renewed fighting in the northern Tigray region raise fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa.
“Ethiopia’s newly deployed military jets will remain more ready than ever to defend the airspace!” Abiy wrote on US social media platform X.
He said the fighter jets were delivered under an earlier agreement with Moscow, and the S-400 air defense systems are expected to arrive later.
“I would like to express my gratitude to my friend, Russian President Vladimir Putin, for his dedication in ensuring we received these warplanes a year ahead of our agreed schedule,” said Abiy.
He described the acquisitions as a major step toward strengthening Ethiopia’s military capabilities and protecting its sovereignty.
READ: Up to 50,000 flee Ethiopia clashes into Kenya, urgently need aid: UN refugee agency
The Russian multirole combat aircraft is designed for air superiority and ground attack missions. The S-400 is a long-range surface-to-air missile system that can engage aircraft and other aerial threats.
Tensions have heightened between Ethiopia and Eritrea, former allies whose relations have deteriorated because of Addis Ababa’s demand for access to the Red Sea and disagreements on security in northern Ethiopia.
Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and Abiy has repeatedly described maritime access as essential to the country’s economic and security interests.
Renewed fighting in Tigray, where Ethiopian federal forces and rival Tigrayan factions have been engaged in hostilities, has also raised concerns about instability along the Ethiopian-Eritrean border.
The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. Eritrean troops later fought alongside Ethiopian government forces during the 2020-2022 Tigray conflict, but relations have since deteriorated.
