articles.title: Russia showcases submarine-launched ballistic missile (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russia showcases submarine-launched ballistic missile (VIDEO)
A Russian nuclear-powered submarine has successfully test-fired an intercontinental ballistic missile, hitting a target around 6,000 km away on the other side of the country, the Defense Ministry announced on Wednesday.
The Bulava missile was launched from a submerged position by the Generalissimus Suvorov strategic missile submarine in the Far Eastern Sea of Okhotsk, near the Kamchatka Peninsula, as part of a scheduled combat training exercise.
The missile’s warheads reached the designated Chizha test range on the Kanin Peninsula in Russia’s Arkhangelsk Region, 5,500-6,000 km from the launch area. The ministry said monitoring data confirmed that the warheads arrived at their target area on schedule, declaring the exercise a success.
The ministry also released dramatic footage of the launch. The video shows the submarine cruising at sea before cutting to crew members operating control systems inside the vessel. A close-up captures the press of a launch button, followed by a nighttime shot of a blazing missile erupting from the water and streaking skyward.
The R-30 Bulava (NATO designation SS-N-32) is a submarine-launched ballistic missile designed to serve as one of the mainstays of Russia’s sea-based nuclear deterrent. Developed by the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology and officially adopted into service in May 2024, the solid-fuel missile has a reported maximum range of around 9,300 km.
Weighing approximately 37 tons, the Bulava is designed to carry multiple independently targetable nuclear warheads. It also incorporates measures intended to help it penetrate missile defenses, including a relatively short boost phase and maneuverable reentry vehicles.
The Generalissimus Suvorov is a fourth-generation Project 955A Borei-A nuclear-powered submarine assigned to Russia’s Pacific Fleet and based in Kamchatka. Built at the Sevmash shipyard, the vessel can carry up to 16 Bulava ballistic missiles, alongside torpedo armaments.
The Borei and upgraded Borei-A submarines form a key component of Russia’s strategic nuclear modernization program, replacing aging Soviet-era missile carriers. Russia currently operates eight submarines of the two classes, with additional vessels under construction.
Wednesday’s launch was intended to test the crew’s combat readiness and the submarine’s missile systems, according to the Defense Ministry.

articles.title: Iran hasn't tried to repair damaged nuclear facilities: IAEA
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran hasn't tried to repair nuclear facilities damaged in US strikes: IAEA chief
The head of the UN nuclear agency said Tuesday there has been no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli military strikes this year or last year.
President Donald Trump has said one of the major reasons the US went to war with Iran on 28 February was to deny Tehran the ability to develop nuclear weapons, even as he has insisted that strikes the US carried out on Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 "obliterated" the country’s atomic program.
During a UN Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks. The IAEA has not been able to verify the status of Iran's stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the US bombed its sites last year.
Grossi said that "since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026."
Trump has consistently downplayed the economic impact of the Iran war, which has emerged as a liability for Republicans heading into next week’s midterm elections, and has argued that higher fuel prices are worth paying to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran. The White House didn’t immediately respond Tuesday evening to a request for comment on Grossi's remarks.
Iran insists its nuclear program is peaceful. Meanwhile, the IAEA says the country has a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity—a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
The UN meeting on Tuesday was called by Bahrain, Denmark, Latvia, France, the United Kingdom and United States after the IAEA referred Iran to the Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Russia and China, allies of Iran, tried unsuccessfully to prevent the meeting.
Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow IAEA inspectors to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.
Iran's UN deputy ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi attacked the council for its silence after the US-Israeli attacks, denouncing their "wars of aggression against Iran" and noted the US is committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
He added that "Israel possesses nuclear weapons, yet your concern is the absence of inspectors in Iran."
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz called Iran a "brutal dictatorship" and asked if the Iranian ambassador wanted to apologise to Bahrain's envoy, a council member, for attacking his country.
"We've heard tireless allegations against the United States," he said. "What we have not heard today is an explanation for Iran's continued failure to satisfy its safeguard obligations."
The IAEA asked Iran for answers, Waltz said, and it would be smart for the Iranian representative to start providing some answers.
"Your lies are no good here," he said.

articles.title: Kiev changes position on security guarantees amid warming Russia-US ties — FT

LONDON, October 28. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky has for the first time acknowledged Russia's demands for security guarantees amid the deterioration of relations between Kiev and Washington and thawing US-Russia ties, the Financial Times reported.
Kiev is afraid that the United States will completely pull support, while Ukrainian officials continue to complain about not receiving enough missiles and the loss of intelligence-sharing.

articles.title: Vladimir Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian Starlink
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.
The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.
“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”
The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US and Ukraine earlier this month.
A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.
Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.
Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.
“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.
Starlink does not work in Russia and its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.
Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.
Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.
“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.
Earlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.
The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.
John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”
The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.
Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.
Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.

articles.title: German drone maker unveils armed version of its Reliant spy drone

Quantum-Systems has unveiled an armed version of its Reliant long-range drone, showing the aircraft fitted with a mixed load of 82 mm mortar rounds and 40 mm grenades.
Dave Sharpin, chief executive of Quantum-Systems Inc., the U.S. arm of the German drone maker, shared images of the configuration on social media on Oct. 28, thanking partners from Orbital for their work on the project. The photos show the munitions carried on the drone’s wing hardpoints, combining two calibers on a single aircraft.
Each caliber gives the drone a different kind of strike: the 82 mm round, the standard size for medium mortars in many armies, carries a heavier explosive charge suited to larger targets, while the 40 mm grenade, the size fired by infantry grenade launchers, is smaller and lighter, so several can be carried and released one at a time against individual targets. Mixing the two lets an operator choose the right weapon for each target found during the same flight.
Reliant is a fixed-wing drone that takes off and lands vertically, so it can launch from a small clearing or a ship deck and then cruise like an airplane without a runway. Quantum-Systems introduced it at SOF Week in Tampa in May 2024 as a Group 2 aircraft with a 3.9 m (12.8-foot) wingspan and more than 10 hours of endurance from a hybrid-electric power system, and in July 2026 it announced an upgraded version with greater payload capacity, a maximum takeoff weight of 45 kg (99 pounds) and integration into the company’s MOSAIC UXS software, which lets operators control several types of unmanned systems together.
The armed configuration grows out of a version Quantum-Systems developed for U.S. customers, with hardpoints on each wing that can carry additional modules and release munitions or smaller drones. The company has also presented Reliant as a carrier for the Archer first-person-view attack drone built by U.S. manufacturer Neros, whose Archer the Pentagon has ordered in large numbers and which the U.S. Marine Corps recently flew with live warheads in Japan.
Reliant sits at the top of Quantum-Systems’ family of aircraft, above the short-range Twister and the mid-range Vector, the reconnaissance drone that made the company’s name in Ukraine. Sharpin has said Vector has flown more than 20,000 combat hours in Ukraine, and the company has fed that experience back into its designs, including after a Vector returned from a mission despite being hit 11 times by small arms fire. Quantum-Systems has also expanded production inside Ukraine, where it now builds Vector fuselages locally.
Quantum-Systems has offered Reliant to the German military as well as to U.S. buyers, and the armed version adds a strike option to an aircraft the company has so far marketed for long-range reconnaissance, surveillance and target acquisition.

articles.title: Russia is building Starlink no foreign company can switch off. Ukraine names 49 firms behind it, and 23 face no sanctions from Kyiv’s allies at all
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) has published the names of 49 Russian and Belarusian companies and institutions building Rassvet, Russia’s low-orbit satellite internet system, on its War&Sanctions portal, the agency said on 28 October. It needs it for its military purposes.
Russian troops ran front-line communications and long-range strike drones on smuggled Starlink terminals until SpaceX blocked them on 1 February 2026. Ukraine still flies on Musk’s network, and on 24 October it got back to full speed after a ten-day cap imposed abroad. Rassvet is meant to give Russia’s army satellite links under its own control.
HUR has said Moscow may struggle to obtain components for more satellites, and its list names the suppliers that sanctions would need to target while the network is still being built.
Terminals for Iskander-M command vehicles
Rassvet is first of all a military communications system. Russia plans to use it for command and control, strike platforms, and drones, and to install terminals in the command-and-staff vehicles of Iskander-M missile systems, HUR says.
The Central Research Institute of Automation and Hydraulics is involved in integrating Rassvet into army communications, including fitting command vehicles, Iskander ones among them, with terminals once 292 satellites are in orbit, according to the portal. The same institute produces guidance components for the Iskander-M and Kinzhal missiles.
Planned coverage takes in Ukraine and the EU first, and once it is wide enough, Russia could use the system in hybrid attacks on other countries. That is why partners should block Rassvet’s access to components, equipment, and software now, the agency said.
Roscosmos launches it, a Belarusian missile maker signs on
The lead company is Bureau 1440, part of the IKS Holding tech group. According to the portal, it is linking its flight control center to systems of the Russian Defense Ministry. Roscosmos launches the satellites into orbit, and its head, Dmitry Bakanov, personally oversees Rassvet.
Meanwhile, Belintersat, Belarus’s national satellite operator, signed a partnership with Bureau 1440 in May 2026 to bring Rassvet into Belarus’s telecom network. It is a branch of the Plant of Precision Electromechanics, Belarus’s lead missile developer and maker of the Polonez rocket launcher.
Another Belarusian firm, Aerospace Instruments, prototypes components for the system.
23 of 49 not sanctioned by Kyiv’s allies
Of the 49, 23, Roscosmos among them, are not under sanctions by any country in the sanctions coalition. The companies involved “must be included in all blacklists” of countries, banks, and businesses, the agency wrote.
32 satellites launched, seven launches to go
Russia launched its first 16 Rassvet satellites earlier this year. Stable communications would need 200–250 in orbit, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, then adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, said in May.
By August, Russia had launched 32 Rassvet satellites and planned seven more launches by the end of 2026, a HUR official told Janes. Only 12 of them, all from the first batch, had reached a sustainable altitude by the end of August, ISW reported.

articles.title: US tells Gulf allies to brace for ‘intense’ war with Iran – WSJ
articles.body:
US tells Gulf allies to brace for ‘intense’ war with Iran – WSJ
The US has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a short but intense military operation against Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
According to the WSJ, US President Donald Trump is leaning toward launching major strikes on Iran’s infrastructure and nuclear facilities, although no final decision has been made. The warnings to Gulf allies reportedly indicate that Israel is also preparing to take part in renewed combat operations.
The US is reportedly deploying an additional Patriot air defense missile battery to the region and moving troops away from vulnerable bases in anticipation of Iranian retaliation. Washington is also replenishing munitions and preparing additional aircraft and warships for possible operations.
Trump has threatened to attack Iran again if it refuses to accept his terms, as negotiations remain stalled, with both sides blaming each other for the impasse. The US last carried out a wave of strikes on Iranian territory on September 1 and has since attacked Iranian tankers and other vessels. Iran has fired on commercial ships attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through a US Navy-designated route, which Tehran considers illegal.
Iranian officials responded to Trump’s threats by pledging to defend the country. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned last week that the US would suffer “an even greater strategic failure” if it opts for renewed military action. State-run broadcaster Press TV, citing a senior Iranian official, reported on Tuesday that Tehran is prepared for an all-out war “without any limitations.”
The prospect of renewed fighting comes amid concerns about dwindling US missile interceptor stockpiles, which Trump has dismissed, insisting that the military has sufficient munitions.
The war remains deeply unpopular among Americans. A Fox News poll published in September found that 71% of registered voters believed the Trump administration lacked a clear strategy for ending the conflict, and 60% said attacking Iran was a mistake. According to a Pew Research Center survey published earlier this month, 65% disapprove of Trump’s handling of operations against Iran, compared with 33% who approve.

articles.title: Italy delays Ukraine military aid package ahead of US midterms: Report
articles.body:
Necva Tastan Sevinc
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Italy’s latest military aid package for Ukraine remains on hold as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government awaits the outcome of next week’s US midterm elections, Italian daily La Repubblica reported Tuesday.
The 13th package is ready but has yet to receive final approval, the newspaper said, citing government sources. Italy’s previous aid shipment to Ukraine was last December, according to the report.
Rome had assured French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that it would approve the package by October, with missile deliveries expected by the end of the month.
However, the parliamentary committee overseeing intelligence services, known as Copasir, had not convened to examine the decree as of Monday evening.
The package includes Aster 30 air defense missiles sought by Ukraine to protect Kyiv and other cities from Russian attacks.
The decree requires signatures from Defense Minister Guido Crosetto, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, and Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti.
Crosetto and Tajani support approval, while some government sources suggested Giorgetti was hesitating over potential opposition from League leader Matteo Salvini, the report said.
The final decision rests with Meloni, and Crosetto had privately warned of a political obstacle that needed resolving.
Approval has already been delayed several times, with expectations shifting from July to September and then until after the League’s party congress.
Government sources now favor waiting for the US midterm elections next Tuesday to assess Washington’s future approach and adjust Italy’s position accordingly.
Domestic political considerations are also contributing to the delay, including opposition to arms supplies from former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte and concerns about giving political momentum to Roberto Vannacci.
Italian officials have informally asked their Ukrainian counterparts to remain patient, according to the report.

articles.title: Turkey warns against further attacks by Russia, Ukraine on Black Sea vessels
articles.body:
ANKARA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler on Wednesday warned Russia and Ukraine against further attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, saying Ankara reserved the right to take legal action against the strikes, in Turkey’s most direct intervention to date.
NATO member Turkey, which has maintained good ties with both Moscow and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has repeatedly called on both sides to halt attacks in the Black Sea that have also struck Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned commercial vessels.
Ankara says it is waiting for responses to a proposal it conveyed to Russia and Ukraine aimed at stopping the intensifying attacks and ensuring the safe shipment of grain from the region.
Speaking in Sofia after a security meeting between defence ministers and military chiefs of Black Sea littoral states Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria, Guler said commercial vessels sailing and operating in the Black Sea had been affected by drone attacks, stray mines and missiles during the conflict.
“We follow with concern the intense attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and call on the sides to act with common sense, in line with the principle of navigational safety in open seas,” he said, adding that another commercial vessel had been struck by three drones inside Bulgaria’s maritime jurisdiction on Wednesday.
It was not clear who carried out the attack on a Greek container ship that was sailing under the Liberian flag in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone.
“We also reserve every legal right regarding attacks on Turkish-flagged or Turkish-owned vessels and follow developments very closely… The necessary warnings are constantly being conveyed to both sides to keep commercial navigational out of the conflict zone and immediately halt attacks on civilian vessels,” Guler added.
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on ships and infrastructure facilitating Russian oil and grain exports since July, when Russia intensified its missile and drone strikes on the main Ukrainian grain export hubs of Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi.
In a late September meeting, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskiy that attacks by Russia and Ukraine on commercial vessels in the Black Sea were inexplicable and steps must be taken to stop them.
Guler also said Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria — which operate a de-mining operation in the Black Sea — agreed it was important to also focus on protecting critical subsea infrastructure.
(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu; editing by Sharon Singleton)

articles.title: Russian nuclear-powered submarine launches Bulava missile from Sea of Okhotsk
articles.body:
MOSCOW, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Russia's nuclear-powered strategic missile submarine Generalissimus Suvorov launched a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from the Sea of Okhotsk toward the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, the Russian Ministry of Defense said Wednesday.
The launch was carried out by the submarine's Pacific Fleet crew as part of scheduled combat training, the ministry said in a statement.
The missile was launched from a submerged position in the Sea of Okhotsk. Monitoring data showed that its warheads had reached the designated area of the test range at the scheduled time, according to the ministry.
The Generalissimus Suvorov is a fourth-generation nuclear-powered strategic missile submarine equipped with modern missile and torpedo systems, as well as navigation, radio engineering and hydroacoustic equipment, the ministry said.

articles.title: Yemeni army claims 239 Houthis neutralized in 749 operations over 24 hours
articles.body:
Yemen’s armed forces said they neutralized 239 Houthi commanders and fighters in 749 operations targeting the group’s military positions across several fronts during 24 hours as part of Operation Dawn of Yemen, Anadolu reports.
Col. Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the armed forces, said on US social media company X that the operations targeted Houthi command centers, fortifications, firing positions, reinforcements and supply routes.
He said the attacks disrupted Houthi field command operations, suppressed firing positions and prevented frontline units from receiving reinforcements and supplies.
The operations resulted in the neutralization of 239 Houthi commanders and fighters, while 117 military vehicles and pieces of combat equipment were destroyed or damaged, according to the spokesman.
Army units and allied Popular Resistance forces continued consolidating their gains and increasing pressure on Houthi positions in southwestern Taiz province, he said.
Al-Nuzaili added that operations continued along the fronts in Al-Jawf, Marib and Al-Bayda provinces, as well as the southern and southwestern fronts.
He said the armed forces would continue operations in accordance with military plans while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
Meanwhile, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed on X that Saudi warplanes and missiles carried out 101 strikes over 24 hours, targeting civilian sites in the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces.
He said the attacks targeted Al-Jawf, Taiz, Amran, Hajjah, Saada, Al-Dhale, Al-Mahwit and Lahj provinces, in addition to the capital.
READ: Houthis call for evacuation of Yemen’s Aden airport amid escalation
Saree claimed the strikes involved F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets that took off from Saudi Arabia’s Khamis Mushait and Taif air bases, as well as missiles launched from Najran.
He also claimed the attacks killed and injured dozens of people, including women and children, but did not provide an exact casualty toll.
According to Saree, the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the beginning of the latest escalation has reached 3,480.
Neither side’s battlefield claims could be independently verified.
The statement comes amid intensified fighting between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital, Sanaa, and large parts of northern Yemen since 2014.
The latest escalation has seen government forces and their allies launch Operation Dawn of Yemen against Houthi positions across multiple fronts, including Taiz, Marib and Al-Jawf.
A Saudi-led coalition has also conducted airstrikes against Houthi military targets amid renewed cross-border missile and drone attacks.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The prolonged conflict has caused one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, leaving millions dependent on humanitarian assistance.

articles.title: Austrian startup shows off APS1 anti-drone turrets in Vienna
articles.body:
- GuardAero presented its APS1 vehicle drone-defense system to Austrian Defence Ministry Secretary General Arnold Kammel at Vienna’s Heldenplatz on Oct. 26.
- The version shown used two rotating turrets with 12 barrels each and camera blocks to identify and shoot down attacking drones.
Austrian startup GuardAero showed its APS1 drone-defense system for military vehicles to Arnold Kammel, secretary general of Austria’s Ministry of Defence, during the Austrian Armed Forces’ National Day display at Vienna’s Heldenplatz on Oct. 26.
The Graz-based company shared images of the presentation on social media, saying APS1 was shown as part of its research project with the Austrian Armed Forces and that the system is made in and for Austria. APS1 is an active protection system, a self-defense unit fitted to a vehicle that detects an incoming threat and destroys it before impact. GuardAero built it specifically to stop drones attacking vehicles at close range.
Photos from Heldenplatz show the system mounted on the turret of a combat vehicle. It uses two separate rotating turrets, each carrying a block of 12 barrels arranged in three rows of four, and each fitted with its own optical sensor. A cluster of camera blocks at the base of the mount handles visual identification of incoming threats.
Small first-person-view drones, flown by a pilot watching a live video feed and steered straight into their target, have become one of the most common threats to vehicles in the war in Ukraine. APS1 is designed as a last line of defense against those drones when they get past other layers of protection.
The system tracks approaching drones with passive sensors, meaning it watches for threats without emitting signals that could give the vehicle away. GuardAero currently uses a shotgun-based kinetic effector, firing shot to knock the drone out of the air. Because the turrets rotate, each can turn its barrels toward a drone coming from any direction.
GuardAero has also fitted APS1 to an Austrian Armed Forces Mitsubishi L200 pickup and has completed several live-fire tests on a dirt road in eastern Austria, shooting down attacking drones. The company says the system is vehicle-independent, so it can be fitted to different platforms, and its current work focuses on integrating it with other military vehicles.
The startup was founded in 2025 and first drew attention when it won the innovation competition at the Austrian Defence Innovation Conference in Klagenfurt in January 2025. It is funded by private capital in the low seven figures, according to Austrian military magazine Militär Aktuell, and in May 2026 it presented APS1 with the Austrian Armed Forces on a military vehicle at the Europa-Forum Wachau technology day. Earlier this month it won the Protection Award at Defence Innovation Pitch Day 2026 in Munich.
Other companies are working on similar close-range shields built around multi-barrel launchers and passive sensors. In the United States, Picket Defense Systems has developed the Inferno RTC, a rotating turret that sweeps its barrels through a full 360-degree hemisphere and fires shotgun-type and small-caliber rounds after detecting drones with acoustic sensors and cameras. Its barrels sit at fixed angles and spin continuously, so the system fires without first turning toward the target, while APS1 swivels its barrel blocks to face an approaching drone. Germany’s Mehler Protection is pursuing the same goal with SCILT, which fires shotgun-type interceptors cued by optical cameras.
APS1 would sit at the bottom of Austria’s drone-defense layers. Higher up, the Austrian Armed Forces are buying 36 Rheinmetall Skyranger 30 turrets on Pandur 6×6 wheeled armored vehicles, combining a 30 mm cannon and Mistral missiles, with the first systems due to arrive in 2027.

articles.body:

• He said Russian President Vladimir Putin had helped ensure the fourth-generation Su-35 military planes were delivered a year earlier than scheduled

articles.title: US hints at expanding Russian diesel deal
articles.body:
US hints at expanding Russian diesel deal
More Russian diesel fuel could enter global markets as part of a trade agreement between Moscow and Washington struck earlier this month, Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said. He claimed the shipments could be a “carrot” for Moscow to scale back fighting in Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump announced the landmark diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on October 9, saying Russia would release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, 500,000 tons in November, another million afterward and potentially 3 million more, depending on refinery capacity.
Trump called lowering fuel prices for American consumers his “greatest priority” ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, where the Republicans are at risk of losing their congressional majority.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky condemned the surprise deal as a “weak decision,” prompting an angry response from Trump, who suggested that Ukraine replace Zelensky with someone willing to negotiate peace with Russia. Trump has also repeatedly pressed Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, something Kiev has refused to do.
Speaking to CNBC on Tuesday, Wright described the diesel deal as an “incentive” for Moscow to stop hostilities with Ukraine, adding that more Russian tankers could “quite possibly” depart under a six-month sanctions waiver.
“It’s trying to put a carrot in front of Russia,” he said, arguing that reduced hostilities would allow Moscow to export more diesel and marginally ease global fuel shortages.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak said on Tuesday that three tankers carrying diesel are already en route to the US, with a fourth expected to depart Wednesday. On Sunday, he offered to supply as much as buyers wanted within Russia’s available export volumes, saying: “We can supply all of it.” He previously said Russian diesel exports could reach 3.5 million tons monthly by year-end.
During a meeting with Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff last week in St. Petersburg, Putin noted that global diesel prices fell 5%-6% after the deal was announced. Earlier this week, Reuters reported that Russia’s daily diesel output rose from 160,000 tons in early October to 180,000 tons after the introduction of new export quotas.
The agreement has nevertheless met bipartisan resistance in Washington, with a group of senators calling it a “gift to our adversary” and a betrayal of Ukraine. Novak pushed back on Tuesday, singling out Democrats and wondering why US lawmakers were acting “not in the interests of the residents of the United States.”

articles.title: Top U.S. general says AI will change how America fights its wars
articles.body:
- Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called artificial intelligence one of his three strategic priorities, after the budget and ahead of operations.
- Caine used the term super intelligence, which a Sept. 29 executive order directs the executive branch to use in place of artificial intelligence.
Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has named artificial intelligence as one of his three strategic priorities, ranking it behind only securing a budget and ahead of ongoing military operations.
Caine made the remarks on Oct. 26 during a fireside chat at the National Defense Transportation Association and U.S. Transportation Command fall meeting in Grapevine, Texas, moderated by Transcom commander Gen. Randall Reed of the U.S. Air Force, according to a Pentagon News account of the session. Throughout the discussion, Caine referred to the technology as “super intelligence,” or SI, the term President Donald Trump is trying to substitute for “artificial intelligence” across the federal government.
“I have sort of three strategic priorities right now, separate from [others]. No. 1 is making sure that we have a budget. … No. 2 is [super intelligence], and No. 3 is ongoing operations,” said Caine.
The wording follows a Sept. 29 executive order that directs the executive branch, to the extent the law allows, to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI.” The order does not create a new category of technology. It defines super intelligence as the same systems already covered by the statutory definition of artificial intelligence in federal law, so when Caine says SI, he is describing the AI tools the military uses and develops today.
Trump first announced the change in his Sept. 22 speech to the United Nations General Assembly, saying all U.S. government documents would switch to the “much more accurate term.” The State Department has since ordered its staff to rename AI-related programs and systems, and military offices have started adopting the language as well; the U.S. Marine Corps aviation acquisition office this month described new maintenance tools it is pursuing as predictive super intelligence technologies.
The term already carries a different meaning in the technology field. Researchers and AI companies have long used superintelligence to describe a hypothetical future system that surpasses human intelligence, and the industry more often uses “artificial general intelligence” for AI that would match or exceed people across tasks. Critics have argued that the government’s branding blurs that distinction, and Trump has responded by calling anyone who uses the term “Artificial Intelligence” an enemy of the White House.
Caine told the Transcom audience that the technology will be essential for the joint force to win tactical engagements, run logistics and sustainment, and carry out command and control, the functions that let commanders direct forces in combat. He described a future conflict in which the number of kinetic and non-kinetic actions moving between the United States and an adversary, from missiles, rockets and bombs to cyberattacks, would be significant enough to require machine help.
“When I think of SI, …it’s going to be a game changer as we move forward,” said Caine.
The chairman stressed that the work involves training leaders as well as systems and models, so that future commanders get decision support while humans stay appropriately involved and the military balances the opportunities against the risks. He said the Joint Staff is already working on that effort.
“It’s going to be an important part of our future, [and] we need to lean in,” said Caine.
The Pentagon’s use of the technology has grown quickly over the past year. In May, Under Secretary of War Emil Michael said the number of department personnel using AI tools rose from about 80,000 to 1.5 million in a single year, spanning enterprise productivity software through classified intelligence analysis. The department is also applying AI to missile defense data fusion and has launched a pilot program that uses AI-assisted tools to manage security classification.
Transcom offers an obvious test case for the logistics side of Caine’s argument. The command moves troops, equipment and supplies worldwide by air, sea and land, and the forecasting, routing and maintenance planning behind that work are the kind of data-heavy tasks where the Pentagon has been most willing to put AI tools into daily use. Caine did not describe specific Transcom programs during the session, according to the Pentagon account.
He closed the point by saying the commercial sector is likely to set the pace if past experience holds, and that the military needs to keep up.
“And we need to match them at the same speed and tempo,” Caine said.

articles.title: Chinese expert points to Japan’s ability to produce thousands of nuclear warheads
articles.body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan possesses more than 40 metric tons of plutonium, theoretically enough to produce several thousand nuclear warheads, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
He pointed out that according to the Japanese authorities, the country possessed 44.4 tons of separated plutonium at the end of 2024, including 8.6 tons stored domestically and 35.8 tons held overseas. In addition, Japan’s stocks of spent nuclear fuel contain about 191 tons of unseparated plutonium.
"The latest report from the Japan Atomic Energy Commission, published in August 2026, says that the total amount of separated plutonium remained at about 44.4 tons at the end of 2025, with 9.9 tons stored in the country and about 34.5 tons held abroad, as the size of the stocks remained vast," Dai said.
"What does this mean? Making a simple nuclear warhead typically requires only a few kilograms of weapons-grade plutonium. According to open sources, Japan’s 44.4 tons of separated plutonium would be enough to manufacture several thousand nuclear warheads," the expert pointed out.
Dai also said that the Japanese authorities justified the country’s substantial plutonium stockpiles by citing plans to use the material as fuel for nuclear power plants. However, this remains a cause for concern amid statements by some Japanese politicians advocating the acquisition of nuclear weapons, the expert added.
"Although most of Japan’s plutonium is reactor-grade, it’s not entirely impossible to use it in nuclear devices. Notably, Japan has the technology and processing facilities needed to separate weapons-grade plutonium, making the distinction between civilian and military use extremely blurred," the expert concluded.

articles.body:

articles.title: Putin to Pezeshkian: Russia honoring all commitments in joint projects with Iran
articles.body:
Putin to Pezeshkian: Russia honoring all commitments in joint projects with Iran
TEHRAN — Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow remains fully committed to all joint projects with Iran, including the continued construction of the Bushehr nuclear power plant, during a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow on Tuesday evening.
The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 8th Summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF).
Pezeshkian thanked Russia for its hospitality and its continued support for Iran in political, security and economic areas, expressing satisfaction that bilateral trade is on an upward and growing trajectory.
He said U.S. unilateral actions in the region have further highlighted the need to strengthen multilateralism and expand cooperation among countries under sanctions.
Regional countries, without reliance on the United States, have the full capability and will to resolve challenges within the region, Pezeshkian stressed.
Pointing to the mutual will of the two countries, he said comprehensive expansion of ties in scientific, economic, industrial, cultural, security and military sectors is achievable.
The Iranian president described the successful holding of Iranian cultural festivals in Moscow, Kazan and Astrakhan as a valuable achievement in bilateral exchanges.
Referring to a report and proposal by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Pezeshkian announced that the necessary permits for establishing a representative office of Russian state radio and television in Iran have been issued, with executive coordination underway.
He also welcomed the holding of a reciprocal Russian cultural and media festival and exhibition in Tehran, calling it an effective step toward deepening cultural and media relations between the two countries.
For his part, Putin said trade between Russia and Iran grew by 10.4 percent in the first eight months of 2026.
He added that work on the Bushehr nuclear power plant is ongoing and that Russia is fulfilling all of its obligations under joint projects with Iran.
Referring to his talks with the Iranian president, Putin also expressed hope that developments in the Middle East move in a positive direction.
He described the GECF summit as constructive, saying Russia is always pleased to host the Iranian president.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday night before departing Russia, Pezeshkian said detailed and in-depth discussions were held during the GECF summit, leading to good understandings, and described the summit as constructive and fruitful.
Referring to his bilateral meetings with the Russian president and the Emir of Qatar on the sidelines of the summit, he said issues related to agriculture, oil and gas, road construction, security matters and bilateral cooperation were discussed. Overall, it was a very good and productive trip, he added.

articles.title: Musk's genius, Rassvet, Akkuyu nuclear plant proposals: Putin's statements
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Entrepreneur, inventor, and Starlink CEO Elon Musk is a genius and Russia is in contact with him, Russian President Vladimir Putin said inspecting an exhibition on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit.
He noted that Russia’s Rassvet system, similar to Starlink, is only taking its fledgling stages. Putin boasted of the system's quality, highlighting that now it's time to put the required satellites in orbit.
He also said that Russia is happy to hear that Turkish companies want to participate in the construction of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant by buying shares in the project.
TASS has compiled the key statements of the head of state.
Digital sovereignty
Russia is one of three countries, along with the United States and China, with full digital information sovereignty: "No one else has a full set of these sovereign technological capabilities."
If a country isn't sovereign digitally, it can't be sovereign in general: "If there is not complete sovereignty in the information sphere, there is no sovereignty. This is impossible in the modern world."
A modern economy cannot exist without modern information technology: "That is, the economy exists, but it is outdated and inefficient. It depends on others, and this dependence will increase."
The impact of social media
Governments should manage social networks in their countries: "I think it would be right for us to have some control over this [the sovereignty and work of social networks]. And think about security issues."
The French government admits that the unrest in the country is due in part to uncontrolled social networks: "The French leadership also points out that the events that are currently taking place in major French cities are influenced by social networks that aren't in France's control. They [the local authorities] have little or no influence on the operation of social networks in their country."
The street protests in Tehran were largely provoked on social networks that were not controlled by the Iranian government: "What was happening on the streets of Tehran at the time of the crisis was largely initiated on social networks that the Iranian government did not manage or control. There was only one thing they could do-shu it all down."
Space cooperation with the United States
Russia’s Rassvet system, similar to Starlink, is only taking its first steps: "This is only our first step. But we are proud that we started doing it and started doing it on our own."
The quality of the Rassvet system is high, now Russia needs to launch the required number of satellites: "The quality is there. Now it's important to move from quality to quantity."
Interaction with Musk
Russia is in contact with the United States on the space issue and, in particular, with the head of Starlink, Elon Musk: "Both we and our American partners value this and, despite all political issues, we work closely with them. Both our Roscosmos and other companies do."
Launching satellites into orbit requires order and discipline: "Because in orbits it is important not to interfere with each other, to observe certain discipline and order.
"Elon Musk is a brilliant man, just really brilliant. How many such [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we are only taking the first steps."
Nuclear power plant construction
Russia successfully competes with Western companies in the nuclear power plant construction market outside politics: "And our competitors, we work with them outside politics, these are French companies, Japanese companies, American companies - they all say they are ready to develop small power plants. But so far, no one has done anything in practice."
Russia is the only country that has not only developed, but also operates small floating nuclear power plants: "This is not just a development, this plant is working. It is located in the north of Russia in the Arctic zone and has been operating and producing energy since 2020. This is quite effective: they are popular under certain conditions."
No other country in the world, including Western ones, has been able to achieve anything like this: "And our competitors, French companies, Japanese companies, American companies - they all say they are ready to develop small power plants. But so far, no one has done anything in practice."
Russia only welcomes the intention of Turkish companies to participate in the construction of the Akkuyu nuclear power station by buying shares in the project: "However, now there are companies inside Turkey that want to participate in this process and are ready to buy out part of the package. We only welcome - please."
Taxation
Russia’s Federal Tax Service is so modern and automated that it resembles a space facility: "Our modern tax service is, maybe I'm exaggerating a little, but not much, very similar to a spacecraft control center."
The Federal Tax Service of Russia is, without a doubt, "one of the most effective in the world."
Russia has good digital taxation technologies, the functioning of fiscal services and customs regulation: "We have good technologies, really good ones, I recommend you get acquainted, send specialists in the field of taxation, fiscal services functioning, customs regulation. Technologies are getting better and better. Moreover, they are not paper-based, they are digital technologies.
"When we agree on joint work with our closest partners, we introduce common standards, I won't speak specifically now either, I won't name the countries, but tax collection increases not by 1-2%, but by tens of percent at once. Very effective tools. And we are ready to share them with you, and these are modern digital tools."
AI in the taxi industry
Artificial intelligence in the taxi industry ensures complete optimization of work: "Artificial intelligence builds optimal routes, gives the customer a taxi that is closer to him. Optimization across the entire service delivery chain."
This is also important from the point of view of passenger safety: "It's always clear in the control center who the driver is, who he took, where he got him from, where he's taking him. This is an extremely important thing and it works very effectively."
Tourism
The Russian tourist flow can become a significant reinforcement for the national economies of African countries: "It is necessary to increase this flow with African countries. Of course, Africa is a unique continent with a unique culture and nature. And we will be able to direct the appropriate flows.
"For some countries, the Russian tourist flow has become an essential sector of their own national economy, even for such a significantly developed country as Turkey," Putin said. "7 million Russian tourists visit Turkey a year, which brings in $12 billion to the Turkish economy thanks to the tourist flow from Russia."
Cooperation on hydrocarbons
De Beers wants to cooperate with Russia and is trying to establish relations, Moscow welcomes this cooperation: "De Beers is a competitor for the [Russia’s] core [company Alrosa], on the one hand. On the other hand, they want to cooperate with us more and more, because problems are being created for them there, in the Western world, and they are trying to establish relations with Russia and our company. We are in favor, we only welcome this cooperation."
Vessels for fishing and processing of fish
Russia builds powerful and efficient vessels for fishing and processing of fish directly at sea, there were no such vessels even in the Soviet times: "Even the Soviet Union did not build such large vessels for the production and processing of fish directly at sea. Modern, efficient vessels are very important."
Indonesia has shown interest in Russian vessels for fishing and processing fish: "We have started building a fishing fleet. Fishing and processing. These are large enterprises for fishing and processing of fish resources. Some of our partners, for example, Indonesia, the president of Indonesia, are very interested."

articles.title: Russia test-fires Bulava from one of its newest missile submarines
articles.body:
- Russia’s Generalissimo Suvorov submarine fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from the Sea of Okhotsk on Oct. 28, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- The missile was launched from underwater toward the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, and the Pacific Fleet said its warheads arrived on schedule.
The Russian Pacific Fleet’s ballistic missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from beneath the Sea of Okhotsk on Oct. 28, sending it across the country to the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The ministry said the launch was carried out from a submerged position as part of the crew’s planned combat training, and the Pacific Fleet said that, according to tracking data, the missile’s warheads arrived in the designated area at the planned time. The flight path took the missile from Russia’s Far East to the far north of its European territory, a route the Pacific Fleet uses to test the readiness of its strategic submarines.
“The crew of the Project 955A Borei-A class strategic nuclear-powered missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov of the Pacific Fleet, in accordance with the combat training plan, test-fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile aimed at the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region,” the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The K-553 Generalissimo Suvorov is one of Russia’s newest strategic submarines and the third of the upgraded Borei-A class, a fourth-generation design from the Rubin Central Design Bureau in St. Petersburg. The Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk laid it down on Dec. 26, 2014, and the Russian Navy commissioned it on Dec. 29, 2022. Before entering service, the submarine fired a Bulava from the White Sea on Nov. 3, 2022, with the warheads striking the Kura test range on the Kamchatka Peninsula, the opposite direction to this week’s flight.
In 2023, the submarine sailed from the Northern Fleet to the Pacific along the Northern Sea Route and arrived at its permanent base in Vilyuchinsk on Kamchatka on Oct. 16, 2023, where it joined the 25th submarine division. TASS reported that the boat’s imported components have been replaced with Russian-made equipment.
Each Borei-class submarine carries 16 Bulava missiles. The Bulava is a solid-fuel missile developed by the Moscow Institute of Thermal Engineering, the design bureau behind the Topol-M and Yars land-based missiles, and it is launched from underwater so the submarine does not have to surface and reveal its position. Each missile can carry multiple nuclear warheads that separate and fly to individual targets, and the Barents Observer has reported that each Bulava carries six. Russia formally accepted the missile into service in May 2024 after years of testing that began with a first launch in 2005.
The Sea of Okhotsk-to-Chizha route has been used before by Pacific Fleet submarines. In December 2020, the Borei-class Vladimir Monomakh fired a salvo of four Bulava missiles from the same sea toward the same range in the Arkhangelsk region, the first time a Borei had launched four missiles in a single salvo.
Russia’s Borei and Borei-A submarines are replacing the Soviet-era Delta-class boats that carried the naval leg of Russia’s nuclear deterrent for decades, with the Generalissimo Suvorov and its sister ships forming the core of the Pacific Fleet’s strategic submarine force at Kamchatka.

articles.title: US envoy should speak based on facts, not fabricated accusations, Iran says
articles.body:
US envoy should speak based on facts, not fabricated accusations, Iran says
TEHRAN — Iran’s Ambassador and Chargé d’Affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, has urged the United States to address the facts rather than level 'fabricated accusations against Tehran,' condemning US and Israeli military attacks against Iran and calling for accountability under international law. In a separate address to the UN General Assembly, Darzi denounced unilateral sanctions as economic terrorism and demanded an end to Washington’s decades-long embargo against Cuba.
Speaking at the conclusion of a UN Security Council meeting on Iran, Darzi directly responded to remarks by US representative Mike Waltz, displaying photographs of Iranians killed in US and Israeli attacks.
 
“Let us speak based on facts, not on fabricated accusations,” the Iranian diplomat said, rejecting Washington’s allegations concerning Iran and its peaceful nuclear program.
Iran challenges Washington’s account of the conflict
Darzi said the US representative had failed to provide credible arguments or justification for 'Washington’s blatant act of aggression against Iran.' Instead, he argued, Waltz had resorted to repeated falsehoods and baseless allegations concerning Iran’s nuclear activities to obscure the facts and evade responsibility.
The Iranian envoy stressed that the United States and Israel had carried out repeated military attacks against Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities, which are under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards.
He maintained that Iran was the victim of the conflict, not its instigator, and accused Washington and Tel Aviv of committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
According to Darzi, the attacks had struck a wide range of civilian targets and essential infrastructure, including residential areas, schools, hospitals, bridges, airports, energy facilities, sports complexes, cultural heritage sites and railway infrastructure.
He described the strikes as flagrant violations of the UN Charter, international law and international humanitarian law, holding the United States and Israel responsible for the consequences of their military actions.
“No amount of propaganda can reverse the facts, erase the suffering of the Iranian people, or absolve those responsible of their international legal obligations,” Darzi said.
He emphasized that those who ordered, carried out or facilitated the attacks must be held accountable, warning against allowing those responsible to escape justice.
The Iranian diplomat also criticized Washington for seeking to portray itself as the victim while, in his account, conducting military aggression and inflicting mass civilian casualties.
He insisted that the distinction between aggressor and victim must not be reversed, arguing that the United States could not carry out attacks against Iran and then use the Security Council to present itself as the injured party.
Darzi said the United States and Israel would ultimately have to answer for their actions and the crimes he accused them of committing against the Iranian people.
Iran condemns sanctions as economic terrorism
In a separate address to the UN General Assembly during a debate on the need to end the US economic, commercial and financial embargo against Cuba, Darzi condemned unilateral sanctions as instruments of coercion that undermine national sovereignty, violate fundamental rights and obstruct economic development.
“Sanctions are examples of economic terrorism, while blockades enforced by armed force constitute acts of aggression under international law,” he said.
Darzi argued that unilateral coercive measures, including so-called autonomous sanctions, threatened multilateralism, destabilized international relations and undermined the principles enshrined in the UN Charter.
He described such measures as a form of collective punishment that imposed hardship on ordinary people, particularly women, children and older persons, while restricting access to healthcare, food and opportunities for development.
Referring to more than six decades of US sanctions and the economic blockade against Cuba, the Iranian envoy said Washington’s policies had inflicted severe suffering on the Cuban population and impeded the country's development.
He rejected the justification of tightening the embargo in the name of promoting democracy, arguing that the humanitarian consequences contradicted the stated objectives of the policy.
“No government is allowed to dictate the political future of a sovereign nation,” Darzi said, describing economic coercion as unlawful, immoral and inhumane.
He called for the immediate lifting of the embargo, full reparation for the damage inflicted on the Cuban people and accountability for those responsible for maintaining the restrictions.
Tehran links sanctions to violations of international law
Darzi said Iran’s opposition to unilateral sanctions was reinforced by its own experience of US economic coercion and military aggression. He reaffirmed Tehran’s unequivocal opposition to sanctions imposed against sovereign and independent states, including Cuba.
The Iranian envoy argued that invoking human rights to justify economic restrictions was fundamentally contradictory when those measures themselves undermined the rights to health, food, development and a dignified life.
He drew a parallel with the US president’s promise of assistance to the Iranian people, recalling the statement that “Help is on its way.” Darzi contrasted that promise with the subsequent US bombing of a primary school in Minab, which, according to the Iranian diplomat, killed 168 children aged between seven and 12.
He cited the incident as an example of the 'contradiction between Washington’s stated humanitarian commitments and its actions.'
Darzi also invoked Articles 1 and 2 of the UN Charter, emphasizing the principles of sovereign equality, international cooperation and friendly relations among nations. He cited Article 2(7) in arguing that unilateral coercive measures violate the principle of non-interference when used to force governments to change their domestic policies.
He warned that sanctions deepen international divisions, fuel confrontation and undermine peaceful coexistence, while imposing the heaviest burdens on vulnerable populations.
Concluding his address, Darzi reaffirmed Iran’s solidarity with the Cuban government and people and urged the General Assembly to press Washington to implement the numerous resolutions adopted by an overwhelming majority of member states calling for an end to the embargo.
He called for intensified international efforts to eliminate unilateral coercive measures, warning that their continuation undermined international law and reflected a failure to uphold fundamental legal and moral responsibilities.

articles.title: US and Japan Finalize Agreement for AMRAAM Facility
articles.body:
At a high-profile meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines this week, U.S. and Japan leaders finalized an agreement to establish a production facility in Japan for the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, following a massive $20.7 billion Pentagon contract to expand production of the missile over the next seven years.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced the agreement in an Oct. 28 press conference after meeting with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Defense Ministers’ Meeting.
The agreement is the culmination of an effort that began in July 2024 under both men’s predecessors.
“We finally reached an agreement on the establishment of a final assembly and inspection facility in Japan for the AMRAAM air-to-air missile, which is essential for the F-35,” Koizumi said, according to a translation of his remarks. “This is a groundbreaking agreement that will not only ensure the acquisition of equipment needed by both Japan and the United States, but will also strengthen Japan’s defense industry base.”
In a readout of the two leaders’ meeting, the Pentagon did not mention the AMRAAM facility but said Hegseth “welcomed Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense industrial capacity, and both leaders committed to continue close coordination on critical munitions production.”
The location for the facility has not yet been announced.
The approval process took more than two years in part because Japan has severe constitutional restrictions on exporting lethal weapons or even coproducing offensive weaponry with allies, which date back to its peace-focused foreign policy following its devastating losses in World War II.
The AMRAAM also contains classified guidance systems and intellectual property that require key safeguards to prevent leaks of crucial information about the weapon.
U.S. and Japanese officials have said the agreement will diversify the AMRAAM industrial base and build regional stockpiles for both the U.S. and its allies at a time when President Donald Trump, and Hegseth and his leadership team at the Pentagon have urged allies to invest more in their own defenses.
AMRAAM has long been the U.S. military’s main dogfighting weapon—the first missiles were delivered in 1988. The latest variant is the AIM-120D, which features GPS guidance and improved range, lethality, and jam-resistance over its predecessors.
All legacy fighters, as well as fifth-generation fighters such as the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II, can carry the AMRAAM.
In late September, the Pentagon and contractor RTX announced a five-year production contract for AMRAAM with two additional option years valued at up to $20.7 billion. The two sides had previously agreed to a framework agreement in February for AMRAAM and other key munitions.
While the contract award—officially published by the Air Force on Oct. 23—does not specify quantities of missiles, the February framework agreement calls for RTX to increase production “to at least 1,900” per year.
Both the length and size of the new contract are far greater than previous deals. Those usually covered a single year, and demand could whipsaw depending on budgetary pressures or service priorities.
As recently as fiscal 2022, the Air Force budget request called for buying just 186 AMRAAMs and the Navy requested none. Those totals wound up changing through reprogramming requests and congressional adds, but generally speaking, procurement stayed at or below 400 missiles between the services from fiscal 2017 to 2022.
AMRAAM Procurement
Source: Department of Defense Program Acquisition Cost by Weapon System reports. 2026 totals not finalized.
This new award expands the Pentagon’s multiyear procurement authorities, covering Lots 41-47. Those lots include fifth-generation technology in AIM-120D-3 variants, such as modernized processors and software-defined measures for the electronic warfare threat.
The deal is part of a broader effort by President Donald Trump’s administration to secure multiyear deals for munitions and aircraft, aiming to break the stop-and-start funding cycles of the past few decades.
The contract also increases output to other countries, with foreign military sales to 16 international partners for additional procurement pipelines included.
“We are accelerating output to record levels to deliver this critical capability for the U.S. services and more than 40 allied nations,” an RTX spokesman told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
“We have invested heavily over the past several years to expand capacity, modernize manufacturing, and strengthen our supply chain,” the spokesman wrote. “RTX proactively sourced $80 million in test equipment before any award. These investments will ramp annual production over the coming years to at least 1,900 AMRAAM missiles.”
The company is currently delivering previously contracted AMRAAMs, but the new multiyear contract helps avoid delivery interruptions, the spokesman wrote.
AMRAAM production has faced bottlenecks from a variety of issues, including subcontractor component supply chain problems and solid rocket motor production lag times.
“Like many advanced defense systems, AMRAAM relies on complex components that have long lead times,” the spokesman wrote. “Through sustained investment, supplier partnerships, and efforts such as new U.S. rocket motor production lines coming online in 2027, we are building faster than ever before.”

articles.title: NATO spots Russian submarine in the High North
articles.body:
A Russian Kilo class submarine has been observed in the High North by Standing NATO Maritime Group 1, according to NATO Maritime Command.
The command said: “SPOTTED: A Russian Kilo-class submarine in the High North, observed by Standing NATO Maritime Group 1 (SNMG1).
“Anti-submarine warfare is a team effort. Ships, submarines, aircraft and helicopters from across the Alliance work together every day to detect, track and, if necessary, counter any threat beneath the surface. Our posture is defensive, our readiness is credible, and our resolve is clear: to deter aggression and keep our one billion people across Europe and North America safe.”
Standing NATO Maritime Group 1 is one of the alliance’s permanently available naval forces, drawing warships from member navies on rotation and operating principally in the North Atlantic and northern European waters. The Royal Navy contributes to it regularly and has commanded it in the past.
The Kilo class is a diesel-electric attack submarine built in large numbers from the 1980s, and the improved Project 636.3 boats are quiet enough on batteries to have earned the nickname Black Hole from American analysts. Russia operates them in the Northern Fleet, the Baltic, the Black Sea and the Pacific, and the type carries torpedoes, mines and the Kalibr land attack cruise missile.
The Defence Committee reported this month that Britain does not have what it needs in the High North, urging ministers to retain Type 23 frigates until the Type 26 arrives and questioning whether the Royal Navy’s attack submarines are putting to sea as often as they should. The committee also called for the return of under-ice submarine skills and warned that Britain sells its nuclear contribution to NATO short.
HMS Prince of Wales is currently in the Arctic and North Atlantic on the second phase of Operation Firecrest with the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless, carrying Merlin Mk2 anti-submarine helicopters among her air group, and RAF Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft operate over the northern approaches from Lossiemouth. NATO warships began the current High North deployment earlier in the year.

articles.title: Iranian foreign minister says Tehran in talks with mediators to implement 7-day plan with US
articles.body:
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Iran is in contact with mediators to review proposals to implement a seven-day plan with the US, Anadolu reports.
Araghchi wrote on US social media company X that Tehran continues to give diplomacy a chance despite tensions with Washington.
“While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed,” he said. “We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week.”
Iran’s seven-day plan, presented to Washington through Qatari mediators in September, proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming negotiations with the US within a week if Washington meets Tehran’s conditions.
The US would take agreed steps during the first five days, including ending hostilities, lifting its naval blockade on Iranian ports, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
