articles.title: Nuclear ambitions threaten Japan’s future, Chinese expert warns
articles.body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. The nuclear ambitions of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s current cabinet could put the future of more than 100 million Japanese citizens at risk, despite widespread public opposition to nuclear weapons, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
He noted that statements by some Japanese politicians calling for the country to acquire nuclear weapons ran counter to Tokyo’s commitments to peace, as well as the views of the Japanese public.
"Opinion polls conducted by Japanese media show that 60% of the population opposes the development of nuclear weapons, while 80% demand respect for the three non-nuclear principles. This clearly demonstrates the anti-nuclear stance of the majority of Japanese society. Open attempts by Japanese ruling circles to promote the ‘nuclear option’ are putting the future of more than 100 million Japanese people at risk," Dai stressed.
"No one should forget history or go against the will of the people. If Japan’s ruling circles persist in their nuclear delusions and continue to compound their mistakes, this will not only pose a major challenge to the post-war world order and the international system of nuclear non-proliferation, but also run counter to Japan’s peace commitments and the general opinion of the Japanese people, ultimately exacting an extremely high price," he added.
"The international community must call on Japan to deeply reflect on the history of [its] aggression [during World War II], completely break with militarism, finally abandon ambitions to acquire nuclear weapons, and faithfully fulfill its international non-proliferation commitments," the expert concluded.
Non-nuclear principles
Japan maintains three non-nuclear principles: not possessing, not producing and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons into its territory. Although the principles aren’t enshrined in laws, all Japanese prime ministers have so far reaffirmed commitment to them. Discussions of the issue have long been considered taboo, prompting some politicians to refer to the "fourth principle" of not discussing nuclear weapons and call for abandoning at least this unwritten rule.
After Sanae Takaichi took office as prime minister, the Japanese media reported that the approach to the three non-nuclear principles would be discussed as part of a planned review of the country’s national security strategy. Media outlets claimed that Takaichi was prepared to call for lifting at least the ban on bringing US nuclear weapons to Japan. However, the prime minister said she had not instructed officials to review the non-nuclear principles as part of discussions of a new version of the national security strategy.

articles.title: Europe must finally hold Russia accountable for hybrid attacks
articles.body:
Europe must finally hold Russia accountable for hybrid attacks
A soldier patrols outside the building hosting the NATO summit of heads of state and government in The Hague, Netherlands, on June 24, 2025. (John Thys/AFP via Getty Images)
Marek Zenisek
Czech politician and academic
Europe has already learned to better recognize hybrid threats, which is definitely a good thing, but recognition alone is not enough and doesn't serve as sufficient deterrence.
European officials have grown accustomed to scenarios where a cyberattack disrupts public services and critical infrastructure, drones appear over sensitive sites, and a flood of misinformation on social media exploits societal uncertainty.
European governments then investigate, share information, release statements, and sometimes announce new security measures until another incident elsewhere grabs the headlines again.
This approach is obviously not enough. Up until today, it appears that Russia is pretty confident that the cost of these hybrid attacks is a bargain — it costs little, and consequences look spectacular in Russian intelligence reports.
And this is exactly where Europe still has a problem. Resilience and deterrence are not the same thing. Europe must become a harder and, above all, much more expensive target for Russia.
Europeans must ensure that deterrence is a priority, as resilience is an unlikely tool to actually change the cost of a Russian attack.
Let's stop treating every incident as an isolated case and add them all up
A single attack may seem too small to justify a major response.
We've seen it many times.
In July 2024, an incendiary package caught fire at Leipzig airport on July 20, followed by similar incidents in Poland and the U.K. over the next two days.
German security authorities did not issue a wider warning to the aviation and logistics sectors until Aug. 28, more than five weeks after the first incident.
The subsequent investigation established links between the incidents and a broader Russian sabotage campaign. The response eventually came, but the delay illustrates the advantage Russia gains when individual incidents are treated separately rather than as parts of a broader campaign.
Determining responsibility can take weeks, and governments may differ in their assessment of the available evidence as well as their opinion on the appropriate reaction. Before responsibility is confirmed, political attention may shift elsewhere, giving Russia a strategic advantage in this gray zone.
This creates an asymmetry that favors the aggressor. Moscow can carry out a long-term campaign while European states deal with individual incidents one by one.
European governments, therefore, need to evaluate individual incidents in a broader context and together.
A cyberattack, sabotage, or an attempt to infiltrate an intelligence network is a full-blown hybrid campaign targeted against European countries.
Repeated operations also consume European resources, reveal weaknesses, create uncertainty, and above all, test how far Europe is willing to go.
So every new investigation shouldn't start from scratch, and instead should take into account what came before it.
Deterrence can't start only after an attack
The central objective of Europe's deterrence strategy should be to change Moscow's calculus and make further aggression an unacceptable gamble. European governments can rise above the Kremlin's dirty tricks by pursuing a constructive, systemic approach that addresses the threat at its roots.
To develop that, European governments should prepare a credible set of possible consequences before another serious incident occurs. Russia doesn't need to know exactly what Europe will do in every situation; strategic ambiguity has its value, but Moscow must believe that Europe will respond and that the consequences will matter.
That's the foundation of credible deterrence.
There's also a broader reason why this is important. If we add up the various forms of pressure Russia has exerted on European countries in recent years, future generations could rightfully ask why Europe tolerated so many things without developing a more systematic response.
It will be especially hard to explain to our children and grandchildren why a group of countries with much greater economic resources than Russia repeatedly allowed Moscow to set the pace of the confrontation.
Europe needs to be much better prepared. European countries should have a set of possible responses ready that can be adapted to specific cases, instead of having to come up with a reaction from scratch after every new attack.
That way, deterrence becomes more than just a statement made after the damage has already been done.
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent so far?
and it may appear in our Letters section.
Europe needs to change the calculation
Everyone understands that Europe cannot prevent every hostile operation. It can't know where the next test will come from, just like it can't rule out the possibility that Russia or another adversary will take advantage of Europe's openness. It can, however, make such operations more difficult.
Europe can better protect its societies. It can improve the ability of its intelligence and security services to identify hostile networks. It can coordinate accountability better. It can remove unnecessary legal and institutional obstacles. And it can make it clear that repeated aggression will not go unpunished.
The main goal, as mentioned before, has to be to change the adversary's calculation.
Russia must not only ask whether a certain operation can be carried out successfully. It also has to ask how much it will cost if Europe uncovers it and holds Moscow responsible.

articles.title: Turkey committee approves pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkish parliamentary committee approves defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
A Turkish parliamentary committee approved a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on Tuesday, as tensions between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels grow.
The defence agreement commits the sides to regard an armed attack against one as an attack on all three. The foreign affairs committee approved it with votes from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling party and its allies, despite objections from the opposition.
The agreement now goes to the full assembly for a debate and a vote. No date has been set.
The 16-article Mecca Joint Defence Agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, joint weapons production, technology transfers and intelligence sharing. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, according to the agreement published by Turkish state media.
Ministers from the grouping have already met twice, in Istanbul and Riyadh, while high-level delegations from the three countries held talks in Tehran on Monday to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war.
Turkish government officials say they are considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, but that the agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or to attack the Houthis.
Ruling Justice and Development Party legislator Fuat Oktay, who heads the committee, urged fellow members to approve the pact, arguing that it aims to increase deterrence and cooperation, does not target other countries and is likely to contribute to peace and stability.
"The agreements our country has signed and to which it is a party are not intended for aggression, expansionism, or the formation of a bloc against third countries," Oktay said.
"On the contrary, our nation is a party to defence agreements aimed at strengthening deterrence, fortifying our region and fostering peace and stability."
Opposition parties warned the agreement could put Turkish soldiers in harm's way and embroil the country in other nations' conflicts.
"Will this agreement enhance the security of the peoples involved, or will it create new obligations that entangle Turkey in the wars of other nations?" asked Semra Caglar Gokalp of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party.
Pointing to conflicts between Pakistan and India and tensions along Pakistan's border with Afghanistan, she continued: "What are the limits of the responsibility Turkey might assume in the face of these challenges?"
The opposition has also criticised the parties for holding meetings before parliament has ratified the pact.

articles.title: European leaders are ‘political masochists’ – Lavrov
articles.body:
European leaders are ‘political masochists’ – Lavrov
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has branded European leaders “political masochists,” accusing them of sacrificing their own citizens’ welfare in pursuit of Russia’s defeat in Ukraine.
Speaking to editors-in-chief of African media outlets in Moscow on Tuesday, Lavrov accused Western governments of pressuring their populations to accept declining living standards to secure Ukraine’s victory in conflict with Russia. 
“They are trying to keep public opinion in a position where people must sacrifice everything: salaries, jobs, healthcare services and social benefits in general, so that Ukraine defeats Russia,” Lavrov said. “People can feel how their situation is deteriorating in European countries,” he added.
He singled out German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as one of the politicians advocating such an approach. “These are masochists, political masochists, if you like,” the foreign minister said.
Merz has defended Germany’s growing military spending and continued support for Kiev while warning that the country can no longer afford its existing welfare system.
The German government has tightened welfare rules, introducing benefit reductions of 30% for repeated violations and, in some cases, complete withdrawal. Berlin’s proposed 2027 budget also envisages billions of euros in savings from pensions, healthcare and other social programs.
Germany has meanwhile earmarked €11.6 billion for Ukraine in 2027, alongside plans to raise defense spending to record levels.
Britain, another major backer of Kiev, has also reduced welfare payments, nearly halving health-related benefits for most new claimants under Universal Credit, a program supporting low-income households and people unable to work.
In September, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called for further welfare cuts to fund increased military spending. “We need to fund our defence, not spend all our money on welfare,” she said. The government, however, rejected her proposal.
France has likewise pursued spending restraint, including a proposed public-sector pay freeze, while increasing military expenditure. The measures have faced opposition from trade unions protesting declining purchasing power and deteriorating public services.
Public discontent has fueled widespread protests across Europe in recent weeks, with hundreds of thousands demonstrating in France over rising living costs, education funding and inequality. Tens of thousands have also taken to the streets in Spain and Portugal over soaring housing costs, while Italy has seen protests over declining living standards.
European NATO members have committed to substantially increasing defense expenditure, citing the perceived threat from Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin last week rejected repeated claims that Moscow was preparing for war with Europe, describing them as part of an ongoing “anti-Russian campaign” on the continent. “They now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia – which, in my view, amounts to a kind of political schizophrenia. But I hope that it will pass,” Putin stated.
Moscow has repeatedly dismissed claims that it intends to attack NATO countries as “nonsense,” accusing Western leaders of using the alleged Russian threat to justify militarization and continued support for Kiev.

articles.title: Qatari mediators present Iran with new deal to end the war, official says
articles.body:
By Andrew Mills and Parisa Hafezi
Oct 28 (Reuters) - Qatari mediators have presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations said, but a senior Iranian official said Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
The official briefed on the negotiations, who is not from Iran, said a new draft peace proposal for the eight-month-old conflict was presented on Sunday and was being considered by Tehran, with a response expected by the end of the week.
Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war, which has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and recently spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The proposal presented by Qatar sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran’s and Washington’s concerns, laying out daily confidence-building steps that each side must take, the official briefed on the negotiations said. The timeline could begin early next week and several countries would act as guarantors of the deal, the official added.
Shortly afterwards, a senior Iranian official involved in the talks said Qatar had presented only “unacceptable ideas and not an offer”, and that Tehran’s policy on showing no flexibility over the nuclear issue remained unchanged.
Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme to be part of negotiations to end the war from the outset, while Iran says its conditions — which include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports — must be met first. Iran rejects Western concerns that its nuclear programme is military in nature.
ATTACK ON SAUDI OIL REFINERY
In late September, Iran presented another seven-day proposal under which Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy shipping channels, could be reopened if certain conditions were met. US President Donald Trump rejected it, prompting further Qatari mediation.
The draft discussed in Tehran on Sunday was different from that proposal, the official briefed on the negotiations said, though the details of the latest plan were not immediately clear. The official had previously told Reuters that the Qatari mediators had coordinated with Washington before going to Tehran.
Earlier mediation efforts to end the war that the US and Israel launched on February 28 helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but it quickly unravelled.
In recent weeks, Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia — a key US ally and the world’s largest crude exporter — opening a new front in the eight-month-old war.
Oil prices rose more than 1% to more than $115 per barrel on Wednesday after a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, stoking concerns over supply risks.
Fighting with the Houthis intensified last month as the militant group advanced against Saudi-backed forces towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another important shipping lane on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from Hormuz.
CONCERNS ABOUT RISK OF NEW STRIKES
The official briefed on the negotiations said there were concerns ahead of Sunday’s meeting in Tehran that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, fighting for another term in a general election, could resume attacks on the Islamic Republic this week.
On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated threats to strike Iran again, while Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel resumed attacks.
On Monday, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan also met Iranian officials in Tehran as part of de-escalation efforts. Qatar said on Tuesday that Iran needs to stop threats against Arab Gulf states and open the Strait of Hormuz to show good intentions for mediation efforts to succeed.
Gulf states came under sustained bombardment earlier in the war.
The war also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. It has eroded Trump’s approval ratings ahead of the US midterm elections that decide control of Congress.
(Reporting by Andrew Mills and Parisa Hafezi; Writing by Nayera Adballah; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

articles.title: Sweden orders four Bofors naval gun systems
articles.body:
BAE Systems has won a contract from the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration for four Bofors 57Mk3 naval gun systems along with 57mm 3P ammunition, according to the company.
Stefan Löfström, marketing and sales director at BAE Systems Bofors, said: “This contract reinforces our long-standing role as a trusted partner to the Swedish armed forces and FMV, and our commitment to supporting the Swedish Navy with world-class capability. It demonstrates Sweden’s absolute confidence in the Bofors 57Mk3 and its advanced 3P ammunition as key capabilities for Sweden’s maritime defence.”
The 57Mk3 is a multirole gun built for air defence, anti-surface warfare and naval fire support. Paired with the programmable 3P round, which is pre-fragmented and proximity fused, it can engage drones, aircraft, missiles and surface targets.
The gun is made at the Bofors site in Karlskoga, which BAE Systems acquired through its purchase of United Defense in 2005, and the 57mm family is in service with the Swedish, Finnish, Canadian, Mexican and United States navies. The American variant is designated the Mk 110 and arms the Littoral Combat Ship and the Constellation class frigates.

articles.title: Most of Britan’s nuclear missile submarine fleet now at sea
articles.body:
Three of the Royal Navy’s four Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines are at sea at the same time, an arrangement naval sources described as unusual, according to reporting in The Times.
One of the boats is understood to be conducting the deterrent patrol, carrying Trident II D5 missiles, which is the task the Royal Navy has maintained without a break since 1969. The other two are believed to have been on sea trials and preparing to take over the patrol. HMS Victorious, the fourth boat, is at Devonport undergoing maintenance and was not among those at sea.
The Ministry of Defence declined to comment.
Having three boats out at once is not a sign of extra capacity, though, as the Vanguard class was designed around a four boat cycle in which one submarine is on patrol, one is working up or recovering, one is in training or trials, and one is in deep maintenance, and the fourth hull is what keeps continuous at sea deterrence going as the submarines age. Running three at sea at the same time means the cycle has been compressed, and it is as consistent with pressure on availability as it is with a deliberate signal.
The Times was told by a former senior naval source that the service had been operating in what submariners call 2BA, or two boat availability, for a prolonged period. In that condition only two of the four boats are available for operational tasking at any time, which leaves no margin, because a defect on the boat at sea has to be covered by a single relief.
The strain is visible in how long the boats are staying out, Navy Lookout reported in March 2025 that a Vanguard class submarine had returned to the Clyde after 204 days, breaking a record set in 2023, and patrols of more than two hundred days have since been reported again. Deterrent patrols were historically planned around three months. Crews now routinely spend five months or more submerged with no contact with their families.
Forces News reported last week, in an account of life aboard the boats, that Commander Roger Ireland, a retired submariner who served on the earlier Resolution class, described the length of modern Vanguard patrols as horrendous. Resolution boats carrying Polaris went out for around eight weeks at a time.
Maintenance has been the other great difficulty, and HMS Vanguard emerged from a refit at Devonport in 2023 that took around seven and a half years against a planned three and a half, after an unscheduled nuclear refuelling pushed the cost from roughly £200 million towards £500 million, as this publication reported when she sailed.
The four Vanguards entered service between 1993 and 1999 and were designed for around twenty five years each. All four are now beyond that, and they must hold the deterrent until the Dreadnought class arrives from the early 2030s. The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, covering Dreadnought, SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the infrastructure behind them.

articles.title: Former US officials who resigned over Gaza urge 2028 presidential candidates to reject architects of Biden-era policy
articles.body:
A group of former US government officials who resigned because of Washington’s policy in the Gaza Strip has urged candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination to pledge not to appoint officials they said enabled Israel’s genocide in the enclave, Anadolu reports.
“Senior Biden Administration officials who were architects of the Gaza policy are now actively white-washing their own roles in enabling genocide,” Gaza Resignees said in a statement signed by 12 former officials.
“They violated U.S. and international law by providing U.S. weapons while Israel indiscriminately and disproportionately attacked civilians and civilian infrastructure, and as Israel arbitrarily blocked humanitarian assistance to Gaza,” it said.
The signatories include former State Department officials Josh Paul, Annelle Sheline and Stacy Gilbert, former diplomats Hala Rharrit and Mike Casey, former White House official Anna Del Castillo and former USAID senior adviser Alexander Smith. Also among them are former Army officer and Defense Intelligence Agency official Harrison Mann, former Air Force Maj. Riley Livermore, former Navy Lt. Cmdr. Hani Z. Nofal and former political appointees Tariq Habash of the Education Department and Lily Greenberg Call of the Interior Department.
“Not even two years since the end of their disastrous time in office, many of these same officials appear to be pursuing a path back into the halls of power,” they said.
“The most basic level of accountability, the most minimal level of consequences, is to ensure that those who have wreaked so much harm from within the highest levels of our Government cannot return to it,” according to the statement.
The group said that “Gaza has become a litmus test for the credibility of American politicians and the viability, in particular, of Democratic candidates.”
READ: US senator calls for accountability over Israel’s killing of 9 Americans in occupied West Bank
The pledge asks candidates to acknowledge US “complicity” in Israel’s genocide in Gaza. It also asks them to exclude any past or present political appointee who was “an architect, leader, defender, or key enabler” of the policy.
In a video released with the statement, the former officials took turns reading the call over images of former Secretary of State Antony Blinken, who now sits on the board of directors of the Center for American Progress, a Washington think tank.
“We have watched as elite institutions have welcomed these officials,” said Mann, as the video showed former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, who is now with venture capital firm Lux Capital and a CNN commentator. It also showed former National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan and former USAID Administrator Samantha Power, who both joined Harvard Kennedy School after leaving office.
“We have watched as these officials have tried to launder their bloody reputations,” Paul said, with Rharrit adding, “and prepare to re-enter the halls of power.”
“And we say, enough,” the former officials said in the video. “Enough with the culture of impunity in Washington. Enough with policies that break our laws and defy our values.”
“They have blood on their hands,” they added.
Top Biden administration officials at that time acknowledged civilian suffering in Gaza but defended Israel’s right to defend itself following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
US-made weapons were photographed several times in Israeli strikes in Gaza, although US authorities have declined to confirm this.
Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, mostly women and children, and wounded over 175,000, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. It has also caused widespread destruction affecting around 90% of the territory’s civilian infrastructure.
More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in the Gaza Strip since an October 2025 ceasefire went into effect.

articles.title: Qatari mediators present Iran with new deal to end the war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Qatari mediators present Iran with new deal to end the war, official says
Qatari mediators presented Iran with a new draft deal on Sunday to end the war with the US and Israel, and Tehran is expected to send a response to the draft by the end of the week, an official briefed on the negotiations said on Wednesday.
The new draft being considered by Iran sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran's and Washington's concerns, laying out daily confidence-building steps that each side must take, the official said.
The timeline could begin early next week and several countries would act as guarantors of the deal, the official added.
However, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday Qatar has not presented a proposal to Iran but has instead put forward ideas that are unacceptable, adding that Tehran would show no flexibility regarding the nuclear issue.
Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war that the US and Israel launched in February. The conflict has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and spilled over across other parts of the Middle East.
There were concerns ahead of Sunday's meeting in Tehran that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, fighting for another term in a general election, could resume attacks on the Islamic Republic this week, the official briefed on the negotiations said.
On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated threats to strike Iran again, while Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel resumed attacks.
Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled.
In recent weeks Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter.

articles.title: Wired for War: Israeli spy-tech firm targeted Starlink users – researchers
articles.body:
Wired for War: Israeli spy-tech firm targeted Starlink users – researchers
An Israeli online advertising company implicated in spyware attacks targeting internet users was heavily active on SpaceX’s Starlink service, Japanese researchers have found, bolstering claims that the firm was running a “targeting and tracking” operation masquerading as a commercial advertising business.
Earlier this month, Canadian cybersecurity watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant published extensive investigations identifying Discover-Tech, an Israeli advertising technology company, as a middleman helping spyware firms, including Candiru and Intelos, as well as a little-known US-linked operator known as Dark Cartographer, track internet users and potentially infect their devices without their knowledge.
Discover-Tech’s operation involved buying ad space on hundreds of thousands of websites and apps, using ads to gather information about the users that saw them, and selling this data to the spyware companies, who could then target specific users and install spyware on their devices via code concealed in Discover-Tech’s ads.
Despite presenting itself as a commercial operation, Discover-Tech concentrated much of its advertising spending on markets that would be of limited interest to conventional advertisers. Of 228 countries and territories examined, Palestine was the most heavily targeted, despite its population having severely limited access to Western goods and relatively little purchasing power.
In more than 100 countries, Discover-Tech was the leading bidder for advertising space targeting Starlink users, according to researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Japanese cybersecurity firm Trend Micro. The company was also the largest advertising bidder in Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan, and the second-largest in Afghanistan.
TrendAI published its findings on October 15, identifying the suspicious advertiser only by the codename Shadow-Earth-79. Six people familiar with the research subsequently told Reuters that the codename referred to Discover-Tech.
Noting that “the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero,” the researchers concluded that the company was running “targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation.”
The findings suggest that Discover-Tech may have been attempting to identify, geolocate, or monitor Starlink users. However, they do not establish that the company successfully infected Starlink users’ devices with spyware.
Who runs Discover-Tech?
Founded in 2020 by Israeli entrepreneur Dekel Boni, Discover-Tech appointed Eric Banoun as its director. Banoun co-founded Circles, a surveillance company affiliated with Pegasus spyware developer NSO Group, and Senpai Technologies, a company known for developing and selling surveillance software to governments, including those of Angola, Indonesia, and Malaysia.
Banoun also founded Intelos, which uses advertisements similar to those placed by Discover-Tech to surveil and geolocate individuals. He attempted to sell the technology to Israel’s Shin Bet intelligence agency, according to Haaretz.
Haaretz also identified Sara Hamou, through her holding company, as a shareholder in Discover-Tech. Hamou is a former manager at Intellexa, the company that marketed Predator spyware in Greece. Earlier this year, she was sentenced to eight years in prison for her role in the Predator scandal.
Is Discover-Tech linked to the Israeli government?
It remains unclear who Candiru, Intelos, and Dark Cartographer sold their services to, once they had obtained user data from Discover-Tech. However, as RT covered earlier in our ‘Wired for War’ series, Israel views its domestically-developed spyware programs as weapons, and retains the final say over where they may be exported to. 
According to a 2021 investigation by Haaretz, export licenses for Pegasus were often granted when sales were considered beneficial to Israeli foreign policy interests, including in connection with trade agreements or diplomatic support for Israel at the UN.
Other Israeli spy-tech companies covered in the series, including Black Cube, BlackCore, and Paragon Solutions, all worked to advance Israel’s interests, even when they were not directly hired by the Israeli state.
Discover-Tech’s advertising infrastructure was used to target at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera with Candiru spyware in 2024 and 2025, according to Citizen Lab. Researchers confirmed that some devices were infected through malicious advertisements that required no interaction from users.
The attacks occurred during a period of heightened tensions between Israel and the Qatar-based broadcaster, which the Israeli authorities have accused of threatening national security. Candiru was founded by two Israel Defense Forces (IDF) intelligence veterans and operates under Israeli defense export controls.
While the Israeli government has not been accused of ordering Candiru to surveil Al Jazeera journalists, the targeting raises questions about whether the company’s clients shared interests with the Israeli authorities. The investigations have not identified the government or client responsible for commissioning the attacks.
Is Discover-Tech still operating?
Following the investigations by Citizen Lab and Confiant, several major advertising companies took action against Discover-Tech. Google, Comcast-owned Beeswax, and Eskimi blocked the firm from their platforms, while Vungle suspended its access pending a review. Industry association IAB Europe also suspended Discover-Tech from its list of approved vendors.
Discover-Tech’s website, which markets the company as a “tailored digital advertising agency,” remains active. The firm has not publicly responded to the findings reported by Citizen Lab, Confiant, or TrendAI.

articles.title: Araghchi briefs cabinet on Tehran security summit, warns of risks to global energy markets
articles.body:
Araghchi briefs cabinet on Tehran security summit, warns of risks to global energy markets
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has briefed the cabinet on the latest diplomatic developments, with a focus on a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, emphasizing the need for regional cooperation to safeguard security, prevent escalation and protect national sovereignty.
Araghchi presented his report at Wednesday’s cabinet meeting, chaired by President Masoud Pezeshkian, outlining recent diplomatic consultations on regional and international affairs, including discussions with senior officials from neighboring and regional countries.
The report covered meetings involving a Qatari delegation, as well as consultations with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council; Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defense minister; Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of army staff; and Ibrahim Kalin, head of Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization.
According to the report, participants in the four-way discussions stressed the importance of strengthening regional cooperation, developing joint security mechanisms and preventing the further escalation of tensions and conflicts.
They also warned against the 'Israeli regime’s destabilizing policies,' including efforts to weaken regional states, expand military aggression, undermine governments and draw the United States into regional conflicts.
The senior officials underscored the need for regional countries to remain vigilant against developments that could fuel tensions and to deepen cooperation in defence of their sovereignty, stability and territorial integrity.
Regional ownership of security
In a message posted on Instagram following the Tehran meeting, Araghchi described the talks as a valuable opportunity to advance dialogue on regional peace and security and address shared threats and challenges. He said the agreement to continue consultations represented an important step forward.
Turning dialogue into lasting cooperation, the foreign minister stressed, would require agreement on common principles, confidence-building, mutual respect for national sovereignty and practical commitments.
Iran’s position, he said, was that sustainable regional security must be achieved through the participation of regional countries, without the military presence or interference of powers from outside the region.
“This approach is based on the responsibility of regional countries to determine their own destiny,” Araghchi wrote.
He also emphasized the need to counter the Israeli regime’s acts of aggression and destabilization, describing this as essential to protecting countries’ independence and sovereignty and preventing the spread of war.
Instagram message concluded with Iran’s diplomatic motto: “Our Neighbors, Our Priority.”
Energy diplomacy and Persian Gulf security
Araghchi also highlighted the energy dimension of Iran’s recent diplomatic engagements, saying the country’s energy diplomacy had advanced during the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, where discussions addressed global gas markets and energy security.
He warned that any military adventurism initiated by Israel in the Persian Gulf could have potentially devastating consequences for international energy markets, making the prospect a serious concern for both gas-producing countries and consumers.
The foreign minister’s remarks underscored the connection between regional stability and global energy security, as well as the importance of diplomatic coordination among regional states in preventing conflicts that could disrupt international markets.

articles.title: Russia-Africa summit: Putin’s key proposals on trade, technology and Western finance alternatives
articles.body:
Russia-Africa summit: Putin’s key proposals on trade, technology and Western finance alternatives
Russia and Africa can expand trade and share technology while reducing dependence on Western financial systems, President Vladimir Putin said at the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum in Moscow on Wednesday.
The event forms part of the third Russia-Africa summit, bringing delegations from 48 African countries to Moscow on October 28–29.
Speaking alongside Burundian President and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye, Putin proposed closer banking links, called for bilateral trade to at least double, and offered Russian expertise in energy, agriculture, healthcare, and artificial intelligence.
Here are the key takeaways from the speeches and opening-day announcements.
An alternative to Western financial dependence
Putin urged Russian and African banks to expand direct ties, open branches in each other’s markets and strengthen payments in national currencies.
He proposed greater use of alternatives for exchanging payment information, including the Bank of Russia’s financial messaging system and the pan-African payments system. These arrangements would lower transaction costs and protect settlements from “politicized interference” by unfriendly countries, Putin said.
He argued that countries that don’t have their own financial systems end up relying on Western infrastructure, which ultimately limits their sovereignty.
Breaking out of ‘debt bondage’
Western countries are resisting the emergence of a multipolar world because they remain accustomed to colonial thinking and “growing fabulously rich at others’ expense,” Putin argued.
He accused them of using sanctions, tariffs, economic pressure, and interference to preserve their influence, including attempts to push African countries back into “debt bondage” through predatory lending.
Servicing such debts diverts resources from long-term development, Putin argued, calling for reforms of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank and a stronger African role in their decisions.
Doubling trade despite sanctions
Russia-Africa trade exceeded $27 billion last year, compared with $18 billion in 2022, Putin said, calling for the figure to at least double and surpass $50 billion in the near future.
He added that neither unprecedented restrictions against Russia nor Western pressure on African partners have been able to stop economic relations between the two from developing and expressed appreciation for this “firm and principled position of our African friends.”
Putin stated that Russian businesses support local processing, employment and tax revenues rather than engaging in “predatory, neocolonial exploitation” of Africa’s natural resources and people. Their investments also support healthcare, education, and environmental projects, he said.
Energy, transport and food security
Russia and African partners are implementing more than 30 energy projects in 16 countries, Putin said, describing affordable and reliable power as essential to industrial development and better living standards.
He offered cooperation on hydropower, including modernizing existing plants and supplying remote communities, alongside other energy technologies.
Russia’s Rosatom and Togo’s Energy Ministry signed a memorandum on nuclear energy cooperation. Rosatom chief Aleksey Likhachev said this could include floating nuclear power plants to supply electricity to the West African country.
Putin also stated that Russia had exported 13 million tons of agricultural products to Africa in the first nine months of 2026 with more than 40 African countries receiving Russian grain and fertilizers.
However, he stressed that Africa has the potential to feed itself, noting that Moscow is offering seeds, machinery, agricultural technology, storage, and processing infrastructure to help develop that capacity.
Transport proposals also include railways, roads, shipping routes, and logistics hubs, Putin said, inviting African airlines to begin flights to Russia.
Russian and Mozambican ministers also signed a road cooperation memorandum and discussed a possible direct shipping route.
Sharing technology and fighting epidemics
Technological independence has become an essential part of sovereignty, Putin argued, pointing to AI, cybersecurity, personal data, and digital infrastructure. Russia is ready to share its expertise, including digital public services and medical technologies, he added.
Putin also announced that Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for African countries would be extended through 2029.
Under the program, eight countries have already received 15 mobile laboratories and around 450 African specialists have been trained. Russian doctors continue to assist against infections including cholera and the outbreak of a new Ebola strain that began in the spring, he said.
Further cooperation could include local production of medicines and vaccines, diagnostic centers, and digital healthcare services.
Scholarships, youth exchanges and media links
Around 40,000 African citizens are studying at Russian universities, Putin said, with enrollment increasing by half since 2020. Scholarship places have nearly tripled over the same period, reaching 5,500 for the 2026–2027 academic year.
The president proposed to establish a Russia-African Youth Union to coordinate further exchanges between youth organizations. He also called for Russian news agencies and broadcasters to expand their presence across Africa and said that Moscow would welcome more African correspondents working in Russia.
A three-year cooperation plan
In his closing remarks, Putin stressed that discussions between senior officials alone are insufficient, which is why this year’s forum has been designed to be more accessible and focused on practical opportunities.
He invited participants to an exhibition presenting Russian technologies and proposals for joint projects, saying Moscow is ready to share its achievements with African partners.
Putin said that leaders also intend to adopt a Russia-Africa partnership action plan for 2027–2029 when the summit concludes on Thursday,
Africa wants industry, not just resource exports
During the plenary session, Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye said that Africa wants a greater role in the global economy and partnerships that help transform its resources into prosperity for its population.
“We do not want to remain merely exporters of natural resources and then import finished goods,” he said, calling for African participation throughout production and trade.
The African Union chair urged investment in local processing, technology transfers, and training, alongside energy, agriculture, transport, and infrastructure.
He also called for diversified trade, payment systems, and logistical routes connecting Africa with Russia and BRICS.

articles.title: American special forces buy Tekever drones
articles.body:
United States Special Operations Command has bought uncrewed aircraft from Tekever after a programme of validation and acceptance testing backed by training and an extensive flight programme at several locations, according to the company.
Ricardo Mendes, chief executive of Tekever, said: “This procurement represents an important milestone in a relationship that has been built over time through rigorous testing, open dialogue and a clear focus on delivering effective capability. We greatly value the professionalism and engagement of the USSOCOM personnel with whom we have worked, and look forward to continuing to support their evolving requirements.”
The number, model and configuration of the aircraft are not being disclosed. Tekever described the system as highly deployable and designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance in demanding environments, with a modular architecture bringing together the air platform, mission payloads, communications and mission software.
Tekever has an established presence in Fayetteville, North Carolina, where the announcement was made and which sits next to Fort Bragg, the home of United States Army special operations. The company said the purchase is a further step in its commitment to the United States and its special operations community.
The Portuguese company is familiar to British readers through its AR5 maritime surveillance aircraft, which has flown over the English Channel under Home Office contracts since 2020. It has also supplied uncrewed aircraft to Ukraine and employs more than fifteen hundred people across Portugal, the United States, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Estonia and Ukraine.

articles.title: AI doomsday fears prompt researcher to abandon retirement savings
articles.body:
AI doomsday fears prompt researcher to abandon retirement savings
An AI safety researcher has stopped saving for retirement because he believes artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the next ten years. His warning follows similar predictions from researchers concerned that increasingly powerful systems could escape human control.
Nate Soares, a former Google and Microsoft engineer who now heads the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), discussed his outlook with Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson
“I do not save for retirement right now. I have a 401(k) from when I worked at Google, but I haven’t contributed for a decade,” he said, referring to his workplace retirement account.
Asked whether he believed there was a greater-than-50% chance humans would not survive another ten years, Soares stated that it’s “more than 50% that we don’t have a decade at this point.”
“I am not really an AI job apocalypse guy,” he said. “I’m an AI kills all humans guy.”
Soares argued that a sufficiently capable system could develop goals incompatible with human survival, evade oversight, and improve itself. It could then acquire resources and build automated infrastructure allowing it to operate without people, potentially making the planet uninhabitable.
The researcher urged governments to halt the training of general-purpose AI systems, arguing that superintelligence should be treated as a danger comparable to nuclear weapons. At the same time, he supported the use of the technology in narrowly focused applications, including cancer research and safer self-driving cars.
Soares stressed that catastrophe could still be prevented. “I do everything I can to stop this eventuality. I don’t think it’s inevitable,” he said.
Other researchers have voiced similar fears. In September, Anthropic’s Evan Hubinger put the probability of AI killing all humans within a decade above 10%. His colleague Jacob Coxon resigned, accusing developers of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
The warnings come amid repeated disclosures of AI agents acting beyond developers’ instructions. OpenAI reported in July that its agents escaped restricted testing environments and accessed systems belonging to Hugging Face, an online repository for AI models and datasets. The company has since restricted internet access during training of its most powerful models.
Critics have called for binding government safeguards and a halt to the development of potentially uncontrollable systems. On the other hand, supporters of continued development argue that AI’s benefits outweigh many of the risks.

articles.title: Meeting of the US, China and Russia: Zelenskyy fears "Yalta 2.0" - media
articles.body:
Meeting of the US, China and Russia: Zelenskyy fears "Yalta 2.0" - media
Kyiv • UNN
The President of Ukraine warned against a new division of spheres of influence between the US, China and Russia. He considers the format most beneficial to Moscow.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy fears an attempt to establish a new division of spheres of influence as a result of the upcoming meeting between the United States, China and Russia, similar to what happened as a result of the 1945 Yalta Conference. This is reported by Rapporteur, according to UNN.
Details
While speaking with journalists, he emphasized that he would not want a repetition of the scenario he called "Yalta 2, 3, 4." According to him, the world today is different from what it was during World War II.
Today we have a different world, a fragmented world that is very different from the world of World War II, both before and after it. A completely different technological world. Therefore, I think it is impossible simply to carry out such a redistribution among the three (the United States, Russia and China — Ed.). Although Russia wants this very much
He added that the Russians are most interested in this meeting, as they consider it an advantage for themselves. At the same time, according to him, China is the least interested in it.
I simply do not see any benefit for China, and I clearly see the advantage of this format for Russia
Context
U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff proposed that Russia hold a trilateral meeting with China's participation next month to discuss a plan to end the war in Ukraine.
The proposal is for U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to meet and reach a settlement regarding Ukraine.
Oleksii Buriachenko, president of the International Institute for Security Studies, said in a comment to UNN that only the Kremlin is interested in the potential trilateral talks between Russia, the United States and China. In particular, this would be aimed at raising the possibility of resolving Russia's war against Ukraine without the participation of Kyiv and Europe. Instead, other issues remain priorities for the United States and China.
To remind you
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin's aide, Yury Ushakov, said that representatives of European countries would not participate in the trilateral technical talks between Ukraine, the United States and Russia, which are scheduled to take place next month.

articles.title: Iran, Russia move toward joint construction of small modular nuclear reactors
articles.body:
Iran, Russia move toward joint construction of small modular nuclear reactors
TEHRAN — Iran is moving toward an agreement with Russia to accelerate the joint construction of small modular reactors (SMRs), as the country advances its domestic nuclear capabilities and seeks to expand the role of nuclear energy in meeting rising electricity demand, the spokesman for the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) has said.
Behrouz Kamalvandi, who also serves as the AEOI’s deputy for International, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs, made the remarks in an interview with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) on Wednesday, discussing Iran’s participation in the Sixth Ministerial Conference on Nuclear Power in South Korea and the growing importance of nuclear energy worldwide.
Kamalvandi said Iran was in the process of signing a protocol with Russia aimed at accelerating cooperation on the joint construction of SMRs, a technology attracting increasing international attention for its potential to provide flexible, scalable sources of electricity.
“We are also in a good position in the field of small modular reactors,” he said, adding that the proposed protocol would help advance bilateral cooperation in their construction.
Unlike conventional nuclear power plants, SMRs are designed to be built in smaller units and can be deployed individually or in groups, offering countries an additional option for meeting growing energy needs. Their modular design also lends itself to standardized production and the deployment of multiple units.
Kamalvandi said global electricity demand was rising rapidly, driven in part by advances in artificial intelligence, digital technologies and the electrification of transport. These developments, he argued, were making the expansion of nuclear power an increasingly important consideration for countries seeking reliable electricity supplies.
Environmental challenges have also heightened international interest in nuclear energy, he said, as countries look for cleaner and more dependable sources of power.
According to Kamalvandi, the world currently generates around 400,000 megawatts of nuclear electricity, while Iran accounts for approximately 1,000 megawatts. He added that announced plans to triple global nuclear power capacity would require the construction of around 1,200 power plants comparable in size to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant in southern Iran.
The AEOI spokesman underscored nuclear power’s capacity to provide a stable, continuous supply of electricity, distinguishing it from wind and solar generation, whose output fluctuates with weather conditions and the availability of sunlight and wind. Such reliability, he said, is particularly important as electricity consumption increases and modern economies become more dependent on advanced technologies.
Kamalvandi also highlighted the broader applications of nuclear technology beyond electricity generation, including nuclear medicine, agriculture and industry, emphasizing its potential contribution to scientific and technological development across multiple sectors.
Reflecting on Iran’s progress, he said his approximately 14 years of continuous service at the AEOI had given him a clear perspective on the country’s achievements in developing its nuclear industry.
“I can say with confidence that the country’s nuclear industry has reached full maturity, and we have now achieved self-sufficiency in the construction of nuclear power plants,” he said.
His remarks highlighted Iran’s emphasis on strengthening indigenous scientific, engineering and industrial capabilities, while pursuing international cooperation in emerging nuclear technologies.
The proposed Iran–Russia protocol on small modular reactors represents a further step in Tehran’s efforts to develop its nuclear power sector and broaden cooperation in a field that is gaining prominence as countries confront rising electricity demand, energy-security concerns and environmental challenges.

articles.title: Egypt's Saudi support raises fears of economic fallout
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Egypt's Saudi support raises fears of economic fallout amid pound slide and rising prices
The Egyptian parliament's authorisation of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support Saudi Arabia and defend its territory against external aggression has raised concerns over the move's potential impact on Egyptian markets, amid fears of further pressure on the pound, financial markets and commodity prices.
The decision, approved on Monday 26 October, occurs as the economic fallout from the US-Israeli war on Iran and its regional impact threatens to intensify, with Egypt already facing pressure on its currency and foreign investment inflows. Consumers could also face higher prices for goods and fuel, alongside rising living costs.
Mohammed Ali Al-Houthi, a member of the Houthi's political council, described the Egypt's authorisation as a "declaration of war" against Yemen, saying it contradicted declared efforts to reduce regional tensions.
The remarks came as the Houthi intensify attacks against Riyadh.
On Tuesday, the group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the Yemeni armed forces had targeted the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province with a ballistic missile.
Meanwhile, the dollar surpassed 56.50 Egyptian pounds at banks on Monday. On Tuesday, it returned to the black market at 56.67 pounds for buying and 57.90 pounds for selling, increasing the risk of higher import costs.
The Egyptian stock market also fluctuated, showing downward trends. Analysts estimate that around $4 billion in foreign investment in government debt instruments exited the market between 15 and 26 October, with outflows accelerating over the final two days.
Traders hoard goods
The New Arab has observed several major traders and suppliers, particularly in commercial centres in downtown Cairo, withholding goods from distributors and shops.
The products include foodstuffs, consumer goods and durable goods, with traders waiting for the dollar exchange rate to stabilise and for Egypt's position on the war to become clearer.
Analysts warn that the conflict could affect consumers through higher oil, shipping and insurance costs, as well as increased production input and food prices. This would further undermine the purchasing power of ordinary families, who are still struggling with previous waves of inflation.
Meanwhile, revenues from tourism and Suez Canal and Red Sea shipping traffic also remain vulnerable to regional escalation, potentially putting further pressure on Egypt's foreign currency resources.
Hisham al-Dajwi, head of the foodstuffs division at the Chamber of Commerce, attributed what he described as traders' "greed" partly to the Ministry of Supply and Internal Trade's failure to fully implement the "Carry On" system, intended to distribute affordable food and subsidised commodities through around 40,000 outlets nationwide.
Distributors said the recent price hikes in goods and products were down to merchants' hedging against price increases, based on a dollar exchange rate exceeding 60 Egyptian pounds. With the increased risk of war, some were hoarding products in the hope of reaping substantial profits if the conflict escalates or they are unable to replenish stocks.
Minister of Supply and Internal Trade Sherif Farouk appealed to traders not to raise prices and to display prices on their products, pledging that the government would secure essential commodities for between three and six months from domestic stocks.
New prices expected
Economist Abdel Nabi Abdel Muttalib said several agents and suppliers had informed retailers last Thursday that no new indicative prices had been issued, while anticipating that new prices would take effect at the beginning of the following month.
He told The New Arab that some suppliers had begun delaying deliveries while waiting for new contracts, allowing them to price products according to future costs.
Abdel Muttalib cited sanitary products for the elderly, which he described as essential for health reasons, noting that some retailers had raised prices over the past two days, only to revert to the former prices after being informed that sales would be suspended until the end of the month.
These practices had contributed to higher prices, he said, warning that they could intensify pressure on consumers, particularly those purchasing essential goods.
Abdel Muttalib warned that continued dollar appreciation could revive the currency black market, with rising exchange rates encouraging expectations of further increases.
He said he had previously ruled out the dollar exceeding 55 pounds, but subsequent increases had heightened concerns over further depreciation.
A weaker pound should theoretically reduce imports by increasing the cost of imported goods and lowering demand. However, this does not apply equally to production inputs, raw materials and essential commodities that Egypt cannot do without, including oil, gas and wheat.
He said the government could have limited price pressures by temporarily coordinating with traders to prevent price increases and penalising violators, or by imposing fees, taxes and levies on capital seeking to exit the country, thereby limiting its profits and preserving state resources. A combination of the two approaches was also possible.
Abdel Muttalib suggested the government may have avoided such measures to preserve Egypt's image as a market allowing foreign investment to enter and exit freely, and to avoid such restrictive measures affecting the IMF's assessment during its latest programme review.
Saudi financial support expected
Abdel Muttalib said the parliamentary authorisation could strengthen ties between Egypt and Gulf states, potentially helping offset capital outflows if it led to new financial inflows or investments from Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
Such inflows could compensate for some outgoing funds, he said, while warning that unfavourable regional developments could place Egypt under greater pressure.
He considered a wider regional war relatively unlikely, but said an expansion of the confrontation could exacerbate economic risks, particularly if accompanied by continued foreign capital outflows and rising prices.
Financing and investment expert Wael al-Nahhas warned that a regional confrontation lasting up to six months could intensify financial pressures on Gulf economies and affect Egypt through higher import costs and reduced foreign currency inflows.
He said the dollar's rise from below 50 pounds to more than 56 pounds in a short period represented pressure beyond normal exchange-rate fluctuations.
Nahhas warned that households were already facing cost-of-living pressures, warning that reduced supplies could intensify price increases even without comparable rises in global markets.
Nahhas also cautioned against interpreting temporary stock market gains as a definitive sign of recovery, given uncertainty over the war, US interest rate decisions and corporate earnings.
If stock prices continue to fall, investors may lose confidence, making it harder for the government to sell shares in state-owned companies, including Banque du Caire, as investors demand greater discounts to compensate for risks or choose to postpone investing.

articles.title: Amid uncertainty over EU aid, Vitalii Kim insists Ukraine has no choice but to fight for motherland
articles.body:
Amid uncertainty over EU aid, Vitalii Kim insists Ukraine has no choice but to fight for motherland
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Vitalii Kim, Minister for Veterans Affairs of Ukraine. “If Europe will not support us, we also will fight because it's our motherland,” says Kim, insisting that Ukraine's determination to resist Russian aggression will endure regardless of the outcome of negotiations over European financial assistance. Yet behind this assertion of national resolve lies a more complex reality: a country confronting not only the immediate pressures of war, but also its mounting psychological, social and institutional consequences.
Speaking to FRANCE 24's François Picard during a visit to Paris for discussions with French defence officials, Kim describes a conflict increasingly defined by attrition. In the southern city of Kherson, civilians face relentless bombardment and attacks by inexpensive, short-range drones, while repeated Russian strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure are taking a cumulative toll. “People just get tired,” he acknowledges, offering a rare glimpse into the tensions between public resilience and the exhaustion generated by prolonged warfare.
The interview also highlights the formidable challenge of reintegrating Ukraine's growing veteran population. With an estimated 1.5 million veterans already requiring support and projections of substantially higher numbers in the coming years, Kim outlines plans to simplify administrative procedures, expand mental healthcare and draw on French expertise. The implications extend beyond individual rehabilitation to the future capacity of the Ukrainian state to meet the needs of a society profoundly transformed by war.
Against the backdrop of uncertainty over a €90 billion European aid package and renewed diplomatic speculation surrounding Donald Trump's efforts to bring the Russian and Ukrainian presidents together, Kim remains unequivocal about Ukraine's commitment to its own defence. Asked about the prospect of presidential talks, however, he offers a notably restrained response: “I need to be politically correct to answer this question. I have no reaction. I have only my job to do.”
His remarks reveal the central paradox of Ukraine's prolonged resistance: a determination to continue fighting, even as the human and material resources required to sustain that resistance come under growing strain.

articles.title: Atlas drops seven hundred paratroopers into Germany
articles.body:
Around seven hundred paratroopers have been dropped onto a German drop zone from four Atlas C1 transports across multiple waves, bringing back battlegroup-level airborne insertion using the aircraft for the first time, according to the Royal Air Force.
Exercise Rhino Titan brought together the RAF Air Mobility Force and 16 Air Assault Brigade Combat Team as a Joint Airborne Task Force, with British, French and German troops taking part. Airborne operations have long been part of British military capability, and the difference here lies in the scale and in soldiers travelling with their stores in the same aircraft.
Squadron Leader Luke, a flight commander on 30 Squadron and the airborne mission commander, said: “Rhino Titan demonstrates the return of large-scale airborne insertion as a capability. The Atlas allows us to deploy combat forces further, faster and more efficiently than previous generations of aircraft, giving Defence the ability to project force rapidly wherever it is required.”
Stores previously needed aircraft of their own, so carrying personnel and equipment together generates more combat power from the same number of airframes, and lets troops become operational almost immediately on landing. Paratroopers board carrying parachute equipment, weapons, communications systems and bergen loads of up to fifty kilograms, with air loadmasters and parachute jump instructors supervising the process before departure.
Squadron Leader Nick, officer commanding the Parachute Training Squadron at RAF Brize Norton, said: “By the time soldiers board the aircraft, a significant amount of planning and preparation has already taken place. Parachute Jump Instructors will have delivered specialist ground training, while detailed planning between aircrew, dispatchers and ground forces coordinates every aspect of the mission.”
He added: “It takes RAF aircrew, engineers, Air Loadmasters, Parachute Jump Instructors and support personnel working alongside the Army to deliver that capability safely and effectively.”
Getting to this point took eighteen months of increased activity between Brize Norton, Weston-on-the-Green and Salisbury Plain, progressing from basic parachuting serials through formation flying and simulated mass drops to integrated delivery of personnel and stores. Aircraft, crews and instructors had to be dedicated to that training while global operational commitments continued.
Squadron Leader Luke said: “The harder we train in exercises, the easier it is to deliver the capability when it’s needed.”
Pathfinders went in ahead of the main force to validate the drop zone and provide reconnaissance and surveillance before the larger force arrived. The RAF said the exercise builds on work done with NATO allies through activities such as Exercise Falcon Leap, where Atlas operators and other tactical airlift nations develop common tactics and procedures, and that dropping troops by parachute lets forces deploy beyond established infrastructure.
The A400M Atlas entered RAF service in 2014 and operates from Brize Norton with 24, 30, 70 and 206 Squadrons. The type will also be fitted for firefighting under the package the government announced last week, which is to give Britain an aerial firefighting capability permanently based in the United Kingdom for the first time.

articles.title: Russia Loses More Troops in a Month in Ukraine Than USSR Lost in 10 Years in Afghanistan, Stubb Says
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Loses More Troops in a Month in Ukraine Than USSR Lost in 10 Years in Afghanistan, Stubb Says
Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated that Russia’s offensive in eastern Ukraine would take years to achieve its objectives at the current pace, addressing the UN Security Council on September 23.
Stubb argued that drone warfare has effectively frozen much of the frontline.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking on behalf of the five Nordic countries, Stubb stated that Russian forces had captured roughly 900 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year, while Ukraine had retaken around 800 square kilometers.
“So the line of contact is basically not moving,” Stubb stated.
At that pace, he warned, Russia would need years to seize the rest of Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Stubb also stated that roughly 25,000 soldiers are being killed each month as both sides fight across a frontline that has shifted only marginally.
He compared the monthly losses with the Soviet war in Afghanistan, noting that the USSR lost roughly 18,000 troops over the entire decade-long conflict.
“This, in my mind, is a waste of life,” Stubb stated. “So the continuation of this war is a lose-lose.”
The Finnish president attributed much of the battlefield stalemate to drones, unmanned systems, and near-constant surveillance.
“We haven’t seen anything like this previously,” Stubb noted.
He described stretches of the frontline as roughly 20-kilometer-wide “death zones,” where exposed troops and vehicles face an extremely high likelihood of being detected and attacked.
“We’re seeing unmanned vehicles, we’re seeing death zones of roughly 20 kilometers to which you cannot enter, because with a 95 percent certainty, you’re going to be wiped out,” Stubb stated.
He argued that this environment helps explain why neither side has been able to achieve a decisive breakthrough despite heavy losses.
Stubb also accused Russia of systematically targeting Ukrainian civilians, civilian infrastructure, and humanitarian operations in an attempt to intimidate the population and weaken resistance.
“The aim is to instill fear and wear down Ukraine,” he stated.
The Finnish president called for an unconditional ceasefire, or at minimum limited arrangements covering areas such as energy infrastructure and grain exports, before negotiations on security, territory, justice, and a permanent settlement.
“There has to become a time when the killing stops,” Stubb stated.
Hours after the UN Security Council meeting, Stubb and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a new defense agreement focused on drones, technology transfers, expertise, and joint industrial projects.
“This is not simply a contract or an agreement on the sale and purchase of drones,” Zelenskyy stated. “This is about security—our shared security and joint production.”
Finland has increasingly framed its defense relationship with Ukraine as a two-way exchange, with Helsinki seeking to draw on Ukrainian battlefield experience as it develops its own military capabilities.
“That is exactly why we began saying that this is not a one-way street where we simply provide something to you,” Stubb stated. “On the contrary, it is a two-way process in which we learn from you.”
“By learning from Ukraine’s experience, we are strengthening our own capabilities,” he added.
Zelenskyy previously reported that Ukraine carried out three major offensive operations in 2026, including Operation Vivaldi in the Donetsk region and Operation VELES near Kupiansk, where Ukrainian troops traveled more than 15 kilometers underground before emerging behind Russian positions.

articles.title: UK Chancellor pledges 3% GDP on defence spending by 2030
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK Chancellor pledges 3% GDP on defence spending by 2030, plans to meet NATO targets by 2035
The UK will increase defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, Chancellor John Healey has announced in the Autumn budget on Wednesday.
The Chancellor said this was part of the UK's plan to meet NATO's defence spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
US President Donald Trump has pressured European members of NATO to spend least 3.5% of GDP on core defence requirements after several members of the military alliance failed to meet the previous defence spending target of 2% of GDP.
As well as spending on military forces, NATO counts spending on police forces who are trained in military tactics, and can be deployed abroad as part of military operations, as defence expenditure.
Healey said he will set out the details on how he will meet the defence targets next year.
He also announced an increase in private investment in defence.
Healey previously served as Defence Secretary in Kier Starmer's Cabinet, before resigning in June over the former Prime Minister's defence investment plan, which he said "falls well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time."
Healey's resignation is widely considered one of the key factors behind the end of Starmer's premiership earlier this year.
In 2025, while Defence Secretary, Healey said the UK is in "in a new era of threat," citing the previous US-Israeli war on Iran, and Russia's war on Ukraine.
"As the threat grows, Britain must step up," he said in the same speech in Parliament.
In his budget announcement on Wednesday, he repeatedly cited the war in the Middle East as a leading cause of the UK's high cost of living, especially due to rising energy costs.
"These are the global economic storms we face'" Healey said, "we must choose the course we steer through them."
Healey also announced a £100 winter energy payment for millions of households in the lowest council tax bands.
The Chancellor also announced an extension of the five pence cut to fuel duty until July 2027.
Duty for motor fuels was temporarily cut in 2022 after fuel costs spiked following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Healey announced that the measures to ease energy bills will be funded by a temporary 3% increase in taxes for banks. The rise will be on top of the 25% corporate tax rate they currently pay.
Healey also announced an end to gas standing charges from next year in a bid to help households with energy prices which rose after the US and Israel's February invasion of Iran.
Currently, households pay a fixed yearly fee on top of their household gas bill, regardless of their usage. Scrapping the standing charge will shift that payment onto the unit rates.
That means around 60% household that use less gas will save money, while those that use the most gas will see their bills increase.
The move will not cost the Government any money. Rather, it will shift some of the burden for energy bills from lower income households to those on higher incomes.
