articles.title: NABU: Ex-Prosecutor General Kravchenko's statement aimed at securing protection in country of residence
articles.body:
A statement by former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko claiming that military personnel from the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine were supposed to have committed acts of violence against him – is an attempt to secure protection in his host country, according to the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU).
"NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) view the statement by the former Prosecutor General, who hastily left Ukraine following the implementation of the NABU and SAPO operation 'Carthage,' as an attempt to secure protection in his country of residence," NABU told Interfax-Ukraine on Wednesday.
The bureau also said Kravchenko's statement regarding NABU and SAPO's involvement in any of the events in question is untrue.
Earlier, Kravchenko posted a statement on his Telegram channel claiming that the General Staff Intelligence Agency servicemen from the Artan unit, who were recently detained in Austria, were planning illegal acts of violence against him. "As is known, two active-duty Intelligence Agency servicemen from the so-called "Artan" group were detained. Their commander, Viktor Torkotuk, was also in Austria at the time of his subordinates' detention. One of the detainees is a former NABU employee who worked in the external surveillance unit," the former prosecutor general said.
He stated: "Back in September, I received information that a group of individuals had been sent to follow me with the intention of committing unlawful acts of violence against me." Kravchenko claims that he was informed at the time that "NABU and SAPO leaders had requested that this group be sent."
Sources at the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ministry of Defense, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine, refuted Kravchenko's claims regarding the alleged involvement of intelligence officers, emphasizing that "no one issued such orders."
"We respect European legislation and our partners. Of course, this is fake news," a source at the Main Intelligence Agency, who spoke to the agency, said.
As previously reported, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) exposed five members of a criminal organization led by an official from the Prosecutor General's Office (Operation "Carthage"), who systematically received illicit benefits for covering up a network of fraudulent call centers and laundered over UAH 42 million through the purchase of real estate – including apartments in the Carpathians – jewelry, and by depositing funds into relatives' accounts.
Amid the scandal over his possible involvement in the Carthage case, Prosecutor General Kravchenko submitted his resignation. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy suspended him from office, and on September 15, the Verkhovna Rada approved Kravchenko's dismissal. In the materials released by the National Security and Defense Council, the key suspect in the case – Serhiy Kropyva, deputy head of the PGO Department of International Cooperation – is identified as Kravchenko's confidant. In particular, according to the investigation, he coordinated household matters and repairs at Kravchenko's home.
Kravchenko has not yet been notified of the charges against him.
At the same time, on September 14, after submitting his resignation letter, Kravchenko signed a notice of suspicion addressed to NABO Director Semen Kryvonos. In response, the NABU and the SAPO stated that they view such actions as a continuation of a systematic attack on independent anti-corruption agencies. On the evening of September 14, the PGO reported that no such charges had been filed.
Kravchenko, for his part, stated that he had left Ukraine, claiming he had gone on a business trip. According to unconfirmed reports, Kravchenko and his wife may be in Vienna (Austria) and are in talks with local law firms regarding asylum.
Acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalsky announced in October that an internal investigation into the departure abroad of former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko is ongoing; the circumstances surrounding the organization of his business trip are being examined, and, in total, eight individuals mentioned in connection with operation "Carthage" have been dismissed from the prosecutor's office.

articles.title: Defence official flagged plans for social media ban request
articles.body:
Defence official who sought to block social media clips claimed she flagged plans with minister
In short:
A senior defence official who sought to block the use of clips from parliamentary hearings on social media claimed in emails she had support from a government minister.
In an email obtained under FOI, Celia Perkins wrote that Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil was "fully supportive" of the plan.
Another government official has since raised concerns that the editing and sharing of social media clips from hearings invited "ridicule and hostility" towards public servants.
A senior Department of Defence official said she had approval from a government minister to try to block the public release of her evidence to a parliamentary hearing due to concerns about "vile" social media commentary.
Deputy secretary Celia Perkins said she had approval from Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil when she told a parliamentary committee hearing last month that she did not "consent" to her evidence appearing on social media.
The request was swiftly rejected by committee chair senator Jess Collins, on advice from parliamentary officials.
"It is our right as senators and members of the public to disseminate the evidence that is provided by the witnesses today in the manner in which we see fit," Senator Collins said.
Emails between Defence officials ahead of the hearing, obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, reveal Ms Perkins told colleagues she raised her plans to make the statement with Mr Khalil and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles's office two days before the hearing.
"(Department secretary Meghan Quinn) is fully supportive, as is AMINDEF. I discussed today in a meeting with AMINDEF and staff from DPMO and his office," she wrote in the email.
"I'll pass the opening statement to them tomorrow."
AMINDEF refers to Mr Khalil, and DPMO is the Deputy Prime Minister's office.
The ABC understands Mr Marles's office provided no input to Ms Perkins's statement before she made it. Comment has been sought from both Mr Khalil and Mr Marles.
During a Senate estimates hearing this week, Senate Clerk Richard Pye was asked about the advice he provided the committee after Ms Perkins request.
"It's absolutely not something that a witness can do," he said.
"It was profoundly unhelpful, I thought on the day, for the matter to be raised in that way without any notice to anybody, not through the secretariat, not to the chair and not to other members of the committee."
But he added that there were genuine concerns about the effect of footage from committee hearings on social media.
"This is not to minimise the fact that there are some people who have been very bruised by their experiences before Senate and House committees and the treatment of footage that has come out of those," he said.
Concerns over 'vile' commentary
The emails reveal some of the reasoning Ms Perkins put forward before her request.
In an email to Ms Quinn a week before the hearing, she raised her plans.
"You may recall after the last hearing we had some unpleasant social media posts and reactions," she wrote.
"I also want to test with you this idea: I'd like to add an explicit statement that the Defence witnesses appearing do not consent to our evidence being reproduced in edited format on social media platforms."
She said the main argument was that she had to maintain a "safe workplace" for Defence staff, and that online commentary could be "distressing".
"Social media posts using footage from previous hearings in edited and embellished formats had generated significant vile, personal commentary that was distressing for staff and invited online bullying," she said.
Ms Perkins also suggested the posts could raise security concerns, including assisting foreign espionage.
"As senior leaders in Defence — we actively discourage security clearance holders from a social media presence that identifies us and our roles — and these post (sic), designed to invite outraged responses, increase the personal risk from malign online actors, including cyber and foreign intelligence threats."
While Ms Perkins's request was immediately shut down, the Secretaries Board, made up of all federal government departmental secretaries, soon after took up the issue, suggesting new standards were needed to guide the use of evidence given to parliamentary hearings online.
This week Steven Kennedy, head of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, told estimates he did not support censoring footage, but did have concerns.
"Conduct that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets witnesses is inconsistent with the behaviour code for parliamentarians," he said.

articles.title: Drones hit another container ship off Bulgaria, defence minister says
articles.body:
Drones hit container ship off Bulgaria, crew safe and ashore
Reuters, Oct 28 - Sea drones struck a container ship off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast on Wednesday, the ship's owner and the government said, the latest in a string of attacks that have raised concerns about the growing scope of Russia's war in Ukraine.
It was not clear who carried out the attack on the Greek ship that was sailing under the Liberian flag in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone (EEZ), or what the vessel's 421 containers were carrying.
"A container ship was hit...with three naval drones, approximately 21 miles southeast of Shabla," Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters on the sidelines of a regional security meeting.
Bulgaria's transport ministry said in a statement that four naval and police boats had been dispatched to assist the vessel, which was travelling from the Israeli port of Haifa to Constanța in Romania, and that the 18 crew members had been evacuated.
The ship's owner, Contships Management, confirmed the attack and a company official said all the crew of 14 Filippinos and 4 Ukrainians, were safe and ashore.
A maritime security source with knowledge of the matter said the ship had been badly damaged and was listing.
INTERNATIONAL CONCERN
Drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria have likely killed some two dozen international seafarers in recent weeks, according to government statements on missing crew members. At least six merchant vessels have been attacked.
The strikes have been in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, an area that stretches beyond Bulgaria's waters but where the country holds sole rights to explore and manage resources.
The attacks have prompted international condemnation and concern about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine. Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has sought allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
Ukraine has blamed the attacks on Russia and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said the attacks appear to benefit Russia, but Moscow has denied involvement.
In a sign of the international concern, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler warned Russia and Ukraine on Wednesday against carrying out attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. He said Ankara reserved the right to take legal action against the strikes. REUTERS

articles.title: Generalissimo Suvorov nuclear-powered submarine test-launches Bulava ICBM

The Pacific Fleet’s strategic nuclear-powered missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov has test-fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from a submerged position in the Sea of Okhotsk toward a test range in the Arkhangelsk Region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The crew of the Project 955A Borei-A class strategic nuclear-powered missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov of the Pacific Fleet, in accordance with the combat training plan, test-fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile aimed at the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region," the ministry reported.

The K-553 Generalissimo Suvorov is a fourth-generation Borei-A class nuclear-powered submarine (designed by the St. Petersburg-based Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering). The submarine was laid down at the Sevmash Shipyard of the United Shipbuilding Corporation (USC) on December 26, 2014, and was commissioned into the Russian Navy in 2022. In October 2023, it completed its transfer from the Northern Fleet to the Pacific Fleet and arrived at its permanent base in Kamchatka. articles.title: Nearly 5,000 tons of nitric acid for Russia’s military-industrial complex. Why did Azot plant become strategic target?
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Azot chemical plant in Novomoskovsk, Tula Oblast, Russia, one of the country’s largest nitrogen-fertilizer producers, on 28 October. The attack set off a major fire at the facility overnight, Exilenova+ reports.
Russia’s munitions need explosives, and those explosives start from nitric acid, a basic industrial chemical. Azot is one of Russia’s biggest sources of it, a plant Ukraine has struck before and hit again overnight.
Nitric acid feeds Russia’s explosives
Military observer Oleksandr Kovalenko explains why the plant matters for Russia. Azot is one of Russia’s biggest producers of ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, and methanol, and in 2023 the company reported supplying more than 60 countries, he says.
For the war economy, he argues, one product stands out from the rest.
“The main reason for its strategic importance is nitric acid and its role in producing explosives for munitions,” Kovalenko says.
The acid goes into the chemical synthesis behind some of Russia’s most powerful explosives, and ammonia, further up the chain, is the base feedstock that the whole of nitrogen chemistry runs on.
Azot supplies the makers, not the munitions
Kovalenko is careful not to overstate what the plant does. Ammonium nitrate, the compound most associated with Azot, is first of all a fertilizer and only secondarily a raw material for industrial explosives.
“The fact of its production alone does not mean the plant makes military munitions,” he stresses.
The same holds for methanol and the plant’s other chemicals, whose military weight depends on which enterprise they are shipped to and what it builds there.
What gives Azot its place in the war machine, in his account, is that it sits one step back from the weapon, feeding the factories that make explosives rather than making them itself.
“Azot does not necessarily produce finished explosives itself. Its role is to supply raw materials to the next-link enterprises that produce energetic materials,” Kovalenko says.
The clearest trace of that role runs through a single customer: recorded deliveries of nearly 5,000 tons of nitric acid to the Sverdlov plant, sanctioned by Ukraine for actions threatening its sovereignty, between 2022 and 2024, with data from 2026 showing the reagent concentrated among a handful of Russian firms.

articles.title: Why Russia still classifies the Taliban as a terrorist organization after suspending its ban on the group
articles.body:
Why Russia still classifies the Taliban as a terrorist organization after suspending its ban on the group
What happened?
We found that in March 2026, the National Antiterrorism Committee published “Collected Information on the Activities of Organizations Designated as Terrorist in the Russian Federation.” Staff at the FSB Research Center prepared it “to inform the public about the crimes” committed by these groups.
The collection covers every terrorist organization added to the FSB’s list by the summer of 2024, including the Taliban movement.
The Taliban also remains on the list of extremists and terrorists maintained by Rosfinmonitoring, Russia’s financial intelligence agency. In the latest version, dated October 23, it appears alongside other movements designated as criminal in Russia:
144. TAGANROG REPUBLIC MOVEMENT* , ;
145. TALIBAN MOVEMENT* , ;
146. TVER LAND MOVEMENT* (TVER PEOPLE’S REPUBLIC; TVER REPUBLIC)
Wait, didn’t the Russian authorities stop treating the Taliban as a banned organization?
That’s right. On April 17, 2025, Russia’s Supreme Court granted a request from the Prosecutor General’s Office to suspend the ban on the Taliban’s activities.
This procedure was added to Russia’s Federal Law on Countering Terrorism only in January of that year. And it was devised specifically for the Taliban!
I see. So the FSB’s collection was just out of date by the time it was published!
No. The collection already mentions the Supreme Court’s ruling on the Taliban; it even specifies that the ruling took effect on May 20, 2025.
Yet the authors continue to call the Taliban movement an international terrorist organization. In the relevant sections, they describe its ideological tenets, propaganda tools, and criminal activities. Here’s how the security service’s experts describe the movement’s main goals and objectives:
The goals are to overthrow secular rule in Afghanistan and establish a state governed by Sharia law. This goal was largely achieved after the movement came to power in 2023. As the fundamentalist state consolidates its position in Afghanistan, efforts are being made to establish relations with foreign countries, including the Russian Federation.
This is confusing… Didn’t the FSB remove the Taliban from its terrorist list in line with the Supreme Court’s ruling?
No! The Taliban remains on the unified federal list of terrorist organizations maintained by the security service. Its entry now mentions both Supreme Court rulings: the one banning its activities in 2003 and the one suspending that ban 22 years later.

So technically, the Taliban is a terrorist organization that’s legal in Russia?

Because the Taliban is still on the list, Russian banks, for example, remain prohibited from doing business with it.

articles.title: Ground crews still excluded from nuclear test medal
articles.body:
There are no plans to extend the Nuclear Test Medal to personnel of 543 and 27 Squadrons who recovered, washed, decontaminated and maintained aircraft used for nuclear cloud sampling between 1966 and 1980, because they did not deploy from the United Kingdom, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Lord Bourne of Aberystwyth, the Conservative peer, asked what progress has been made on extending eligibility to those personnel, in light of representations from nuclear test veterans involved in intelligence gathering of foreign nations’ atmospheric tests.
Lord Coaker, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Nuclear Test Medal (NTM) eligibility has been broadened to include UK personnel who deployed in support of United States atmospheric nuclear tests, and UK personnel who were deployed from the UK in support of operations to monitor atmospheric nuclear tests conducted by France and China up to 1974 and 1980 respectively.
“Ministry of Defence officials will continue to keep the eligibility criteria under review to ensure that they are as comprehensive and inclusive as they can be given the current boundaries. There are no current plans to expand the criteria to include personnel who did not deploy from the UK in support of either UK or other nations atmospheric testing.
“Any formal proposal for the expansion of the NTM eligibility criteria would need to be endorsed by the Committee on the Grant of Honours, Decorations and Medals (HD Committee) and approved by His Majesty The King.”
Everything turns on deployment, because aircrew flown out to sample the clouds produced by French and Chinese tests qualify, while the people who met those aircraft on return and handled contaminated airframes do not, because they stayed at their home station.
Number 543 Squadron flew the Victor B2(SR) in the strategic reconnaissance role until 1974, and 27 Squadron took on the maritime radar reconnaissance and air sampling task with the Vulcan B2(MRR) thereafter. The Nuclear Test Medal was instituted in 2022 for veterans and civilian staff who took part in Britain’s atmospheric testing programme, after decades of campaigning.

articles.title: Saudi diplomatic push exposes divisions among Iran hardliners
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi diplomatic push exposes divisions among Iran hardliners
A diplomatic initiative involving Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan has exposed divisions among Iranian hardliners, with influential conservative figures disagreeing over whether the talks represent recognition of Tehran's regional influence or an attempt to force concessions over Yemen.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistani military chief Asim Munir visited Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior security officials.
The meeting, held amid renewed threats of US and Israeli military action against Iran, concluded with an agreement to continue discussions on regional security.
According to Reuters, citing a Pakistani official, Munir presented Tehran with a proposal to end hostilities that had received US President Donald Trump's approval.
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Qatar could reportedly act as guarantors of an agreement, although no diplomatic breakthrough was announced.
The initiative has generated contrasting reactions among Iranian political figures, according to Iranian media reports.
Iran's state-run Iran newspaper welcomed the visit, declaring that regional security was impossible without Tehran's participation.
Abdollah Ganji, a former editor of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-affiliated Javan newspaper, similarly portrayed the talks as recognition of Iran's regional importance.
Writing on X, Ganji suggested that Tehran was becoming central to an emerging regional security arrangement opposed to Israel.
However, Hossein Shariatmadari, the influential editor of the hardline Kayhan newspaper, questioned the intentions of the visiting governments.
Shariatmadari argued that Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were too closely aligned with Washington to act as credible mediators.
He also challenged the optimism expressed by Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who had presented the meeting as an opportunity to establish a new regional security framework.
Shariatmadari warned that the initiative could weaken Iran's position by relieving pressure on Washington while encouraging Tehran to distance itself from regional allies.
Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, meanwhile, advocated a broader regional security arrangement based on non-aggression, confidence-building and economic cooperation.
Much of the controversy concerns Yemen's Houthi movement, which has renewed attacks against Saudi Arabia amid continuing tensions over the country's unresolved conflict.
Saudi Arabia led a military intervention in Yemen beginning in 2015, launching a devastating bombing campaign and imposing restrictions on the country's ports and borders that contributed to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
Although large-scale fighting diminished following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, the conflict remains unresolved, with the Houthis controlling much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
The movement maintains close political and military ties with Iran but has its own domestic political objectives and decision-making structures.
Shariatmadari warned that the diplomatic initiative could result in pressure on Tehran to abandon the Houthis, something he insisted Iran would not do.
Hardline parliamentarian Mahmoud Nabavian defended the movement, arguing that attacks against Saudi Arabia would continue while restrictions on Yemen remained in place.
Former parliamentary national security committee chairman Heshmatollah Falahatpisheh, however, suggested that resolving the Yemen conflict was a central priority for Saudi Arabia and its regional partners.
The diplomatic initiative comes as Washington reportedly prepares for another military campaign against Iran following the 3 November US midterm elections.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that the Trump administration had warned Gulf governments to prepare for a possible short but intense military operation.
The prospect of renewed fighting has increased the urgency of regional diplomacy, even as Iranian political figures disagree over whether negotiations could protect Tehran's interests or undermine its regional alliances.

articles.title: Iran war leaves ‘forever cruise’ residents stranded
articles.body:
Iran war leaves ‘forever cruise’ residents stranded
A cruise ship selling “permanent homes at sea” has abruptly suspended operations, leaving around 200 residents stranded in Cambodia as its operator blamed soaring fuel costs caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The 200-meter (656-foot) Odyssey, with a capacity for 650 passengers, departed Belfast in October 2024 on a “continuous” round-the-world “forever cruise.” It offered cabins for rent, purchase, or lifetime ownership starting at $59,999 and reaching $440,000, plus monthly fees for meals, drinks, Wi-Fi and other services.
On Monday, Florida-based operator Villa Vie Residences (VVR) ordered passengers – some of whom reportedly sold their homes or spent their life savings on cabins – off the ship during a stop in Cambodia’s Sihanoukville. They had just seven hours to pack and leave, passenger Randy Cassingham reported on his cruise blog.
Cassingham shared a message from VVR CEO Kathy Villalba saying the company was “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations” and that the Odyssey would enter a “temporary layup,” with crew remaining aboard. Other residents, many of whom also run travel blogs, confirmed the account.
Sihanoukville deputy governor Long Dimanche confirmed Tuesday that the vessel, which arrived from Thailand on October 23 with 203 passengers and 156 crew, was due to sail to Vietnam later this week, but instead disembarked all passengers. Some have since flown out of Cambodia, while others remain in Sihanoukville, he said in a statement to local media.
Passengers voiced their anger online. Cassingham blamed a “cascade of problems,” including a flawed business model and management mistakes, and accused the company of doing “absolutely nothing to help.” Another resident, Holly Hennessy, told CNN that problems had been mounting for months.
“It’s been incredibly tough since the war,” she said, adding that residents had been asked to pay a fuel surcharge in May, while the ship had reduced air conditioning to save energy.
Fellow residents Lynette and Johan, who run the YouTube vlog Living Life on a Cruise, also described months of financial uncertainty. Johan said he felt “really drained” and worried about those who had invested their life savings in the cruise.
VVR denied abandoning passengers, saying it was arranging temporary accommodation and disembarkation assistance. Company founder Mikael Petterson told Bloomberg that VVR would cover local lodging and transportation costs, but not passengers’ travel out of Cambodia.
In a statement on Tuesday, the company blamed “extraordinary” fuel costs tied to the Iran war, saying monthly fuel expenses had surged from $1,800 to as much as $8,000 per cabin in parts of Asia since February. Slower sailing and longer port stays had failed to contain costs.
“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said, announcing plans to restructure and seek financing within 60 days.
The cost of war
The US-Israeli war on Iran has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities and shipping have further strained supplies, threatening the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Despite Gulf exports reportedly recovering to 80% of pre-war levels, Brent crude recently approached $117 per barrel.
US President Donald Trump has rejected Tehran’s latest settlement proposal and last week threatened another offensive. He also blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, rather than the Iran war, for the latest spike in fuel prices. Trump subsequently lifted restrictions on Russian diesel exports to the US in an effort to ease shortages, and Moscow said on Tuesday that three diesel tankers were already heading to America.
The move offers little immediate relief to the Odyssey, however, which refuels at ports along its route. Cambodia, for instance, relies entirely on imported petroleum products, with gasoline prices up 33.7% and diesel 46.7% since the Middle East escalation, according to its Ministry of Commerce. Marine gasoil, which powers the ship, has nearly doubled to $1,321 per metric ton in Singapore, the world’s largest refueling hub, according to ClearLynx.

articles.title: Why Moscow shouldn’t fear a Democratic victory in the US midterms
articles.body:
Why Moscow shouldn’t fear a Democratic victory in the US midterms
When Donald Trump returned triumphantly to the White House in January 2025, his supporters believed they could finally finish what he started during his first term and reverse the Democrats’ social engineering agenda, commonly known as ‘wokeism’, curb illegal immigration, accelerate technological development, and above all, ‘make America great again’.
Trump moved quickly on the first two priorities, as he revoked 78 of Joe Biden’s executive orders, tightened border controls and gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) greater resources and powers to conduct raids in sanctuary cities, where the local authorities limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
But Trump’s determination to achieve everything at once, from restructuring the federal government and securing favorable trade deals to pursuing ambitions involving Greenland and Venezuela, has kept American politics in a state of turmoil, while his confrontational approach has also unsettled allies and opponents abroad.
The decision to launch joint military operations with Israel against Iran has proven particularly divisive as it fractured Trump’s conservative coalition, with some supporters accusing him of betraying his promise to end America’s ‘endless wars’, while others fear the political consequences for Republicans in the approaching midterm elections.
The Iran war has also hurt American consumers. Over the past year, gasoline prices have risen by 38% and diesel by 71%, while food prices have increased by 2.5%.
The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz isn’t solely responsible, but Democrats and sympathetic media outlets have made it central to their criticism, while they also point to an increase of $3.8 trillion in the national debt since Trump’s return, allegations of corruption within his administration, and questions about the competence of senior officials, particularly Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Republicans, including those who oppose the Iran war, are trying to redirect voters towards the administration’s achievements – despite the turbulence, the US economy has grown by 3.2% since the end of 2024, and investment is booming in certain sectors, particularly technology, while illegal crossings at the southern border have reportedly fallen by 95%.
Vice President J.D. Vance, who is increasingly discussed as Trump’s successor, has urged Americans to give Republicans another chance, or at least another two years, to complete what they have begun – but for now, that opportunity appears uncertain. Yet contrary to expectations, losing control of Congress wouldn’t necessarily be a disaster for Trump.
Even with Republican majorities in both chambers, he has preferred to govern through executive orders, issuing more than 290 since January 2025, and this is hardly unprecedented. Bill Clinton issued 364 over his eight years in office, including during periods when Republicans controlled Congress.
For presidents, demonstrating immediate effectiveness and scoring political points often matters more than ensuring continuity.
Democratic threats to impeach Trump and members of his administration may sound formidable, but removing officials from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate, a much higher hurdle, and even if Democrats capture both chambers, converting their numerical advantage into meaningful political influence will not be straightforward.
They could, however, obstruct legislation, block nominations to senior administration positions and the federal judiciary, and subject the White House to sustained congressional scrutiny.
Their minimum objective would be to turn Trump into a lame-duck president for his remaining two years, but this strategy carries risks of its own – in the 2028 presidential campaign, Republicans can argue that the Democrats prevented them from completing their program.
For Moscow, however, the consequences of the midterms could be considerably more serious.
A Democratic-controlled Congress would almost certainly seek to complicate relations with Russia, and there remains a strong desire in Washington to obstruct Trump’s apparent ambition for a new Yalta involving Russia, China, and the US. Equally persistent is the determination among influential American political circles to inflict a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia.
This could explain the Trump administration’s intensified diplomatic activity over Ukraine, given whatever opportunities exist for reaching an agreement today could narrow considerably after the new Congress takes office in January 2027.
The urgency could also reflect an attempt to secure lasting advantages for the administration before the political landscape changes.
The argument that there’s little time left, and that Moscow must therefore accept an agreement now or face worse conditions later, shouldn’t be allowed to overshadow Russia’s own interests.
Russia has an objective interest in normalizing relations with the US, but a settlement of the Ukraine conflict must be based on mutually beneficial terms, rather than unilateral concessions extracted under the pressure of America’s electoral calendar.
Ultimately, as Americans prepare to vote in the midterms, Russia should be concerned less with Trump’s political fortunes than with protecting its own interests.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team

articles.title: Israel opposition holds narrow edge over Netanyahu, polls show
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel opposition holds narrow edge over Netanyahu in first projections
Israeli voters on Tuesday gave opposition parties a narrow edge over ICC fugitive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, initial projections showed, after a decades-high turnout in the country's first election since the outbreak of the genocidal war in October 2023.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister who has led the country for nearly two decades, had run on promises to fight enemies from Hamas to Iran and had spent election day raising fears of the strength of Israeli Arab voters.
Early projections broadcast by Israeli television networks showed that the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right former military chief, had a narrow edge over Netanyahu's bloc, which includes the far-right.
Early exit polls showed Arab parties made sweeping gains, likely giving them a critical role in the next parliament.
With no single party winning a majority, Israeli politicians will likely spend weeks in high-stakes negotiations to cobble together a coalition.
The country's main pollsters, Channels 11, 12 and 13, projected the opposition bloc to win 52 to 53 seats, and Netanyahu's bloc to win around 50, although his Likud would be the largest single party in parliament, with 24 or 25 seats.
In a dash to secure as many votes as possible, Netanyahu had charged that Israeli Arabs were out to "steal the election" and his Likud party unsuccessfully asked election authorities to keep polls open past 10:00 PM (2000 GMT).
His efforts led the opposition to charge that he was looking for pretexts to challenge the results.
"We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," a visibly tense Netanyahu told supporters as he tried to bring up turnout in a Likud stronghold.
Nationwide turnout as of 8 PM stood at nearly 75 percent, the highest in decades.
Arab minority in spotlight
Some 7.3 million people were eligible to vote, with tens of thousands of Israelis estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.
Throughout his career, he has repeatedly raised the spectre of Arab voters as a threat. He warned Tuesday of Arabs voting by the busload, writing on social media that Israel could wake up to a "government of the left wing and Muslim Brotherhood".
Netanyahu said that three senior officials of the United Arab List had been arrested with envelopes full of cash in the south.
The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, said that police had "caught individuals who tried to bribe voters", adding that the unidentified suspects were not at polling stations and were caught near their homes.
He said the matter was a localised case and under investigation.
United Arab List head Mansour Abbas, who could emerge as a kingmaker in a close election, accused Netanyahu of "lying and inciting" to mobilise his voters.
Exit polls from the main Israeli television channels showed the two Arab lists winning 17 or 18 seats in the 120-member parliament between them, up from 10 in the last election in 2022.
In Tel Aviv, left-wing party The Democrats, which is part of Eisenkot's opposition bloc, said police had arrested a man with a knife who had moved threateningly towards its leader Yair Golan.
"Incitement and violence will not intimidate us," Golan said in a statement, blaming the incident on the "poison machine" of Netanyahu.
Netanyahu last returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket and have aggressively championed settlements in the West Bank.
In the last days of the campaign, he posted an image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv and talked up his endorsement by US President Donald Trump, who is also fond of alleging election fraud.

articles.title: Harassed by Russian drones, Ukraine’s trains keep on rolling
articles.body:
By Yurii Kovalenko
ON A TRAIN BETWEEN DNIPRO AND ODESA, Ukraine, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Ukrainian beauty salon owner Antonina Viter is getting used to having her travel plans disrupted by the threat of Russian drone attacks, as she criss-crosses the country by rail to keep her business going.
“Every third trip, we end up evacuating once, twice or even three times,” she explained on board a train from the southeastern city of Dnipro to Odesa on the Black Sea.
“What can you do? How else do you get to your client?”
Kyiv has set new rules for rail passengers during air-raid alerts and, sure enough, soon after she spoke, the 36-year-old was standing outside under a pitch-black October sky, wrapped in a blanket, waiting for the “all-clear”.
In a country long reliant on its vast rail network, hours-long delays and repeat evacuations when air-raid sirens sound are another way in which Russia’s escalating missile and drone attacks are wrecking everyday life for civilians.
New Russian jet-powered drones that are hard to shoot down have attacked everything from shopping centres and filling stations to power plants and other critical infrastructure. And the railways are no exception.
UKRAINIAN RAILWAYS ATTACKED 1,700 TIMES THIS YEAR
The state operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, says Russia has attacked more than 1,700 rail facilities this year, including stations, locomotives and passenger wagons. Russia says its targets are objects used by Kyiv’s military.
A trip on the line from Dnipro to Odesa, some 400 km (250 miles) to the southwest, showed how Ukrainians are coping with those disruptions.
The outward journey featured eight evacuations of roughly 30 minutes each, the return journey - one more.
Direct attacks, like the drone strike that killed two train drivers on the Dnipro-Odesa line on August 13, are an ever-present threat.
But air-raid alerts can unexpectedly double the travel time on any route, and some stations in the east and south have been shut indefinitely as fighting creeps closer.
The prospect of being hit is one that 41-year-old IT worker Larysa Konstantynova - who was travelling from Dnipro to Odesa with her teenage son at the start of a holiday trip to Europe - prefers not to think about.
Like Viter, who travels at least six times a month to manage two salons in Kyiv and Dnipro, she says she is adapting.
“It’s how your mind works: you just try to be positive and survive with the way things are.”
Other attacks have included a strike on a Warsaw-bound train near the Polish border in September.
For some, overnight rail journeys - once opportunities to unwind with few distractions - are now spent in anxious anticipation.
During air raid alerts, passengers can be jolted awake and forced to scramble into fields or up and down embankments, sometimes with children or pets in tow. In the winter, temperatures are often below freezing.
RAILWAY JOURNEYS HAUNTED BY RISK OF RANDOM DEATH
Huddled outside her train with a colleague, Viter tracked a nearby drone on a cell-phone app after hearing its distinctive ‘whoosh’ overhead.
It was the third evacuation in two hours.
“Better to stand in a field for an hour than to risk never getting to see the next hour,” she said, knowing she had to teach a beauty workshop in Odesa the next day.
In fact, although delays of 5 to 12 hours are not unusual on the Dnipro-Odesa route, this train arrived just an hour and 20 minutes late.
Nevertheless, the risk of random death has soared as Russia has broadened its drone and ballistic-missile campaign, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of air defence missiles.
More than 50 railway workers have died on duty this year alone, according to Ukraine’s infrastructure minister, and dedicated staff have had to adapt their routines to maintain a network that appears to be close to their hearts.
At the beginning of each journey, conductors sweep through the carriages closing curtains to block out light that might alert a Russian drone.
“They can see us, so we have to hide a bit,” said train attendant Olha Boniuk, 49, with the air of a mother soothing her child.
After each evacuation, chief conductor Mykola Zakharchenko, 47, sits in his cramped booth diligently recording the interruption.
All the same, he smiles recalling conversations with passengers, and still enjoys watching dawn break through the carriage window: “Train work, as they say, is romance.”
Locomotive driver Mykola Kovalenko put it another way.
“If I quit,” he said, “who will drive the trains?”
(Additional reporting by Thomas Peter; Writing by Dan Peleschuk; Editing by Mike Collett-White and Kevin Liffey)

articles.title: Iranian foreign minister says Tehran in talks with mediators to implement 7-day plan with US
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Iran is in contact with mediators to review proposals to implement a seven-day plan with the US.
Araghchi wrote on US social media company X that Tehran continues to give diplomacy a chance despite tensions with Washington.
“While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed,” he said. “We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week.”
Iran’s seven-day plan, presented to Washington through Qatari mediators in September, proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming negotiations with the US within a week if Washington meets Tehran’s conditions.
The US would take agreed steps during the first five days, including ending hostilities, lifting its naval blockade on Iranian ports, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
On the sixth day, Iran would reopen the strait to normal commercial shipping, while negotiations between Tehran and Washington toward a comprehensive agreement would resume on the seventh day.
The proposed measures remain subject to agreement.
On Oct. 8, Araghchi said Tehran was reviewing Washington’s response to the proposal, with messages continuing to be exchanged through mediators.
The latest remarks come amid diplomatic efforts to maintain a fragile ceasefire between Iran and the US following months of military confrontation.
The two countries signed the Islamabad Memorandum on June 18 following negotiations mediated by Pakistan and Oman.
That agreement addressed several disputed issues, including maritime security in the strait, sanctions relief and the withdrawal of US naval restrictions.
Oman, Pakistan and Qatar have maintained diplomatic contacts aimed at resolving differences between Tehran and Washington.

articles.title: Iraq sacks four top officers over 'insult' to US flag
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq sacks four senior officers over 'insult' to US flag
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed four senior Interior Ministry officers for failing to prevent members of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) from "desecrating the US flag" during a military parade in Baghdad last month, according to an official document obtained by The New Arab.
The decision, believed to be the first of its kind in Iraq, also orders an investigation into the officers over alleged security negligence during celebrations marking the end of the US-led coalition's military presence in the country.
The dismissals were outlined in an official document issued by the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces and signed by General Abdul Amir al-Shammari.
Those removed include Brigadier General Dawood Salman Dawood Hassan, director of the second security sector, and Brigadier General Riyadh Jizan Rasan Salloum, an officer at Baghdad's Rusafa Police Command.
Colonel Dhulfiqar Awda Kitab, commander of the fifth Rusafa Emergency Police Regiment, and Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Saleh Muhaidi, an intelligence officer in the same unit, were also dismissed.
According to the document, the officers failed in their security duties by allowing PMF members to desecrate the US flag during a parade held on 30 September to mark "Sovereignty Day".
The document described the incident as an "irresponsible act that harms international relations and Iraq's standing abroad".
Al-Zaidi also instructed security forces in Baghdad's Rusafa district to strengthen their readiness and monitoring to prevent similar incidents during demonstrations and public gatherings.
US flag driven over during military parade
Videos circulated from the Sovereignty Day celebrations showed military vehicles belonging to Iraqi armed factions driving over a US flag laid on the ground in central Baghdad.
The incident drew criticism from US figures and prompted Iraqi authorities to take action.
On 4 October, Major General Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for Iraq's commander-in-chief, announced the arrest of individuals accused of desecrating the flag, stressing that authorities would not tolerate violations of public order or existing laws.
Although disciplinary action against senior officers over such an incident is unprecedented, similar acts have occurred during previous demonstrations and military parades.
Members of the PMF and other armed factions, many aligned with Iran, have repeatedly painted US flags on roads and walked over them during public events as an expression of hostility towards Washington.
The New Arab contacted three officials close to Prime Minister al-Zaidi, all of whom declined to comment formally on the dismissals.
However, one official said the decision was intended to prevent actions that could damage Iraq's relations with Washington or other countries.
"The decision is a government measure aimed at preventing insults to Washington, as well as preventing similar incidents that could target other countries," the official said.
The official added that dismissing the officers would strengthen security forces' ability to enforce discipline and prevent similar incidents.
The arrests have already drawn criticism from Iran-aligned armed groups.
Abdul Qader al-Karbalai, a military aide to the Nujaba Movement, previously described the arrests of PMF members accused of desecrating the US flag as a "dangerous precedent" that could not be ignored.
The group's secretary-general, Akram al-Kaabi, also posted a video on X showing himself walking over a US flag.
He accompanied the footage with the words, "Your crimes are beneath our feet", in an apparent protest against the Iraqi government's arrests.

articles.title: Syria and Jordan reopen border crossing after deadly air strikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria and Jordan reopen border crossing after deadly air strikes that killed seven civilians
Syria and Jordan resumed passenger and commercial traffic through the Nasib border crossing on Wednesday, following a temporary closure triggered by Jordanian air strikes in southern Syria that killed seven civilians, including children.
The reopening comes as Damascus and Amman agreed to establish a joint security committee to investigate the strikes, which targeted areas in the southern Syrian provinces of Daraa and Suwayda on Monday.
Mazen Alloush, director of international relations and cooperation at Syria's General Authority for Land and Sea Ports and Customs, confirmed that passenger movement and commercial activity had returned to normal on Wednesday morning, according to the Syrian state news agency SANA.
Syrian authorities had suspended traffic in both directions on Tuesday, citing concerns for the safety of travellers and border personnel following the strikes.
The Nasib crossing, which connects southern Syria with Jordan, is a major route for passenger travel and overland trade between the two countries.
The reopening signals an effort by both governments to contain tensions following the Jordanian military operation, which Damascus said had not been coordinated with Syrian authorities.
Joint investigation into deadly strikes
The decision to establish a joint security committee followed a telephone conversation between Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and his Jordanian counterpart Ayman Safadi.
According to a joint statement issued by the two foreign ministries on Wednesday, the committee will examine the circumstances surrounding Jordan's recent military operations inside Syrian territory and assess their consequences.
It will also develop mechanisms for field and intelligence coordination to address security threats and prevent further civilian casualties.
Both ministers emphasised their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations and resolving disagreements through dialogue, recognising the interconnected security interests of their countries.
Jordan's armed forces said Monday's strikes targeted sites linked to the Islamic State group (IS), which it accused of posing an imminent threat to Jordanian security.
The operation followed a deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the Jordanian city of Karak on Friday, which killed at least nine people and wounded 34 others.
IS claimed responsibility for the church attack, prompting Jordanian security forces to launch an investigation and arrest three suspects.
Jordan subsequently carried out air strikes against what its military described as IS hideouts in southern Syria.
However, the strikes also hit civilian areas, killing seven people, according to Syrian civil defence authorities. Five members of one family, including three children, were among those killed.
Syrian emergency and disaster management teams responded to attacks at four locations in Daraa and Suwayda.
Jordanian authorities initially maintained that the operation had been coordinated with Damascus, but Syrian officials disputed that account.
Safadi later expressed deep regret over the civilian deaths during his conversation with al-Shaibani, while reaffirming Jordan's commitment to Syria's sovereignty and stability.
He maintained that the strikes had been based on intelligence concerning suspected threats to Jordan.
The disagreement over whether the operation had been coordinated highlighted tensions between the neighbouring countries, despite their stated commitment to security cooperation.

articles.title: Israel deadlocked: Do the Arabs hold the key to defeating Netanyahu?
articles.body:
Netanyahu’s Israel deadlocked: were the elections ‘stolen by the Arabs’?
Israel’s parliamentary elections are over, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been wounded, but not defeated. His battle to form a government and stay in power is just beginning.
The final results of the Israeli election won’t be known until Thursday, when Israel’s Central Election Committee (CEC) finishes tallying so-called ‘double envelope’ ballots cast by soldiers, diplomats living abroad, prisoners, and other voters unable to make it to polling stations on election day.
However, with more than 85% of votes counted as of Wednesday evening, a picture of political deadlock is becoming clearer, and neither Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, nor the center-left to center-right bloc of his opponents, are on track to win a majority in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset. Either bloc must secure 61 out of 120 Knesset seats to form a government.
What are the results of the Israeli election?
Netanyahu’s Likud remains Israel’s largest political party, and is projected to win 26 seats, down from 32 in 2022.
Yashar, led by Netanyahu’s chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is in second place with 21 seats.
Both politicians lead large and potentially fractious blocs. Together with four far-right and religious parties – Otzma Yehudit, United Torah Judaism, Shas, and Religious Zionism, Netanyahu’s bloc controls 53 seats, ten short of a majority.
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc comprises Yashar, former Prime Ministers’ Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s B’Yachad party, Yair Golan’s Democrats, and Yisrael Beytenu, a right-wing party led by former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman. Together, this bloc controls 48 seats.
What about the Arabs?
Israel’s two main Arab parties, Yousef Jabareen’s Joint List and Mansour Abbas’ Ra’am, have almost doubled their representation in the Knesset. Driven by anger over Netanyahu’s war on Gaza and his appointment of overt Jewish supremacists to cabinet positions, voters in Arab-majority districts turned out in record numbers to award the Joint List and Ra’am 12 and seven seats respectively, up from a combined ten seats in 2022.
With a combined 19 seats, the Arab parties could play the role of kingmakers when coalition talks begin. However, they would likely find few allies within either Jewish-led bloc.
Will Netanyahu work with the Arabs?
Netanyahu has explicitly ruled out cooperation with either Arab party, both of which have condemned his war on Gaza. “It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he said after polls closed on Tuesday.
In the run up to the vote, the Israeli prime minister framed the election as a choice between “Me and [US President Donald] Trump, or Eisenkot and Abbas,” and accused his opponents of plotting to recognize a Palestinian state after entering a government with the Arabs.
In a statement on Wednesday, Netanyahu claimed that “the elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties,” and that Likud had uncovered evidence of vote-buying, “threats and violence against polling station members,” and repeat voting in Arab districts. The PM called on police and Israel’s Shin Bet intelligence agency to conduct a “thorough investigation” into his claims.
Eisenkot’s party warned on Tuesday that Netanyahu would attempt to delegitimize the election. “Netanyahu is panicking and has begun making up stories and claiming that the election is being stolen,” Yashar said in a statement. “This is no accident. He is already laying the groundwork to challenge the election results.”
What about the opposition?
Eisenkot, Liberman, and Bennett have all ruled out cooperation with the Arabs, with Eisenkot declaring on election night that he intends to form “a Zionist government.” Democrats leader Yair Golan, on the other hand, has called on the anti-Netanyahu bloc to reach out to Ra’am and the Joint List for the sake of ousting Netanyau. Partnership with the two Arab parties would give the bloc 65 seats – a clear majority.
“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid,” he wrote on social media on Wednesday morning. “We have a majority. We have responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel’s Arab citizens.”
Abbas has said that he is willing to enter government with the anti-Netanyahu bloc, while Jabareen has said that his Joint List lawmakers would “pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government” by refusing to oppose a minority government in exchange for some concessions on Palestine and funding for Arab communities.
Who will form a government in Israel?
Israeli President Isaac Herzog will ultimately decide which political leader stands the best chance of forming a stable government, and task them with forming a coalition. Herzog has called on all parties to enter negotiations “with an open mind.” As the political horse-trading begins, three potential outcomes are laid out below:
Netanyahu wins back the right
Netanyahu could secure a majority by striking a deal with Bennett and Liberman to peel B’Yachad away from the opposition bloc. Both are right-wingers, but both campaigned on ousting Netanyahu and forcing military conscription on Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Haredi communities. In this case,, Netanyahu would likely lose the backing of the two ultra-Orthodox parties in his coalition, United Torah Judaism and Shas.
Swapping these parties for B’Yachad would leave Netanyahu’s bloc even further away from a majority, meaning one side would have to compromise on their core campaign promises to make this arrangement work.
Eisenkot joins the Arabs
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc could quickly secure a majority and form a government, but only if he, Bennett, and Liberman decide that taking power is worth cooperating with, or securing the abstention of, the Arab parties.
Doing so would carry political consequences for everyone involved. At a time when public support for a two-state solution has collapsed and fewer Israelis than ever believe that they “cannot coexist peacefully” with their Palestinian neighbors, Eisenkot, Bennett, and Liberman would risk alienating their right-wing voters.
Likewise, Arab voters could see any partnership with the Israeli-right as a betrayal by the Joint List and Ra’am. Earlier this week, Joint List parliamentary leader Ahmad Tibi alluded to this fear, telling Türkiye’s Anadolu news agency that he does not want his party “to be responsible for incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque, a war in Gaza, the continuation of Jewish terrorism and settlement activity, or house demolitions.”
Entering a government with Eisenkot and the right-wing opposition would make the Joint List “collectively responsible” for these crimes, he explained.
Could a grand Zionist coalition emerge in Israel?
A unity government – in which Netanyahu and Eisenkot rotate the premiership with the support of Bennett and Liberman – may seem like an obvious solution for everyone involved. Likud, Yashar, B’Yachad, and Yisrael Beytenu are all aligned on security matters, and entering a grand coalition would allow Netanyahu to cast off his ultra-Orthodox and far-right partners, while Eisenkot could sever ties with the Democrats and Arabs.
Such an arrangement is not without precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz – a centrist ex-general – reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
However, the Netanyahu/Gantz coalition fell apart in less than a year, at a less polarized time in Israeli politics. This time around, all of Netanyahu’s opponents have focused their campaigns around deposing the prime minister, with Eisenkot accusing him of corruption, incompetence, and ignoring “dozens of warnings” prior to Hamas’ attack on Israel in 2023.
“I unequivocally pledge that I will not serve under Netanyahu in a rotation agreement. Period,” Eisenkot told Radio 103 last week. “If that were to happen, you would see me resign an hour later.” Eisenkot did not explicitly rule out working with Likud, if Netanyahu were to retire.
The alternative for Israel: deadlock and elections
Should none of these arrangements work, Israel could be thrust into another election cycle. Repeat elections and failed coalition talks were a leitmotif in Israeli politics until the October 7 attack and subsequent wars ushered in a period of relative stability: in the four years before 2022, Israel went through five elections.
Herzog has made it clear that he wants to avoid such an outcome. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said on Tuesday. However, unless Israel’s main parties can find some kind of compromise, another election may be inevitable.

articles.title: How US midterms could fracture bipartisan support for Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How US midterms could fracture bipartisan support for Israel
Washington, DC - Across the United States, many candidates who support Palestinian human rights are set to score wins in the country's midterm elections in November, reflecting a big shift in US public opinion on Israel amid the war on Gaza.
The House of Representatives will likely see an influx of progressive Democrats critical of Israel who won primaries against pro-Israel opponents.
And two Senate candidates - Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine - who have accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza are locked in close races that could see them clinch seats in the upper chamber of Congress.
Abdelhalim Abdelrahman, communication director for American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), says US voters are starting to make the connection between foreign and domestic policy.
Progressive candidates have "done an excellent job exploring the intersection between the genocide in Gaza and Israel's broader destabilising conduct in the Middle East with the affordability crisis in America", Abdelrahman told The New Arab.
Since the start of the war on Gaza, the US government has provided Israel with more than $21 billion in military aid at a time when Americans are struggling with skyrocketing inflation.
The war on Iran, which the US launched jointly with Israel, put further strain on the cost of living and pushed energy prices to record highs.
"Every single day Americans are waking up to videos and pictures of the Israeli government bombing civilian infrastructure, killing Palestinian children, spreading crimes across the Middle East," Abdelrahman said.
"Meanwhile, the average American cannot afford rent. The average American has seen their wages stagnate. This funding of the Israeli government has cost the American people tons of money."
Dwindling support for Israel
Public opinion in the US has been turning against Israel for years, polls show - a trend that was accelerated by the well-documented Israeli atrocities in Gaza over the past three years.
A Pew Research Center survey in July suggested that 63 percent of US adults have unfavourable views of the Israeli government.
"The American people have come to their own conclusions that it's a great moral hazard to this country to have a government that wilfully ignores the will of the American people," said Abdelrahman.
"Now more Americans sympathise with Palestinians. Now more Americans are calling for arms embargoes and sanctions on Israel."
During the primary season, pro-Palestine progressives won House races in districts from New York to California through Michigan and Colorado.
In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani's victory last year ushered in what appears to be a new era of progressive politics in the largest city in the US. Candidates backed by the mayor won three major House contests, ousting two staunchly pro-Israel incumbent Democrats.
Darializa Avila Chevalier - who participated in the encampment against the war on Gaza at Columbia University - defeated Adriano Espaillat.
Brad Lander, an Israel critic, won his primary against Congressman Daniel Goldman, who has been one of the most uncompromising pro-Israel Democrats.
Separately, Mamdani-backed state legislator Claire Valdez won the contest for an open US House seat.
All three are running in safe Democratic seats; they are all but certain to win in the general elections on 3 November.
In Pennsylvania, State Representative Chris Rabb, a vocal opponent of Israeli policies, also won the primary in a safe Democratic district. In Colorado, progressive candidate Melat Kiros beat incumbent Diana DeGette.
Several similar storylines played out across the country, setting the stage for the most pro-Palestine Congress in US history that will take office next year to chisel a sizable gap in the near-unanimous bipartisan support that Israel has enjoyed on Capitol Hill for decades.
AIPAC 'is on its heels'
These victories came despite tens of billions of dollars spent by pro-Israel groups - spearheaded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) - to defeat candidates who support Palestinian rights.
Usamah Andrabi, spokesperson for Justice Democrats, a leading left-wing group that backed many of the pro-Palestine candidates that won this year, said overcoming AIPAC's spending took years of organising and building awareness about the role of the pro-Israel lobby group.
In 2024, AIPAC spent record amounts of money in primaries and successfully toppled two Justice Democrats-backed incumbents - House members Cori Bush and Jamal Bowman.
Andrabi said it took multiple election cycles to turn AIPAC's endorsement into "a toxic kiss of death" for Democratic campaigns.
"We suffered some really terrible losses, but this lobby is on its heels," Andrabi said.
AIPAC has been trying to conceal its spending on behalf of candidates by funnelling money to subsidiaries with generic-sounding names, known as shell PACs - a tactic that Andrabi said shows the unpopularity of the pro-Israel group.
Andrabi told The New Arab that the rise of numerous progressive candidates across the country was a product of the anger of Democratic voters after President Donald Trump won in 2024.
"Democratic voters woke up in 2025 realising that the Democratic establishment was wholly unfit and unprepared to defend our communities against Republican extremism and fascism," he said.
Andrabi added that while Gaza may not have been a top priority for all voters, support for Israel featured heavily in many contests because candidates were able to draw a line between foreign wars and domestic issues.
"It's not that every single district and every single voter in this country, the most important issue on their mind is, 'How do we end the genocide in Gaza?' But our candidates were connecting the dots, like Darializa did, who led with the slogan of 'babies, not bombs,'" Andrabi said.
"Why are we spending billions of dollars bombing hospitals and schools and killing babies abroad when the same government is defunding our schools and our jobs and our hospitals at home, and we can't afford to put a roof over our head or food on the table?"
The progressive newcomers will increase the number of legislators in Washington who are willing to push for a break from unconditional support for Israel in US policy. However, the contingency remains a minority within the Democratic caucus.
But Andrabi said the progressive bloc will have a "monumental impact" in the next Congress by highlighting where the Democratic base stands.
As Democratic voters sour on Israel, some lawmakers who have avoided criticising the US ally throughout their years-long careers have backed measures to hold the Israeli government accountable for its abuses over the past year.
Last month, 46 out of 47 Democrats in the Senate voted for a bill to compel the State Department to investigate increasing Israeli violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killing of US citizens.
Abdelrahman, of AMP, said he hopes the next Congress upholds Washington's own laws prohibiting aid to human rights abusers.
"Previous administrations and previous iterations of the American Congress have sidestepped justice and accountability for the sake of protecting Israel, and what we hope to see is that the status quo is broken," he said.
Ali Harb is a journalist based in Washington, DC. His work focuses on US foreign policy, elections, and Arab American communities
Follow him on X: @Harbpeace

articles.title: Blind Ukrainian man faced conscription – court papers
articles.body:
Blind Ukrainian man faced conscription – court papers
A blind Ukrainian man was allegedly held for days at a conscription center despite being clearly unfit for military service, according to court papers.
The case, reported by Ukrainian media on Wednesday, stems from a complaint filed by the unidentified man with a district court in Odessa seeking an official investigation. A judge ruled in his favor last week, ordering the authorities to look into the allegations, a decision that was made public shortly afterward.
According to the complaint, the man has been visually impaired since childhood and was exempted from military service as early as 1994, with his status reaffirmed in 2020 and 2023. Despite this, he says draft officials refused to recognize his condition and held him for almost five days.
He was allegedly seized on a street in Odessa in March, held incommunicado without being formally booked, and released only after intervention by his lawyer.
The regional branch of the State Bureau of Investigation, which had earlier refused to register his complaint, was ordered by the court to reverse that decision. The man had separately secured a court ruling ordering his removal from a list of people wanted for draft evasion.
Kiev relies on compulsory mobilization of fighting-age men to sustain its war effort against Russia, but the campaign has been marred by widespread corruption among draft officials and public perceptions that the system is deeply unfair. The government has responded to draft evasion with heavy-handed enforcement that has repeatedly involved the illegal use of force by military officials.
Illegal detention at recruitment centers has become a recurring problem, according to the office of Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmitry Lubinets.
In one high-profile case reported by Lubinets in June, 21 men were found to have been illegally held in poor conditions at a conscription center in Uzhgorod, some for more than 50 days.
In another case, the three-day detention of 39-year-old Aleksey Ivanko at a Kharkov recruitment center in May 2025 ended with him jumping from a third-floor window to his death. Lubinets said in his annual report that his office found no evidence Ivanko had been physically abused by draft officials, but concluded there had been no legal grounds to restrict his freedom and that the prolonged confinement had contributed to the circumstances of his death.

articles.title: Kiev receives 12 Patriot missiles per month from US, but fires more than 30, Zelensky says
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky says that Ukraine receives an average of 12 Patriot missiles per month from the United States, but fired 35 in October alone.
"There are documents on US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s desk that he has signed. Maybe he thinks he’s signed everything, but that’s not the case. He signed off on a US package of 12 missiles. Fine. But this month I’ve fired 35. And the question concerns the 23 missiles that I obtained through other channels," the UNIAN news agency quotes Zelensky as saying.
He did not identify which countries provided the 23 missiles.
Earlier, Kiev had repeatedly reported a shortage of interceptor missiles for its air defense system. On October 15, CNN, citing sources, reported that Ukraine’s stockpile of Patriot missiles had been completely depleted. Later, Vladimir Zelensky criticized delays in the delivery of American interceptor missiles purchased with funding from European Union countries under the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism. He accused Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth of holding up the delivery of missiles for the Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems by a month.

articles.title: Exclusive: Putin 'wanted very much' for Melania Trump to broker Oleshky ceasefire, first lady adviser says
articles.body:
Exclusive: Putin 'wanted very much' for Melania Trump to broker Oleshky ceasefire, first lady adviser says
Russian President Vladimir Putin "wanted very much" for U.S. First Lady Melania Trump to mediate the ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, Marc Beckman, her exclusive senior adviser, told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 28.
"President Putin wanted very much for her to participate and also wrote a formal letter explaining that she… would be recognized as the exclusive intermediary from Russia," Beckman said.
Beckman said the Russian military proposed moving the ceasefire forward by two days and expanding its geographic scope beyond Oleshky into other parts of Kherson Oblast to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and evacuation preparations. Ukraine agreed to the proposal.
He described the changes as a sign of good faith, saying both sides had cooperated in implementing the agreement so far. "Their actions will speak for themselves ultimately, but what we've seen so far is tremendous cooperation from both sides," he said, adding that both parties had upheld the ceasefire's terms to date.
But concerns have been raised about Russia's true motives in agreeing to the ceasefire, as well as its agreement to allowing Trump to mediate it.
"They know exactly what they are doing," John Foreman, CBE, a former UK defense attache in both Kyiv and Moscow, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Allowing Melania to take the credit bolsters their credentials to the MAGA base as peacemakers before the midterms," he added.
Oleshky, which had a pre-war population of around 24,000, has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
The ceasefire — announced by the White House on Oct. 23 as being mediated by Trump and soon confirmed by Ukraine and Russia — is in its second day as of Oct. 28, and is expected to last into early November, as aid is brought in, key roads are demined, and residents are evacuated.
read also
The Trump-mediated ceasefire comes after international attention to the plight of civilians trapped under Russian occupation.
Earlier this month Pope Leo called Putin and requested a ceasefire. Putin responded by blaming Ukraine for the situation.
Beckman said that as well as the Vatican, "both sides were unable to bring in the United Nations, and… the Red Cross" as mediators.
Ukraine has also warned that Russia could exploit the evacuation for propaganda purposes.
Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos.
"Key Russian media figures are already starting to spread the narrative that Russia is 'rescuing' the residents that it has been terrorizing," Peter Pomerantsev, executive editor of The Reckoning Project, wrote in an op-ed for the Kyiv Independent.
On the Ukrainian side, Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary commissioner for human rights, is expected to arrive in Oleshky within the next 36 hours and lead the effort on the ground, Beckman said.
Beckman said Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in person in Belarus to sign the ceasefire agreement.
Representatives from both Russia and Ukraine had independently asked him to keep certain details of the ceasefire agreement confidential, citing the sensitivity of the information. He declined to disclose those details, saying both sides had emphasized the need for discretion.

articles.title: Lviv Oblast administration head: Controversial resolution on Year of UPA not yet in force
articles.body:
Lviv Oblast administration head: Controversial resolution on Year of UPA not yet in force
Maksym Kozytskyi, Head of Lviv Oblast Military Administration, has written a letter to Wojciech Saługa, Marshal of the Silesian Voivodeship in Poland, drawing attention to the fact that the resolution declaring 2027 the Year of the UPA The UPA, or Ukrainian Insurgent Army, was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union in the region has not yet been signed and has not come into force.
Source: Polish Press Agency (PAP) citing the Chancellery of the Marshal of the Silesian Voivodeship, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Kozytskyi expressed his conviction that the decisions of local authorities should take into account the interests of Ukraine's foreign policy and good neighbourly relations with Poland.
"I would like to inform you that the resolution of the Lviv Oblast Council referred to in your letter has not yet been signed and has not come into force. I am convinced that the decisions of the authorities at all levels must take into account the interests of Ukraine's foreign policy and good neighbourly relations with the Republic of Poland," Kozytskyi wrote.
He also stressed that he is aware of the sensitivity around issues of remembrance for the Ukrainian and Polish peoples, as well as the importance of discussing them in an atmosphere of mutual respect, openness and readiness for understanding.
Kozytskyi also recalled the importance of the long-standing partnership with the Silesian Voivodeship and thanked it for the support provided to Ukraine and the assistance to residents of Lviv Oblast and Ukrainian citizens who found refuge in the Silesian Voivodeship and across Poland during the Russian aggression.
Background:
- On 20 October, Lviv Oblast Council voted to designate 2027 as the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, one of its commanders-in-chief Roman Shukhevych and Oleh Olzhych. The decision immediately drew criticism from Polish officials.
- Later, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk stated that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had made it clear he would not support further steps by the Lviv Oblast Council regarding the declaration of 2027 as the year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych.
- Meanwhile, Kraków's new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, has proposed suspending the city's partnership with Lviv in response to the Lviv Oblast Council's decision.
