articles.title: Lib Dems want six more frigates and new shipyards
articles.body:
Three more Type 31 frigates, three more Type 26 frigates and four new shipyards should be funded through defence bonds and delivered by the mid-2030s to counter the threat from Russia, according to the Liberal Democrats.
The party published the proposal alongside polling it commissioned, which found that sixty per cent of people think the government is not doing enough to protect Britain’s critical infrastructure, including undersea cables, from Russian attack.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson, said: “After years of the Conservative Party underinvesting in our military, we are now dangerously exposed and woefully unprepared. Russia is actively, and brazenly, testing the limits of our naval defence capabilities – but Labour has dragged its feet on investing properly in our defence.
“We cannot afford to sit on our hands while Putin’s aggression intensifies and our national security weakens. We need a plan which gives confidence to British industry and allows our manufacturers to get on with delivering for Britain’s long-term security.
“By investing now in six new warships and by expanding our ship-building capacity with four new British shipyards, we can regenerate our fleet, protect our vital underwater infrastructure, and ensure Britain has the defence capabilities we need to stand up to the Kremlin.”
The party said it would raise the Digital Services Tax from two per cent to ten per cent and use part of the proceeds to cover crewing and maintenance. It acknowledged that no estimates exist for the in-service costs of either the Type 31 or the Type 26, despite parliamentary questions pressing the government for them, and extrapolated an assumed £20 million a year for each ship from 2018 estimates for the Type 23 and Type 45, giving £120 million a year for six ships in 2034/35 terms.
On the threat, the party cited the Royal Navy spending twenty five per cent more time monitoring Russian vessels around British waters, a Russian warship firing warning shots at a yacht off the Isle of Wight in June, and a Russian attack submarine and two intelligence submarines loitering over critical undersea cables in the North Atlantic for a month in May. It also raised Russian escorts for sanctions-busting tankers passing through the Channel.
The polling was carried out by Savanta, which interviewed 2,234 United Kingdom adults online between 29 May and 1 June this year, weighted to be representative by age, sex, region and social grade. Respondents were told that the head of the United Kingdom’s intelligence and security agency has warned of relentless attacks from Russia on critical infrastructure, and asked whether the government is doing enough to protect it. Five per cent said definitely, twenty two per cent probably, thirty nine per cent probably not and twenty one per cent definitely not, with fourteen per cent unsure. Concern ran highest among older respondents, at sixty seven per cent of those aged fifty five and over against fifty one per cent of those aged eighteen to thirty four.
The Defence Committee reported last week that dramatic progress is needed in building up British forces and ships for the High North, and the Liberal Democrats argued that the Strategic Defence Review set a compelling vision for the hybrid Navy while the Defence Investment Plan failed to provide the resources to rebuild the fleet.

articles.title: Russian Billionaire Takes Tiny Norwegian News Outlet to Court in London
articles.body:
Russian tycoon Vitaly Orlov is suing The Barents Observer, a small Norwegian news outlet, over its reporting on sanctions against his fishing company.
The Barents Observer is a six-person non-profit newsroom in Kirkenes, a town of about 7,000 people in Norway’s far north. But the lawsuit isn’t taking place there — or even in Norway. Instead, Orlov has lodged a defamation suit in the High Court of London.
“We don’t even have money for plane tickets to go to the court,” said Editor in Chief Thomas Nilsen.
“It’s just not possible for us to defend ourselves against all of the claims,” he told OCCRP’s Norwegian media partner, NRK, adding that if Orlov is awarded some legal costs, The Barents Observer “will go bankrupt.”
Orlov’s fishing company, Norebo JSC, said in a statement provided to OCCRP that the choice of London as a venue for the lawsuit was related to the fact that The Barents Observer publishes in English.
“The Barents Observer is a Norwegian publication that publishes in English and now complains at being sued in England. This is the very country The Barents Observer has courted,” the company said.
The legal claim by Orlov’s lawyers, from the London firm Devonshires, states that The Barents Observer website received 190,000 hits from the U.K. in 2025, according to a web analytics firm.
But U.K. readers make up only 5 percent of The Barents Observer readers, according to a letter the publication sent to the court.
“It is difficult to understand the logic behind Vitaly Orlov bringing his grievances before a court in England,” The Barents Observer stated in its letter.
The Barents Observer noted that it is based in Norway, and that Norebo is already engaged in a lawsuit against the Norwegian government in response to its ban on company vessels using its territorial waters and ports.
Orlov is claiming damages as a result of “serious harm” to his reputation caused by five news stories published by The Barents Observer between May 2025 and January this year. The news reports covered the E.U. sanctioning of Norebo, but also included information about Orlov himself.
The E.U. sanctions notice does not mention Orlov, and he has not been sanctioned. The sanctions notice alleges that Norebo vessels showed “movement patterns [that] align with malign objectives.”
“The movement patterns have been linked, including by Member States and the authorities of third states, to the Russian state-sponsored surveillance campaign that employs inter alia, civilian fishing trawlers, to conduct espionage missions directed against civilian and military infrastructure in the North and Baltic Sea,” the sanctions notice states.
In the claim brought to the High Court of London on behalf of Orlov, Devonshires lawyers note that “Norebo disputes the designation and has brought annulment proceedings before the General Court of the European Union.”

articles.title: EU burying its own economy – Putin (VIDEO)
articles.body:
EU burying its own economy – Putin (VIDEO)
The EU is burying its own economy by rejecting Russian energy supplies, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said.
European nations have faced soaring energy costs since imposing sweeping sanctions on Russia and its hydrocarbon exports following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Brussels has pledged to eliminate Russian gas imports entirely by 2027, despite opposition from several member states.
Speaking at the eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow on Tuesday, Putin warned that efforts to push Russia out of the global gas market were hurting European industries and households.
“[Europe] is dealing a blow to its own industry and social sector by abandoning Russian energy supplies and tearing up long-term contracts,” he said.
There is a saying in Russia: ‘Don’t dig a pit for someone else, or you might end up there yourself.’ In my view, that is precisely what has happened today in the countries of the European Union.
Putin also accused European nations of hypocrisy over their approach to fossil fuels, arguing that they had built their own prosperity on resources they now discourage developing countries from using.
“The economy of modern Europe was built precisely on coal and hydrocarbons,” he said.
Yet those same countries reopened coal-fired power plants “when they found it more difficult to address their own energy challenges,” Putin added.
European gas prices surged to their highest level since December 2022 on Monday, briefly exceeding €97 ($108) per megawatt-hour as supply disruptions linked to the Iran war and forecasts of colder weather rattled markets, according to Trading Economics.
Germany, Europe’s largest industrial economy, has been particularly hard hit by the loss of Russian gas. The country suffered two consecutive years of economic contraction in 2023 and 2024, while its energy-intensive industries, particularly chemicals and metals, have struggled with higher production costs.
German industry is shedding around 15,000 jobs a month, Tanja Goenner, head of the Federation of German Industries, warned in July, citing structural weaknesses, US tariffs and mounting competition from China.
Economic pressures have also fueled public anger across Europe. Rising living costs, stagnant wages and government policies have triggered protests in France, Belgium, Italy and other countries this month, with demonstrators demanding relief for struggling households.
